Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: In project scheduling terms, what does the technique of time boxing primarily help a project team to control?
o: The reporting format used for progress updates
The quality standards applied to the outputs
The number of stakeholders that are consulted
The elapsed time devoted to a piece of work
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Time boxing controls the elapsed time given to a piece of work by fixing the period and flexing scope within it.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Beyond simply naming suppliers, what does a well-considered procurement strategy aim to achieve for a project?
o: The elimination of every risk associated with using suppliers
The detailed daily task schedule for the internal project team
A guarantee that no external suppliers will be needed at all
Value for money and a sound, consistent approach to sourcing external work
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A procurement strategy aims to secure value for money through a sound, consistent approach to sourcing external work.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: How does working in fixed time boxes help a team guard against work expanding without limit?
o: The immovable deadline forces the work to be contained within the period
It fixes the scope so that nothing can ever be added
It allows the deadline to move whenever more work appears
It removes the need to prioritise any of the work
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: The fixed, immovable deadline contains the work within the period, guarding against uncontrolled expansion or scope creep.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A team is given two weeks to complete as much as possible from a defined set of features. Which technique is being used?
o: Critical path calculation
Time boxing
Milestone tracking
Float analysis
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: This is time boxing: the duration is fixed at two weeks while the scope achieved within it is allowed to vary.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What is the main purpose of applying resource optimisation techniques when planning a project schedule?
o: To set the thresholds at which changes must be formally approved
To define how the project team will communicate with its stakeholders
To forecast how inflation will affect the overall project budget
To use resources efficiently and avoid periods of over- or under-allocation
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource optimisation adjusts the schedule so that resource demand is balanced, avoiding overloads and idle periods.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager sequences activities and sets their timings before delivery begins. Which project management activity is being carried out?
o: Scheduling
Risk analysis
Quality control
Benefits management
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Determining the timing and sequence of activities, and the resources needed, is the purpose of scheduling.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager finds that a key resource is assigned to several tasks on the same day. Which technique should resolve this?
o: Milestone tracking
Scope definition
Earned value analysis
Resource levelling
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource levelling reschedules activities to resolve over-allocation, accepting that the end date may be affected.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What is a key benefit of agreeing a procurement strategy at the start of a project?
o: It removes the need to monitor suppliers once contracts are signed
It gives a structured, consistent approach to acquiring goods and services
It replaces the need to produce a business case for the project
It guarantees that internal resources are always selected in preference
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: An early procurement strategy provides a consistent, transparent framework for obtaining resources and services externally.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: How does a time-boxed activity differ from a conventionally scheduled activity in terms of what is fixed and what flexes?
o: Both its scope and its end date are entirely fixed at the outset
Its scope is fixed and its end date flexes to suit the remaining work
Its end date is fixed and its scope flexes, rather than time flexing to fit scope
Neither its scope nor its end date is ever actually defined
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: In time boxing the end date is fixed and scope flexes; conventional scheduling instead lets the timeline extend to fit the scope.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What is a key difference between resource levelling and resource smoothing?
o: Levelling adjusts quality, whereas smoothing adjusts cost
Levelling may change the critical path, whereas smoothing does not
Levelling applies only to Agile, whereas smoothing applies to linear
Smoothing adds team members, whereas levelling removes them
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Levelling can extend the schedule and alter the critical path, whereas smoothing works within float and preserves the end date.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Resource levelling and resource smoothing are the two main examples of which scheduling activity?
o: Resource optimisation
Critical path analysis
Change control
Configuration management
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource levelling and smoothing are the two principal resource optimisation techniques used within scheduling.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Why does an approach based on time boxing depend heavily on clear prioritisation of the work to be done?
o: Because the scope is fixed and therefore cannot ever be reduced
Because prioritisation removes the need to set any deadline at all
Because the period is simply extended to accommodate all of the work
Because only the highest-priority items can be guaranteed within the fixed period
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: With time fixed, prioritisation ensures the most valuable items are completed first, as not all scope can be guaranteed in the period.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which of the following would you typically expect to find within a procurement strategy?
o: Preferred contract types and the criteria for evaluating suppliers
The models used to support development of the project team
The amount of float available on each of the project's tasks
The categories used to prioritise the identified project risks
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A procurement strategy defines how suppliers will be chosen, including preferred contract types and evaluation criteria.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What is a key advantage of using time boxing in project delivery?
o: It ensures delivery is prioritised within a fixed timeframe
It guarantees that the full scope will always be delivered
It removes the need for configuration management activities
It extends deadlines to allow further stakeholder approval
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Fixing the time forces prioritisation and focus, improving predictability of delivery within the agreed period.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which description best reflects the level and focus of a project's procurement strategy?
o: A high-level plan for how a project will source what it needs externally
A detailed cost estimate for every item the project will purchase
A log of goods received and inspected against their specifications
A list of the internal skills the project team already possesses
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A procurement strategy is the high-level approach to sourcing externally, not a detailed estimate, receipt log or skills list.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A sprint ends before all of its assigned tasks are finished. In a time-boxed approach, what happens next?
o: The team is formally penalised for missing the target
The sprint is extended until every task is complete
The incomplete tasks are permanently abandoned
The remaining work is re-prioritised for a future sprint
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Time boxing fixes the time, so unfinished work is reassessed and, if still needed, carried forward and re-prioritised.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: In critical path analysis, what is true of the activities that lie on the critical path?
o: They each hold generous amounts of spare float
They may be delayed freely without consequence
They have zero float and cannot be delayed
They are optional and can be removed if needed
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Critical path activities have zero float; delaying any of them extends the overall project duration.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A client insists a release must launch on a fixed date, accepting that some lower-priority features may not be ready. Which technique fits?
o: Resource levelling
Critical path analysis
Time boxing
Analogous estimating
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Holding the launch date fixed while allowing lower-priority features to drop is time boxing.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: On a supplier contract with staged deliverables, milestones are frequently used to trigger which of the following events?
o: The identification of new project-level risks
Automatic changes to the project's agreed scope
Staged payments once agreed points are reached
The levelling of over-allocated project resources
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Milestones mark agreed points of achievement and are often used contractually to trigger staged payments on their completion.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What is meant by the term 'time boxing' in project management?
o: Fixing the time allocated to an activity and allowing scope to vary within it
Assigning extra resources to the activities with the longest durations
Holding a reserve of unused time to draw on during emergencies
Extending the project deadline to accommodate additional scope changes
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Time boxing fixes the duration of an activity or phase, with the scope delivered varying to fit within the allotted time.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Because a time box cannot be extended, what is the likely fate of the lowest-priority items if time runs short?
o: They automatically become the highest-priority items
They are delivered by lowering the required quality
They are dropped or deferred to a later time box
The time box is lengthened until they are all finished
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: With the deadline fixed, the lowest-priority items are dropped or deferred to a later time box rather than the period being extended.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Why might resource smoothing alone fail to resolve a serious over-allocation of resources?
o: Because it always pushes the completion date far into the future
Because it deletes tasks from the schedule to reduce demand
Because it ignores the project's float when moving activities
Because it only moves tasks within float and cannot exceed the end date
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Smoothing is constrained by the end date and float; where demand still exceeds capacity, levelling may be needed instead.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A planner links dependent activities to find the longest path through the network. What are they determining?
o: The minimum time in which the project can be completed
The total cost of all the project's resources
The number of stakeholders needing consultation
The quality standards for each deliverable
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: The critical path is the longest sequence of dependent activities, which determines the shortest possible project duration.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager prepares a one-page summary schedule for executives showing only the key dates. What are these key dates called?
o: Baselines
Dependencies
Work packages
Milestones
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Key dates shown on a summary schedule are milestones, giving senior stakeholders a high-level view of progress.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Selecting the type of contract and reimbursement approach for external work forms part of which project document?
o: The responsibility assignment matrix
The procurement strategy
The work breakdown structure
The issue log
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Contract and reimbursement types are decisions set out within the procurement strategy.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Why is knowing the critical path valuable when managing a project's timescale?
o: Because activities on it can slip without any effect
Because delay to any of its activities delays the whole project
Because it lists every risk recorded in the register
Because it removes the need to monitor other activities
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Activities on the critical path have no float, so any delay to them directly delays the project completion date.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager prepares a Gantt chart to show when specific tasks will be carried out. Which aspect of scheduling does this support?
o: Financial and cost reporting
Task sequencing and time planning
Assignment of team roles
Identification of project risks
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A Gantt chart is a scheduling tool that displays the order of tasks and when each is planned to take place.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: How do milestones assist a project manager specifically when reporting the status of a project to its stakeholders?
o: They provide clear reference points showing whether delivery is on track
They record the full technical specification of each project deliverable
They set out the communication methods to be used for each group
They list the individual costs of every one of the project's activities
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Milestones give clear, recognisable reference points against which achievement can be reported, showing stakeholders whether delivery is on track.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project team documents its overall approach to using external suppliers before any contracts are signed. What have they produced?
o: A configuration management plan
A procurement strategy
A benefits realisation plan
A stakeholder engagement matrix
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Documenting the overall approach to sourcing from external suppliers is the procurement strategy.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Critical path analysis shows a task that can be delayed without affecting the overall project timeline. What is this an example of?
o: Float
Budget slippage
Configuration drift
Scope creep
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Float, or slack, is the amount of time an activity can be delayed without affecting the project's completion date.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: In the context of project management, how is a 'procurement strategy' best defined?
o: A schedule showing when each supplier's work will take place
A record of the threats and opportunities affecting suppliers
A matrix assigning internal team members to each work package
The overall approach to obtaining goods and services from suppliers
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A procurement strategy sets out the overall approach a project will take to acquiring the goods and services it needs.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which of the following best describes the purpose of a project milestone?
o: To track the unresolved risks within the project
To assign specific tasks to individual project team members
To measure product quality against the baseline specification
To mark a significant point or achievement within the schedule
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Milestones are zero-duration events that flag key points such as phase completions or major approvals within the schedule.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: In which type of project life cycle is time boxing most commonly applied?
o: Linear
Iterative or Agile
Extended
Sequential
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Time boxing is a core practice of iterative and Agile approaches, where time is fixed and the scope delivered is flexible.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which of the following is NOT a purpose of critical path analysis?
o: Identifying the longest sequence of dependent activities
Revealing which activities have float available
Justifying the project's investment to the sponsor
Determining the shortest possible project duration
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Critical path analysis addresses scheduling, not investment justification, which is the role of the business case.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: How does critical path analysis help a project manager decide where to concentrate limited resources?
o: By ranking stakeholders according to their influence
By showing which activities have the greatest cost
By highlighting the activities that cannot afford to slip
By listing the risks with the highest impact scores
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: By highlighting zero-float activities, critical path analysis shows where resources must be protected to avoid delaying the project.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A schedule shows that two activities must finish before testing can begin. What does this illustrate?
o: A task dependency
A work breakdown structure
A project benefits map
A scope verification check
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A dependency exists where one activity cannot start until another is complete; scheduling identifies these relationships.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A deadline is fixed and cannot move, but resource peaks must be reduced. Which optimisation technique should the project manager apply?
o: Crashing, adding cost to shorten the critical path
Resource levelling, accepting a later completion date
Fast tracking, overlapping activities to save time
Resource smoothing, using float without changing the end date
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: When the end date must hold, smoothing evens out resource peaks using available float without delaying completion.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project needs a specialised system that only two suppliers can provide. What should guide the selection of a supplier?
o: The stakeholder communication plan
The lessons learned log
The project issue log
The procurement strategy
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: The procurement strategy sets out the supplier selection criteria and contract preferences that inform such a decision.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which of the following is a key outcome of performing critical path analysis?
o: A detailed quality assurance plan for deliverables
An understanding of which tasks have scheduling flexibility
A stakeholder influence and interest chart
A revised procurement contract for the main suppliers
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Critical path analysis distinguishes tasks with float from those without, showing where the schedule has flexibility.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: How does a milestone differ from an ordinary task within a project schedule?
o: Milestones consume project resources, whereas ordinary tasks do not
Milestones are used only within quality control activities on a project
Milestones must be repeated within every phase of the project life cycle
Milestones have zero duration and mark significant events, unlike tasks
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A milestone is a zero-duration marker of a significant event or decision point, whereas a task represents work that consumes time and resource.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: When resource smoothing is applied and the project end date must not change, what typically happens to the schedule?
o: Non-critical tasks are rescheduled within their float to even out resource demand
All tasks are moved onto the critical path so delivery is faster
The scope of several tasks is reduced to lower overall resource demand
Additional staff are recruited so that the work can be shortened
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Smoothing keeps the end date fixed by rescheduling non-critical activities within their available float to level resource demand.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What is the primary purpose of a milestone in a project schedule?
o: To mark the completion of a significant stage or deliverable
To allocate the project budget across its work packages
To record the daily effort logged by each team member
To calculate the total float available on the critical path
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A milestone is a key point in the schedule, usually marking the completion of a significant deliverable or stage; it has zero duration.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Critical path analysis shows a non-critical task has five days of float. What does this tell the project manager?
o: The task can slip up to five days without delaying completion
The task must be finished five days earlier than planned
The task lies directly on the project's critical path
The task should be removed from the schedule entirely
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Float is the time an activity can be delayed without affecting the project end date; five days of float means that much slippage is tolerable.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A schedule is revised to delay a task by three days so a shared specialist can finish another job first. Which technique is this?
o: Time boxing
Resource levelling
Resource smoothing
Risk transfer
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource levelling resolves a resource conflict by moving task timings to match availability, even where this affects the schedule.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which of the following best describes the primary purpose of scheduling within a project?
o: To track the project's risks and open issues
To confirm that the business case is financially viable
To identify the key stakeholders of the project
To sequence activities and allocate time for their completion
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Scheduling sequences activities and assigns durations so the project can be planned and delivered within an agreed timeframe.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A critical activity is forecast to overrun by two days. According to critical path analysis, what is the likely effect?
o: The project end date slips by two days unless recovered
The project end date is unaffected because of float
Only non-critical activities are delayed by two days
The project baseline automatically re-sets itself
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A slip on a zero-float critical activity pushes out the project completion date unless corrective action recovers the time.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: During delivery a planned milestone is not achieved on its target date. What does this most usefully signal to the project manager?
o: That the project's budget has automatically been increased
That progress may be slipping and corrective action may be needed
That the project's scope has been formally reduced
That the risk register no longer needs to be maintained
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A missed milestone is an early signal that progress is slipping, prompting the project manager to consider corrective action.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager uses critical path analysis to find which tasks must finish on time to avoid delaying the project. What is being managed?
o: Critical path activities
The quality of project resources
The overall project budget
Formal stakeholder approval
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Critical path activities have zero float, so they must be completed on time to prevent the project end date from slipping.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which underlying principle lies at the very heart of the time boxing scheduling technique?
o: The time available is fixed and the scope is adjusted to fit it
The scope is fixed and the time is extended until it is complete
The cost is fixed and the quality is reduced to meet it
The team size is fixed and the deadline moves to suit it
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Time boxing fixes the period and flexes the scope to fit, rather than extending time to complete a fixed scope.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What is a typical output of applying resource optimisation techniques to a project?
o: An updated communication plan for the project’s stakeholders
A revised schedule that balances resource demand against availability
An approved business case setting out the project’s justification
A prioritised list ranking the project’s stakeholders by influence
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource optimisation produces a revised schedule in which resource demand is balanced against the resources available.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: When applying resource smoothing to a schedule, which constraint must always be respected?
o: The stakeholder analysis must be fully revised before smoothing begins
The project sponsor must approve each individual resource change first
The risk register must be cleared of all entries before smoothing starts
The available float must not be exceeded, so the completion date is protected
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource smoothing works only within available float; the critical path and the project end date must remain unchanged.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What key benefit does effective scheduling provide to a project manager?
o: Improved levels of motivation across the project team
Easier negotiation with influential project stakeholders
Reduced financial risk within the project business case
Clarity on task dependencies and the overall project duration
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Scheduling makes dependencies visible and establishes how long the project will take, supporting sound planning and control.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which of the following statements best describes the main outcome of carrying out critical path analysis on a project?
o: It identifies which activities directly control the project duration
It calculates the financial return forecast for the project
It assigns responsibilities using a RACI matrix
It documents the change requests raised during delivery
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Critical path analysis identifies the activities that control the overall duration, distinguishing them from those with float.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What is the main purpose of a procurement strategy in project management?
o: To schedule the internal resources needed to complete project tasks
To identify and document the risks that face the project
To define how goods and services will be acquired from external suppliers
To assign roles and responsibilities to project team members
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A procurement strategy sets out how external products, services and resources will be obtained to support delivery.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager wants to know whether current progress is ahead of or behind plan. Which tool most directly supports this?
o: The stakeholder matrix
The risk register
The schedule
The business case
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: The schedule provides the time baseline against which actual progress is measured, showing whether work is ahead of or behind plan.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Why might a project manager include milestones within a project schedule?
o: To provide clear checkpoints for monitoring and reporting progress
To increase the total number of activities shown on the plan
To remove the need for a formal project management plan
To guarantee that the project finishes ahead of schedule
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Milestones give recognisable checkpoints against which progress can be monitored and reported to stakeholders.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Several workstreams must all reach a common checkpoint before integration testing begins. How is this checkpoint best represented in the schedule?
o: As a milestone
As the critical path
As a resource histogram
As a work package
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A shared checkpoint marking a key point that workstreams must reach is represented as a milestone; it has no duration itself.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which of the following statements best describes what a schedule provides to those delivering a project?
o: A record of quality standards the outputs must meet
A list of stakeholders and their communication needs
A justification of why the project should be funded
A time-based plan of activities, dependencies and resources
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A schedule is a time-based plan showing activities, their dependencies, durations and required resources.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: What is the primary purpose of critical path analysis in project scheduling?
o: To identify the sequence of tasks that determines the project's duration
To define the overall scope of work for the project
To establish the stakeholder communication methods
To allocate team roles and responsibilities to members
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Critical path analysis identifies the longest chain of dependent tasks with zero float, which sets the minimum project duration.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager decides to buy in specialist development work from an outside supplier. Which document guides this approach?
o: The change request log
The risk register
The work breakdown structure
The procurement strategy
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: The procurement strategy defines whether work is delivered internally or bought externally, and the criteria for doing so.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Short, fixed-length cycles such as sprints in an iterative delivery are an application of which scheduling technique?
o: Resource levelling
Parametric estimating
Time boxing
Critical path analysis
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Sprints are fixed-length cycles, a direct application of time boxing within iterative delivery.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Resource levelling is most accurately described as which kind of scheduling technique?
o: Resource-limited, adjusting the schedule to available resources
Scope-limited, deleting tasks until demand is affordable
Time-limited, never allowing the completion date to change
Quality-limited, adjusting specifications to save resources
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource levelling is resource-limited, adjusting the schedule to fit the resources available, which may extend the duration.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Resource smoothing evens out resource peaks by rescheduling activities within which scheduling allowance?
o: Their mandatory dependencies
Their available float
The project's cost baseline
The critical path duration
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource smoothing reschedules activities within their available float, evening out demand without moving the end date.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager uses a milestone to record the formal approval of the completed design phase. What does this milestone provide?
o: A checklist of quality requirements
An overview of team responsibilities
A schedule marker that shows progress
A register of the project stakeholders
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A milestone marks a significant scheduled event, such as a phase completion or approval, providing a clear indicator of progress.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project manager wants to know where to focus attention to protect the completion date. Which analysis best supports this?
o: Critical path analysis
Stakeholder analysis
Cost-benefit analysis
PESTLE analysis
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Critical path analysis reveals the activities that must not slip, showing the project manager where to focus to protect the end date.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: When resource levelling is applied because resources are limited, what is the likely effect on the schedule?
o: The project end date may be extended to fit resource availability
The critical path is removed from the schedule entirely
The scope automatically expands to absorb the spare capacity
The project cost is guaranteed to fall to its lowest level
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource levelling is resource-limited, so activities are rescheduled to available resources and the end date may move out.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Why might a project manager choose resource levelling rather than resource smoothing?
o: To reduce the number of stakeholders involved in the project
To remove the need for regular progress reporting during delivery
To keep the project's original end date fixed whatever the resource position
To resolve resource over-allocation even if the project end date must be extended
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Levelling prioritises resolving resource over-allocation and may extend the schedule, unlike smoothing which protects the end date.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Why is identifying the critical path important to the success of a project?
o: It enables better control of time-sensitive tasks that affect the duration
It improves the project's overall stakeholder engagement strategy
It determines which procurement options the project will use
It ensures only the most skilled members are assigned to tasks
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Knowing the critical path lets the project manager focus attention on the tasks that directly drive the completion date.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Why is a milestone shown on a schedule with zero duration rather than as a bar spanning several days?
o: Because it always has the most float of any scheduled item
Because it marks a single point in time and represents no work itself
Because it can never appear anywhere on the critical path
Because it is the most expensive element in the schedule
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A milestone marks a single point in time and involves no work, so it has zero duration, unlike an activity shown as a bar.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Why is scheduling considered essential to managing the delivery of a project?
o: It defines the overall scope of the work the project will deliver
It establishes the cost breakdown structure for the whole project
It provides a framework to monitor progress and identify delays early
It removes the need for a project manager to oversee delivery
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A schedule sets out when activities occur, giving a baseline against which progress is monitored and delays identified and managed.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which statement best describes resource smoothing as a method of resource optimisation?
o: Adjusting activities within their available float to reduce peaks in resource demand
Extending the schedule as required to remove all float from the plan
Adding extra staff directly to the activities on the critical path
Cutting lower-priority activities in order to shorten the schedule
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource smoothing reschedules activities within their available float to even out peaks in demand without extending the project end date.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Why is producing a realistic schedule important before a project moves into delivery?
o: It removes the need to identify any project risks
It provides a basis for coordinating resources and tracking progress
It guarantees the project will finish under budget
It replaces the requirement for a project sponsor
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A realistic schedule allows resources to be coordinated and progress to be measured against a time baseline throughout delivery.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which of the following is a direct purpose of scheduling in a project?
o: To forecast when the project is likely to complete
To define the behavioural balance of the team
To record issues that have already occurred
To decide which supplier should win a contract
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: By setting out activity durations and dependencies, the schedule forecasts completion dates and supports planning of resources.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: How does a procurement strategy differ from an individual supplier contract?
o: The strategy binds a named supplier; the contract only sets aims
The strategy sets the overall sourcing approach; the contract governs one agreement
The strategy lists internal roles; the contract lists project risks
The strategy records goods received; the contract sets the budget
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: The procurement strategy is the overarching sourcing approach, whereas a contract is the specific agreement with a single supplier.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A procurement strategy sets out, among other things, decisions about which of the following?
o: Which project risks should be escalated to the sponsor
Which milestones will be used to monitor project progress
Whether the project makes items in-house or buys them externally
Which quality tests each deliverable must pass before handover
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Make-or-buy decisions are a core element of the procurement strategy's approach to sourcing.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A project plan shows 'design approved' as a milestone. What does this most likely represent?
o: The total cost of the design phase of the project
The list of resources assigned to the design work
The completion of a significant deliverable or decision point
The amount of effort required to produce the design
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: A milestone marks a significant achievement or decision point, such as an approval, rather than effort or cost.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Why are milestones useful when monitoring the ongoing performance and progress of a project?
o: They allocate individual tasks to named members of the project team
They reveal slippage by comparing planned and actual achievement dates
They remove the need for any formal progress reporting on the project
They provide the deadlines by which supplier contracts must be signed
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Milestones mark key events, so comparing planned and actual dates highlights schedule slippage and emerging risk to delivery.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A milestone marks the end of the testing phase. What typically happens once this milestone is achieved?
o: A completely new stakeholder engagement plan is produced
The project automatically moves straight into closure
The next phase of the project is authorised to begin
The project's risk register is permanently archived
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Milestones frequently act as gates, confirming that work is complete and authorising the project to move into the next phase.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: A team adjusts the start times of non-critical tasks to even out resource demand without delaying completion. Which technique is this?
o: Float analysis
Change control
Procurement scheduling
Resource smoothing
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Resource smoothing uses available float to reduce peaks in resource demand while keeping the project completion date unchanged.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Which of the following would a project's procurement strategy normally NOT be expected to address?
o: The detailed test scripts for verifying each deliverable's quality
Whether to make items in-house or buy them externally
The types of contract to use with external suppliers
The approach to selecting and managing suppliers
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Test scripts belong to quality control; a procurement strategy covers make-or-buy, contract types and supplier management.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Without any schedule, a team is unsure which tasks to start and when. Which core purpose of scheduling is being demonstrated by its absence?
o: Defining the acceptance criteria for quality
Recording configuration items under version control
Approving the project's overall business case
Establishing the sequence and timing of activities
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Scheduling establishes the order and timing of activities; without it, the team cannot know what to do when.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: In a delivery approach that uses time boxing, which element is deliberately held fixed throughout the work?
o: The size of the team that is assigned to the work
The duration of the period allotted to the work
The total budget that is available to the project
The full set of features that are to be delivered
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: In time boxing the time period is fixed; scope is the variable that flexes so the deadline is always met.

Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.q: Deciding whether to use a single supplier or several competing suppliers is a decision captured within which document?
o: The procurement strategy
The risk register
The quality plan
The communication plan
Resource, Scheduling & Optimisation.w: Supplier relationship decisions, including single versus multiple sourcing, form part of the procurement strategy.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical use of a risk register?
o: Recording the agreed response for each risk
Tracking the status and ownership of identified risks
Authorising payments to the project's suppliers
Providing a basis for reviewing risks at meetings
Risk & Issue Management.w: The register manages information about risks; authorising supplier payments is a financial and procurement matter, not a register function.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A newly logged issue has just been assessed for its impact. According to the process, what happens at the next stage?
o: Its probability of occurring is analysed and scored
It is logged in the issue register before any assessment
It is identified and recorded for the very first time
It is resolved, or escalated if it is beyond the manager's authority
Risk & Issue Management.w: After assessment, the process moves to resolving the issue or, where it exceeds the manager's authority, escalating it.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which pairing correctly matches the terms 'risk' and 'issue' to their defining feature?
o: Risk = has occurred; issue = might occur
Risk = might occur; issue = has occurred
Risk = certain benefit; issue = certain threat
Risk = external only; issue = internal only
Risk & Issue Management.w: A risk is a possible future event that might occur, whereas an issue is something that has already happened.

Risk & Issue Management.q: An issue has occurred within a project. Which process is used to resolve it?
o: Configuration management
Change control
Issue management
Risk management
Risk & Issue Management.w: Issue management is the structured process for recording, assessing and resolving problems once they have occurred.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A risk recorded earlier in the project has now actually happened. In project terminology, what has it become?
o: An assumption
An issue
A milestone
A constraint
Risk & Issue Management.w: When a risk materialises it becomes an issue: a problem that has occurred and now requires management action.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which statement correctly reflects the relationship between a risk and an issue on a project?
o: An issue can always be prevented through effective mitigation planning
A risk is always a negative event that will harm the project
A risk and an issue are always recorded within the same register
An issue represents a realised risk or a newly arising problem
Risk & Issue Management.w: An issue is something that has happened now, arising either from a risk that has materialised or from a new event, unlike a risk which is uncertain.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A team colour-codes its risks red, amber and green to show their severity. What is this an example of?
o: Qualitative risk analysis
Quantitative risk analysis
Configuration management
Critical path analysis
Risk & Issue Management.w: Ranking risks by descriptive categories such as red, amber and green is a form of qualitative risk analysis.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Why is risk management important to the successful delivery of a project?
o: It removes the need for stakeholders to be involved in the project
It ensures that all project issues are completely avoided altogether
It guarantees that the project will succeed and meet every objective
It allows uncertainties to be identified and controlled before they occur
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risk management enables uncertainties that could affect objectives to be identified, assessed and responded to proactively.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which action is most appropriate during the risk closure stage of the risk management process?
o: Reviewing the outcomes and updating the lessons learned
Increasing the project's contingency budget for reassurance
Converting each closed risk into a formal change request
Assigning new owners to risks that have already expired
Risk & Issue Management.w: Closure involves recording outcomes and capturing lessons learned to improve risk handling on future projects.

Risk & Issue Management.q: An organisation with strong risk management is more likely to achieve its project objectives. Why is this the case?
o: Risk management removes every possible threat before it can occur
Risk management removes the need for a project sponsor
Risk management guarantees delivery below the approved budget
Uncertainty is actively managed, improving the chance objectives are met
Risk & Issue Management.w: Actively managing uncertainty improves the likelihood that the project's objectives are achieved.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A team identifies that early supplier delivery could let them finish sooner and plans to take advantage. Which purpose of risk management does this show?
o: Exploiting opportunities as well as managing threats
Avoiding the need to update the risk register
Eliminating all uncertainty from the schedule
Recording issues after they have already occurred
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risk management addresses positive uncertainty too, so planning to capture a beneficial outcome is exploiting an opportunity.

Risk & Issue Management.q: During testing, a defect is discovered that prevents the product from being deployed. How should this be classified?
o: As an issue, because it has occurred and must be resolved
As a risk, because it may affect deployment later
As a baseline, because it defines the tested product
As an assumption, because it was expected during testing
Risk & Issue Management.w: The defect has already occurred and is blocking deployment, so it is an issue that must be managed to resolution.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A supplier misses a key delivery, so the project manager records it and assigns it to the procurement lead. Which stage of issue resolution is this?
o: Analysis of the issue's impact on objectives
Identification and assignment of the issue
Closure of the issue once it is verified
Resolution of the issue through corrective action
Risk & Issue Management.w: Logging the issue and giving it an owner are part of the initial identification and assignment stage of the resolution process.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A high-impact risk was reduced by early action, and the manager records this in the register. Why does this matter?
o: It automatically triggers a review of the team's performance
It provides an audit trail of the risk treatment actions taken
It ensures the stakeholder matrix is kept fully up to date
It activates a formal contract change notice with suppliers
Risk & Issue Management.w: Recording responses and their outcomes in the register provides transparency and an audit trail that supports future learning.

Risk & Issue Management.q: How does the risk analysis stage differ from the risk identification stage?
o: Both stages only find risks, but identification also selects the responses
Identification finds the risks, whereas analysis assesses their probability and impact
Both stages only assess impact, but analysis is done after closure
Identification assesses probability and impact, whereas analysis simply lists the risks
Risk & Issue Management.w: Identification discovers and records the risks; analysis then evaluates each one's probability and impact so they can be prioritised.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which sequence best represents the stages of a typical risk management process?
o: Concept, definition, delivery and handover
Logging, escalation, resolution and reporting
Identification, assessment, response and closure
Planning, execution, monitoring and closure
Risk & Issue Management.w: A typical risk management process runs from identification, through assessment (analysis) and response, to closure.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Why is risk management considered a proactive discipline throughout the delivery of a project?
o: It focuses purely on logging issues after they occur
It records lessons learned solely at project closure
It only reacts once problems have already materialised
It anticipates and addresses uncertainty before it affects objectives
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risk management is proactive because it identifies and responds to uncertainty before it can affect project objectives.

Risk & Issue Management.q: In what way does an effective risk management process improve decision-making on a project?
o: It replaces the need for a project board to make decisions
It removes uncertainty so no judgement is required
It ensures decisions are only made at project closure
It provides a structured understanding of threats and opportunities to inform choices
Risk & Issue Management.w: By assessing threats and opportunities, risk management gives decision-makers a structured basis for informed choices.

Risk & Issue Management.q: What is the main objective of risk analysis in project management?
o: To approve outstanding change requests more quickly
To assess the likelihood and impact of each identified risk
To transfer every identified risk to external suppliers
To remove all uncertainty from the project's plans
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risk analysis evaluates how likely each identified risk is to occur and how much it would affect the project's objectives.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which of the following best describes the escalation step in the issue resolution process?
o: Recording the lessons learned after the issue is resolved
Logging the issue formally when it is first identified
Raising the issue beyond project authority for a decision
Assigning the issue to a stakeholder for resolution
Risk & Issue Management.w: Escalation is used when an issue exceeds the project manager's authority and requires a decision from a higher level of governance.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project team meets regularly to review threats and plan responses before they occur. What core purpose of risk management does this serve?
o: Reducing the impact of uncertainty on project objectives
Transferring all responsibility for outcomes to the sponsor
Recording issues only after they have disrupted delivery
Guaranteeing that the original plan will never change
Risk & Issue Management.w: Regularly reviewing and responding to threats in advance reduces the impact of uncertainty on the project's objectives.

Risk & Issue Management.q: During a review, a project manager updates the status of several risks in the register. Why is keeping it current important?
o: It guarantees no new risks will ever emerge
It transfers all risks to the project sponsor
It ensures decisions are based on up-to-date risk information
It removes the need to hold any further reviews
Risk & Issue Management.w: A regularly updated register keeps risk information current, so responses and decisions reflect the project's actual exposure.

Risk & Issue Management.q: What is the primary purpose of a risk register in project management?
o: To record and manage identified risks and their planned responses
To record the availability of staff across the project
To maintain the project's formal change control log
To monitor the day-to-day tasks of the project team
Risk & Issue Management.w: The risk register is the tool used to document identified risks, their status and their planned responses.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project passes a risky component to a specialist third party under contract. Which risk response is being used?
o: Acceptance
Mitigation
Transfer
Avoidance
Risk & Issue Management.w: Transfer shifts responsibility for a risk to another party, commonly through a contract or insurance.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project's main server crashes, halting all progress. How should this event most accurately be classified?
o: As a risk, because it may affect the schedule
As a constraint, because it limits progress
As a milestone, because it marks an event
As an issue, because it has already occurred
Risk & Issue Management.w: The crash has already happened and is affecting delivery, so it is an issue to be managed and resolved rather than an uncertain future risk.

Risk & Issue Management.q: During which stage of the issue resolution process is the effect of the issue on project objectives determined?
o: Closure
Analysis
Resolution
Identification
Risk & Issue Management.w: The analysis stage examines the severity and implications of the issue for the project's objectives before deciding how to address it.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which statement correctly reflects how a project issue should be treated once it has been identified?
o: It must be actively managed and resolved, and escalated where necessary
It should be ignored until it possibly occurs at some later point
It should be recorded only within the project's risk register
It should be treated as a guaranteed benefit for the project
Risk & Issue Management.w: An issue is a current problem requiring active management, resolution and, where appropriate, escalation; it is not a future or beneficial event.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A key risk recorded in the project's risk register has now materialised. What should happen next?
o: It should be ignored because it has already been analysed
It should be closed and recorded as a completed milestone
It should be deleted from the risk register without further action
It should be reclassified as an issue and managed accordingly
Risk & Issue Management.w: Once a risk actually occurs it becomes a current problem, so it is reclassified as an issue and handled through the issue management process.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project's main server crashes during a product launch. What should the project manager do first?
o: Replace the server without recording what happened
Log the issue and assess its impact on the project
Escalate the problem straight to the project sponsor
Cancel the launch until the server is restored
Risk & Issue Management.w: The first step is to formally log the issue and assess its impact so that an informed decision on the response can be made.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which statement best reflects a purpose of risk management that goes beyond simply avoiding threats?
o: It removes all uncertainty from the project
It also identifies and helps exploit potential opportunities
It guarantees the project will finish under budget
It transfers accountability for outcomes to suppliers
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risk management addresses uncertainty in both directions, seeking to exploit opportunities as well as reduce threats.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A new starter asks what separates an issue from an assumption in project terms. Which explanation is correct?
o: An issue is a problem that has occurred; an assumption is something taken to be true for planning
An issue is a benefit; an assumption is a cost to be recovered
An issue and an assumption mean effectively the same thing
An issue is a future possibility; an assumption is a current problem
Risk & Issue Management.w: An issue is a problem that has already occurred, whereas an assumption is something accepted as true for planning purposes; they are different concepts.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Why is a structured issue management process valuable to a project manager?
o: It fixes the project scope so no changes are ever needed
It ensures problems are logged, assessed and resolved consistently
It replaces the need for a risk register entirely
It guarantees the project will finish under budget
Risk & Issue Management.w: A structured process ensures issues are captured, evaluated and resolved in a consistent, controlled way.

Risk & Issue Management.q: How does effective risk management support communication within a project?
o: It removes the need to hold regular project team meetings
It removes the need to hold a contingency budget in reserve
It gives the team a shared understanding of potential challenges and responses
It allows difficult decisions to be deferred until project closure
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risk management aligns the team around known uncertainties and agreed responses, supporting open and transparent communication.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Why is the closure stage important within the issue resolution process?
o: It confirms the issue is resolved and records any lessons learned
It assigns the issue to an owner for the very first time
It decides whether the issue should be escalated further
It determines the issue's likely impact on the schedule
Risk & Issue Management.w: Closure confirms the issue has been dealt with and captures lessons that may help on future work.

Risk & Issue Management.q: How can a well-run risk management process increase stakeholder confidence in a project?
o: By showing threats are being identified and actively managed
By promising that no risks will ever occur
By hiding potential threats from the project board
By removing the need for any progress reporting
Risk & Issue Management.w: Demonstrating that risks are being systematically identified and managed reassures stakeholders that the project is under control.

Risk & Issue Management.q: What characteristic must an event have before it can be classed as a project risk?
o: It must be uncertain and capable of affecting the project's objectives
It must lie entirely outside the project team's ability to control
It must occur only during the execution phase of the project
It must be guaranteed to happen at some point during the project
Risk & Issue Management.w: A risk must be uncertain and able to affect objectives, whether positively or negatively.

Risk & Issue Management.q: In APM terms, the potential of an event to affect the achievement of objectives is known as what?
o: A risk
A benefit
A dependency
An issue
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risk is the potential of an event or situation to affect the achievement of objectives.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Why is a risk described as 'uncertain' rather than definite?
o: Because it can never affect the project's objectives
Because it is always guaranteed to occur eventually
Because it may or may not happen in the future
Because it has already happened and been recorded
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risk carries uncertainty: it is a possible future event that may or may not materialise.

Risk & Issue Management.q: What is the primary purpose of issue management within a project?
o: To develop contingency plans for anticipated external risks
To estimate the overall duration of the project's activities
To record, evaluate and resolve events that have already occurred
To identify and assess possible future threats to the project
Risk & Issue Management.w: Issue management provides a structured approach to capturing, assessing and resolving events that have already happened during the project.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager maintains a risk management process throughout delivery. What is this mainly intended to achieve?
o: Better-informed decisions by anticipating and managing uncertainty
A permanent record of every completed project activity
The removal of any need for quality management
A reduction in the total number of project stakeholders
Risk & Issue Management.w: Ongoing risk management supports informed decision-making by anticipating uncertainty and planning responses.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project team uses a probability and impact matrix to assess its risks. What are they doing?
o: Creating the risk register
Performing risk analysis
Prioritising the lessons learned
Carrying out risk identification
Risk & Issue Management.w: A probability and impact matrix is a standard method of carrying out qualitative risk analysis.

Risk & Issue Management.q: What is the primary purpose of the risk identification stage?
o: To capture and record potential future events that may affect objectives
To assign risk owners and set aside their mitigation budgets
To resolve every open issue before project execution begins
To remove all uncertainty from the project management plan
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risk identification focuses on uncovering and recording potential future events that could affect the project's objectives.

Risk & Issue Management.q: The project's actual spend has now exceeded its approved budget and finance has flagged it. How is this best classified?
o: A dependency
A risk
A tolerance
An issue
Risk & Issue Management.w: A confirmed overspend that has already happened and needs action is an issue, not a risk, which remains only a possibility.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager arranges a backup supplier agreement in case the main vendor fails to deliver. Which risk response is this?
o: Risk acceptance
Risk transfer
Contingency planning
Risk avoidance
Risk & Issue Management.w: Preparing a fallback to be used only if the risk occurs is a contingency (fallback) response.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which word most accurately captures the essential nature of a project risk?
o: Certainty
Deliverable
Milestone
Uncertainty
Risk & Issue Management.w: A risk is fundamentally an uncertain event, distinguishing it from certainties, deliverables or milestones.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which of the following best defines a project issue?
o: A problem that has already occurred and requires resolution
A possible delay that could arise during execution
An uncertain event that may affect the project in future
A threat for which a mitigation strategy must be planned
Risk & Issue Management.w: In APM terms an issue is an event that has already happened, or is happening now, and must be resolved, unlike a risk which is an uncertain future event.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Why is risk analysis carried out before deciding on responses in the risk management process?
o: So that every identified risk can be immediately closed
So effort can be focused on the most significant risks first
So that the responses can be chosen at random for fairness
So that the project budget can be finalised and fixed
Risk & Issue Management.w: Analysis prioritises risks by probability and impact so that responses target the most significant threats.

Risk & Issue Management.q: What is the purpose of producing a risk response plan?
o: To document the acceptance criteria for the project's final deliverables
To define how the team will react once issues have been logged
To develop the project's work breakdown structure
To set out the actions that will reduce, avoid, transfer or accept each risk
Risk & Issue Management.w: A risk response plan records the agreed action for each risk, whether to reduce, avoid, transfer or accept it.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A supplier fails to deliver components on time, delaying the schedule. What is the role of issue management in this situation?
o: To revise the scope so the affected tasks are removed
To document the issue, assign ownership and track its resolution
To plan the resources needed for the next project phase
To reassess the project's future risks and update tolerances
Risk & Issue Management.w: Issue management handles real disruptions such as a missed delivery by logging them, assigning an owner and tracking them through to resolution.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which of the following is NOT a standard step in the issue resolution process?
o: Analysis
Closure
Rescheduling
Identification
Risk & Issue Management.w: Rescheduling may be a consequence of resolving an issue but is not itself a formal step in the issue resolution process, which runs from identification to closure.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Why are risks and issues typically tracked separately on a project?
o: Risk tracking is optional, whereas issue tracking is mandatory
Issues must always be resolved before the project can start
They follow different lifecycles and require different treatment
Only risks can be escalated to senior management for a decision
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risks are analysed and planned for as uncertain future events, while issues are resolved as current problems, so they need separate processes and records.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Why does an effective issue management process assign a clear owner to each logged issue?
o: So that the issue can be ignored until the project closes
So that responsibility for resolving the issue is unambiguous and it is progressed
So that no record of the issue needs to be kept
So that the issue is reclassified as a future risk
Risk & Issue Management.w: Assigning an owner makes resolution responsibility unambiguous, ensuring the issue is actively progressed to closure.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A risk plan notes that poor weather may delay construction. What benefit does identifying this early provide?
o: It removes the impact of every environmental risk on the project
It gives the team time to prepare responses before any delay occurs
It removes the need for configuration control during the project
It guarantees that the project will remain within its agreed scope
Risk & Issue Management.w: Identifying risks early is the purpose of risk management: it allows responses to be planned before problems arise.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Why does an identified project issue demand immediate management attention rather than monitoring alone?
o: Because it is a problem that has already occurred and is affecting the project
Because it is a benefit expected only after the project closes
Because it is a constraint that was fixed at the project's outset
Because it is an uncertain event that has not yet happened
Risk & Issue Management.w: An issue has already occurred and is affecting the project, so it demands action now, unlike a risk which is only monitored as a possibility.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A team decides to take no pre-emptive action against a possible delay to key components. Which risk response is this?
o: Transfer
Acceptance
Avoidance
Mitigation
Risk & Issue Management.w: Acceptance means acknowledging a risk and taking no pre-emptive action unless it actually materialises.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which of these statements describes a genuine project risk rather than a current problem?
o: Adverse weather might delay outdoor work next month
The budget was exceeded during the last reporting period
A team member resigned from the project last week
A supplier has already failed to deliver essential materials
Risk & Issue Management.w: Only the weather statement is an uncertain future event; the others have already occurred and are issues.

Risk & Issue Management.q: What is the key difference in timing between issues and risks?
o: Both issues and risks relate only to events after project delivery
Risks relate to the future, whereas issues occur in the present or past
Both issues and risks are recorded only once lessons are learned
Issues relate to the future, whereas risks occur in the present or past
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risks are anticipated future events, whereas issues are events that have already happened and are affecting the project.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which statement best describes how a risk register is used across the life of a project?
o: It is completed once at initiation and then archived
It is a living document reviewed and updated throughout
It is produced only after the project has closed
It is used solely to record issues that have occurred
Risk & Issue Management.w: A risk register is a living document, reviewed and updated throughout delivery as risks change, close or newly emerge.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project without any issue management process is most likely to experience which of the following?
o: A permanent reduction in all project risks
Unresolved problems that grow and threaten objectives
A guaranteed increase in delivered benefits
An automatic improvement in team morale
Risk & Issue Management.w: Without issue management, problems go unaddressed and can escalate to threaten the project's objectives.

Risk & Issue Management.q: What is the main purpose of risk management on a project?
o: To improve the chance of meeting objectives by managing uncertainty
To eliminate every possible risk before the project begins
To transfer all responsibility for the project to the sponsor
To replace the need for a project management plan
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risk management aims to increase the likelihood of achieving objectives by identifying and responding to uncertainty, not to remove all risk.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which statement correctly describes a project issue?
o: It is an uncertainty relating to the project business case
It is an unplanned event that has occurred and needs management attention
It is a scheduled event that is recorded in the risk register
It is a constraint that has been imposed by the project sponsor
Risk & Issue Management.w: An issue is an actual, unplanned event affecting the project that requires management action to resolve it.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager revises the likelihood rating of an existing risk after new information arrives. Where is this recorded?
o: In the project issue log
In the stakeholder register
In the risk register
In the schedule baseline
Risk & Issue Management.w: The risk register is kept up to date throughout the project to reflect changes in likelihood, impact and status.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A stakeholder demands that an issue be escalated before any assessment has been made. What should the project manager do?
o: Close the issue without recording any further detail
Assign the issue to a team member without logging it
Analyse the issue first to decide whether escalation is needed
Escalate the issue immediately as the stakeholder requests
Risk & Issue Management.w: The issue should be analysed first so the project manager can judge whether it genuinely exceeds project authority and warrants escalation.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which sequence correctly reflects the stages of a typical issue resolution process?
o: Analysis, then identification, then escalation, and finally resolution
Identification, then analysis, then resolution, and finally closure
Identification, then resolution, then analysis, and finally closure
Escalation, then identification, then resolution, and finally closure
Risk & Issue Management.w: Issues are first identified and logged, then analysed, resolved through agreed action and finally closed once addressed.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which statement best defines a 'risk' in the context of project management?
o: A confirmed problem that requires immediate resolution by the team
An uncertain event that, should it occur, would affect the project's objectives
A completed task that is currently waiting for formal approval
A cost overrun that has already occurred and cannot be recovered
Risk & Issue Management.w: A risk is an uncertain future event that may have a positive or negative effect on project objectives.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A software defect has been fixed, tested and verified. What is the final step in the issue resolution process?
o: Escalation of the issue to a higher authority
Closure of the issue, recording it as complete
Reassessment of the issue's potential impact
Reopening the issue for further investigation
Risk & Issue Management.w: Once an issue has been resolved and verified, it is formally closed and recorded as complete.

Risk & Issue Management.q: The team agrees and carries out corrective actions to remove the effect of a logged issue. Which stage of issue resolution does this describe?
o: Identification
Resolution
Logging
Escalation
Risk & Issue Management.w: Agreeing and carrying out the corrective actions to deal with the issue is the resolution stage.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A data breach has just occurred and is disrupting the project. In risk terminology, how is this event now best classified?
o: An issue, because it has already occurred and requires action
A risk, because it might affect the project
A constraint, because it limits the project
An assumption, because it was anticipated
Risk & Issue Management.w: An event that has already occurred and is affecting the project is an issue requiring resolution, not a future uncertainty.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Delivered equipment has arrived damaged and cannot be installed, stopping the next task. Why is this an issue rather than a risk?
o: Because it has already happened and is now impacting delivery
Because it relates purely to a much later delivery phase
Because it has no measurable effect on the project at all
Because it is at this stage still only a future possibility
Risk & Issue Management.w: The event has occurred and is affecting the project now, which makes it an issue; a risk would still only be a potential event.

Risk & Issue Management.q: The development team reports a defect that is preventing key features from working. How should this be treated?
o: As an issue, because it is already affecting the project
As a change request, because the scope has altered
As a constraint, because it limits the design
As a risk, because it may affect the project later
Risk & Issue Management.w: A defect that is actively preventing features from working has already occurred, so it is an issue that must be managed and resolved.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Why does a risk register support effective communication about risk on a project?
o: It records only the risks the sponsor wishes to see
It replaces the need for any progress reporting
It provides a shared, consistent record all parties can reference
It hides risk information from the wider stakeholders
Risk & Issue Management.w: By holding risk information in one consistent place, the register gives stakeholders a shared reference for discussing and reviewing risk.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A supplier has failed to deliver a critical component, halting project work. How should this be classified?
o: An issue, because the problem has already occurred
An assumption, because it was expected during planning
A risk, because it might affect the project later
A milestone, because it marks a point in the schedule
Risk & Issue Management.w: A problem that has already happened and is affecting the project is an issue, not a risk.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A team holds a brainstorming session to work out what could prevent successful delivery. Which risk management stage is this?
o: Risk analysis
Risk response
Risk closure
Risk identification
Risk & Issue Management.w: Brainstorming is a common technique used during risk identification to surface possible risks.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Why is it important to formally close risks during the risk management process?
o: To prevent risks from being escalated to the project’s stakeholders
To transfer the lessons learned directly into the project issue log
To reduce the number of meetings the project team must hold
To keep the risk register accurate and focused on active threats
Risk & Issue Management.w: Closure removes risks that are no longer relevant, keeping the risk register current and focused on active threats and opportunities.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A team recognises that a supplier might fail to meet its deadlines. Which stage of risk management does this demonstrate?
o: Risk identification
Risk acceptance
Risk avoidance
Risk exploitation
Risk & Issue Management.w: Spotting a potential future threat before it materialises is an example of risk identification.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which of the following is typically recorded during the closure stage of issue resolution?
o: The stakeholder responsibility matrix for the project
The proposed escalation route for the issue
The date the issue was resolved and the actions taken
The estimated likelihood of the issue recurring later
Risk & Issue Management.w: At closure the resolution date and a summary of the actions taken are recorded to confirm the issue is complete.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project team recognises potential cyber-attacks as a threat to delivery. What has this activity achieved?
o: It has identified a risk
It has closed the risk
It has analysed the risk's impact
It has accepted the risk
Risk & Issue Management.w: Recognising cyber-attacks as a possible future threat means the team has successfully identified a risk.

Risk & Issue Management.q: How does a risk register support accountability within a project's risk management?
o: By assigning an owner responsible for each risk
By removing the need to assign any risk owners
By recording only risks that have already occurred
By listing the project's stakeholders and their interests
Risk & Issue Management.w: The register names a risk owner for each entry, making individuals accountable for monitoring and responding to their risks.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager keeps a single document listing each risk, its owner and its planned response. What is this document?
o: The quality plan
The communication plan
The business case
The risk register
Risk & Issue Management.w: A risk register is the central record of identified risks, their assessment, owners and planned responses, supporting ongoing risk management.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which of the following is commonly used as a tool for identifying project risks?
o: SWOT analysis, examining strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats
Critical path analysis, identifying the longest sequence of activities
Earned value analysis, comparing planned and actual project performance
MoSCoW prioritisation, ranking requirements by their relative importance
Risk & Issue Management.w: SWOT analysis is a recognised technique during the identification stage of the risk management process for surfacing threats and opportunities.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A possible delay to delivery is identified because a supplier may be overloaded with work. How should this be classified?
o: As a milestone, because it marks a delivery point
As a risk, because it has not yet happened
As a change request, because the plan must alter
As an issue, because it is affecting the project now
Risk & Issue Management.w: The delay is only a possibility that has not yet occurred, so it is an uncertain future event and is therefore a risk.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which of the following is an example of the risk response known as avoidance?
o: Removing a high-risk feature from the project's scope entirely
Accepting the possibility of a small delay to final delivery
Buying insurance to cover possible damage to project equipment
Increasing the budget to cope with late supplier deliveries
