Risk & Issue Management.w: Avoidance removes the threat completely, for example by taking the risky element out of scope.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager reviews risks at every team meeting rather than only at the outset. What benefit does this ongoing review bring?
o: It removes the need to maintain a risk register
It transfers all accountability for risks to the sponsor
It provides early warning of new and changing risks so responses stay current
It guarantees that no risks will materialise during delivery
Risk & Issue Management.w: Reviewing risks regularly gives early warning of new and changing risks, keeping planned responses current throughout delivery.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Midway through delivery a team spots a new threat that was not previously listed. Which stage does the process return to?
o: Analysis
Identification
Response
Closure
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risk management is iterative; a newly spotted threat re-enters the process at the identification stage before being analysed and responded to.

Risk & Issue Management.q: One event may happen next quarter; another has already stopped work today. How should each be classified respectively?
o: The first as an issue; the second as a risk
Both as risks, since both affect the project
The first as a risk; the second as an issue
Both as issues, since both are recorded
Risk & Issue Management.w: A possible future event is a risk; one that has already occurred and stopped work is an issue.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which statement best corrects the misconception that risk management removes all risk from a project?
o: It guarantees the project will meet every objective
It ensures no threats will ever materialise
It manages uncertainty to acceptable levels rather than removing it entirely
It transfers every risk to an external supplier
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risk management reduces and controls uncertainty to acceptable levels; it cannot eliminate all risk from a project.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager maintains a risk register and reviews it each week. How does this best support project success?
o: It removes all remaining assumptions from the project management plan
It allows risks to be monitored continuously and responses to be actioned
It ensures the lessons learned are all documented before work begins
It prevents any further change requests from being raised during delivery
Risk & Issue Management.w: Regular review of the risk register lets the team act on emerging threats and opportunities before they escalate.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which of the following would you NOT normally expect to find recorded in a risk register?
o: The actual durations recorded for completed project tasks
A clear description of each identified risk
The probability and impact scores for each risk
The named person who owns each identified risk
Risk & Issue Management.w: Actual task durations belong to the schedule, not the risk register, which focuses on uncertainty and responses.

Risk & Issue Management.q: During which stage would a project manager draw on lessons learned from earlier projects to spot potential risks?
o: Risk acceptance
Risk response
Risk closure
Risk identification
Risk & Issue Management.w: Lessons learned from previous projects are a useful input to risk identification, helping surface recurring or overlooked risks.

Risk & Issue Management.q: How does a risk differ from an assumption on a project?
o: A risk is always true; an assumption is always false
A risk is an uncertain future event; an assumption is taken to be true
There is no difference between the two terms
A risk has occurred; an assumption cannot occur
Risk & Issue Management.w: A risk is an uncertain event that might happen, while an assumption is something accepted as true for planning.

Risk & Issue Management.q: How does effective risk management benefit a project?
o: It removes all uncertainty from the project environment
It shifts every decision onto the individual team members
It reduces the impact of threats and helps exploit opportunities
It allows the project to ignore its business case
Risk & Issue Management.w: Managing risk reduces the effect of threats and helps the project take advantage of opportunities, improving the chance of success.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Considering how projects define their terms, which of the following situations most clearly represents an issue?
o: A supplier might raise its component prices next quarter
A required approval has been refused, halting the next stage
Bad weather could delay some outdoor work later in delivery
A team member may possibly leave before delivery ends
Risk & Issue Management.w: A refused approval that has halted progress has already happened, making it an issue; the others are uncertain future events, or risks.

Risk & Issue Management.q: As soon as a problem is confirmed to be affecting the project now, where is it first recorded in the resolution process?
o: In the benefits plan at closure
In the business case during escalation
In the risk register during analysis
In the issue log at the identification stage
Risk & Issue Management.w: A confirmed issue is first recorded in the issue log as part of the identification stage of the process.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which of the following best defines an 'issue' in a project?
o: A technique used to break down the scope of the work
A planned milestone marking the end of a project stage
An uncertain event that may or may not happen in future
A problem that has occurred and requires management action
Risk & Issue Management.w: An issue is a problem that has already happened and needs resolving now, unlike a risk, which is an uncertain future event.

Risk & Issue Management.q: During which stage of the risk management process are risks assessed for probability and impact so that they can be prioritised?
o: Identification
Response
Analysis
Closure
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risk analysis assesses probability and impact, enabling risks to be prioritised for attention.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Where would a project manager typically record and track a problem that has already arisen during delivery?
o: In the risk register
In the issue log
In the communication plan
In the business case
Risk & Issue Management.w: A problem that has arisen is an issue and is recorded and tracked in the issue log, distinct from the risk register used for potential events.

Risk & Issue Management.q: After logging an issue, the project manager works out how seriously it affects cost, time and quality. Which stage of issue resolution is this?
o: Closure
Escalation
Identification
Assessment
Risk & Issue Management.w: Determining the effect of a logged issue on the project's objectives is the assessment stage.

Risk & Issue Management.q: At what point in the issue resolution process is ownership of the issue formally assigned?
o: During the analysis of the issue
Only if the issue is escalated
During the closure of the issue
Immediately after the issue has been logged
Risk & Issue Management.w: Once an issue has been identified and logged, ownership is promptly assigned so that resolution can be driven and tracked.

Risk & Issue Management.q: The team records that adverse weather might delay outdoor work next month. How is this best classified?
o: An issue, because it is affecting delivery now
A change, because it alters the agreed scope
A risk, because it is uncertain and may occur in future
A constraint, because it limits the schedule
Risk & Issue Management.w: An uncertain future event that may or may not happen is a risk, distinguishing it from an issue that has occurred.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which of the following would you normally expect to find recorded against each entry in a risk register?
o: The exact wording of the project's business case
The full technical specification of every deliverable
The behavioural role of the person raising it
The risk's probability, impact and planned response
Risk & Issue Management.w: Each register entry typically records the risk description, its probability and impact, a risk owner and the agreed response.

Risk & Issue Management.q: What is normally the first step in a typical issue resolution process?
o: Escalating the issue directly to the project board
Closing the issue as soon as it has been recorded
Implementing a resolution before any assessment is made
Identifying and logging the issue in the issue register
Risk & Issue Management.w: The issue must first be identified and formally logged so that it can then be assessed, owned and tracked to resolution.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Within issue management, what is the purpose of having a defined escalation route?
o: To identify uncertain events long before they occur
To decompose the project's scope into work packages
To raise problems beyond the manager's authority to those who can resolve them
To measure the benefits delivered after project closure
Risk & Issue Management.w: An escalation route lets issues beyond the project manager's authority reach those who can resolve them.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A newly identified threat to the schedule needs capturing. Where should the project manager record it and its planned response?
o: In the business case
In the quality plan
In the communication plan
In the risk register
Risk & Issue Management.w: Newly identified risks, with their assessment and planned responses, are captured in the risk register.

Risk & Issue Management.q: How does a 'risk' differ from a 'certainty' in project management terms?
o: A risk lies outside the manager's control, whereas a certainty does not
A risk concerns team behaviour, whereas a certainty concerns the sponsor
A risk involves uncertainty, whereas a certainty does not
A risk always leads to failure, whereas a certainty leads to success
Risk & Issue Management.w: The defining feature of a risk is uncertainty: it may or may not occur, unlike a certainty.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project's approval board is asked to decide how to resolve an issue affecting several workstreams. This situation best represents:
o: Issue escalation
Scope management
Risk reassessment
Stakeholder mapping
Risk & Issue Management.w: When an issue exceeds the project team's authority and is referred upward for a decision, this is issue escalation.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A high-impact, low-probability risk has been identified. What should risk analysis then help the team decide?
o: Whether to accept, avoid, reduce or transfer it as the response
Whether to delay the whole project until the threat has passed
Whether to ignore the risk simply because it is unlikely to occur
Whether to remove the affected deliverable from the project
Risk & Issue Management.w: Analysis of likelihood and impact informs the choice of an appropriate response, such as accept, avoid, reduce or transfer.

Risk & Issue Management.q: According to APM terminology, a risk may have what kind of effect on project objectives?
o: Only a negative effect, never a positive one
No effect on objectives whatsoever
Either a positive or a negative effect
A guaranteed effect that is always realised
Risk & Issue Management.w: APM defines risk as covering both threats and opportunities, so its effect may be negative or positive.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which of the following best illustrates a risk on a project?
o: The project sponsor has already resigned from their post
A key supplier has already defaulted on an agreed delivery
The team has already exceeded the budget agreed for the phase
Adverse weather could delay the construction work later in the year
Risk & Issue Management.w: Adverse weather is an uncertain future event that may delay delivery, so it is a risk; the others have already happened and are issues.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager reviews a checklist of common threats to spot what could affect the project. Which stage of risk management is this?
o: Risk response
Risk closure
Risk analysis
Risk identification
Risk & Issue Management.w: Using prompt lists or checklists to find potential threats is part of the risk identification stage.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Why does a risk require a different management response from an issue?
o: A risk affects benefits while an issue never does
A risk is recorded but an issue is deliberately ignored
A risk needs planned responses in case it occurs; an issue needs action now
A risk is owned by suppliers and an issue by customers
Risk & Issue Management.w: A risk is managed through planned responses ahead of time, whereas an issue has occurred and requires immediate resolution.

Risk & Issue Management.q: An issue is beyond the project manager's authority to resolve, so it is referred to the sponsor. Which stage of the process is this?
o: Closure
Identification
Escalation
Assessment
Risk & Issue Management.w: Referring an issue to a higher authority when it exceeds the manager's remit is the escalation stage.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A regulatory change that was once a major risk is now confirmed not to apply to the project. What should happen?
o: The risk should be re-analysed and given a new impact score
The risk should be formally closed in the risk register
The risk should be transferred to the project sponsor
The risk should be reprioritised as a high-impact risk
Risk & Issue Management.w: As the threat no longer applies, the risk should be formally closed and recorded in the register.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which statement best describes the difference in timing between an issue and a risk?
o: An issue is a future possibility, whereas a risk is a current event
An issue is a current or past event, whereas a risk is a future possibility
Both an issue and a risk describe events that may occur in future
Both an issue and a risk describe events that have already occurred
Risk & Issue Management.w: An issue is a present or past event requiring resolution, while a risk is an uncertain event that has not yet occurred.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager puts an agreed contingency arrangement into action and monitors whether it is working. Which part of the process is this?
o: Analysing the risk's probability
Identifying new risks
Closing the risk register
Implementing the risk responses
Risk & Issue Management.w: Carrying out and monitoring the agreed responses is part of implementing the risk responses within the process.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which of the following would NOT be classed as a project risk?
o: Potential cost savings from adopting a new item of technology
Confirmed damage that has already occurred to a delivery vehicle
Expected delays caused by forthcoming changes in legislation
Possible supplier delays arising from future industrial action
Risk & Issue Management.w: A confirmed event that has already happened is a current issue, not an uncertain future event, so it is not a risk.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Issue management differs from risk management chiefly because it deals with what?
o: Uncertain events that have not yet happened
Problems that have already arisen and now need resolving
The measurement of benefits after handover
The decomposition of deliverables into work packages
Risk & Issue Management.w: Issue management addresses problems that have already occurred, whereas risk management handles uncertain future events.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which of the following best describes the difference between an issue and a risk?
o: A risk relates to cost, whereas an issue relates to quality
A risk must be escalated, whereas an issue does not
A risk is recorded in the schedule, whereas an issue is not
A risk is a future uncertainty, whereas an issue is a current problem
Risk & Issue Management.w: A risk is an uncertain future event, while an issue is a problem that has already occurred and must be resolved.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A developer flags a design flaw that could delay testing if it is not addressed. How should this be managed?
o: Record it in the risk register, as it is a possible future event
Add it to the work breakdown structure as a new task
Escalate it immediately to the project sponsor for a decision
Record it in the issue register, as it has already occurred
Risk & Issue Management.w: Because the delay has not yet happened and would only occur if the flaw is not addressed, it is an uncertain future event and belongs in the risk register.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager introduces an issue log and escalation route. What purpose does this primarily serve?
o: It records the estimated cost of each work package
It sets the acceptance criteria for the final product
It forecasts uncertain events that may occur later
It ensures current problems are captured and dealt with promptly
Risk & Issue Management.w: An issue log and escalation route ensure current problems are captured and resolved promptly, the aim of issue management.

Risk & Issue Management.q: After a response reduces a risk's likelihood, what should happen to that entry in the risk register?
o: It should be moved into the project's issue log
It should be updated to reflect its revised assessment
It should be left unchanged to preserve the original
It should be deleted immediately from the register
Risk & Issue Management.w: The register is updated so that the revised probability and residual exposure are recorded, keeping the risk picture accurate.

Risk & Issue Management.q: What takes place during the closure stage of the issue management process?
o: Assignment of ownership to a responsible person
Formal verification and sign-off that the issue is resolved
Implementation of the corrective action needed
Initial logging of the issue when it is first identified
Risk & Issue Management.w: Closure confirms and records that the issue has been resolved, with the necessary verification and sign-off completed.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A positive risk that could benefit the project if it occurs is often referred to as which of the following?
o: An issue
An opportunity
A threat
A constraint
Risk & Issue Management.w: In APM terms a positive risk is an opportunity, whereas a negative risk is a threat.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which two elements together characterise a risk when it is first defined on a project?
o: Its uncertainty of occurring and its potential effect on objectives
Its exact cost and its confirmed completion date
Its assigned owner and its reporting frequency
Its approval status and its version number
Risk & Issue Management.w: A risk combines uncertainty of occurrence with a potential effect on objectives, unlike a certainty or fixed fact.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Having assessed its risks, a team decides how to treat each one, choosing to reduce, transfer, avoid or accept. Which stage is this?
o: Risk response
Risk analysis
Risk identification
Risk closure
Risk & Issue Management.w: Deciding how to treat each risk — reduce, transfer, avoid or accept — is the risk response stage.

Risk & Issue Management.q: What is typically carried out during the resolution step of the issue management process?
o: Assigning the issue to a responsible team member
Determining the overall severity of the issue
Recording the issue formally in the register
Taking corrective action to resolve the issue
Risk & Issue Management.w: The resolution step involves implementing the planned corrective action to deal with and close out the issue.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A product fails final testing because of a missed requirement, so the project manager formally records and recognises it. Which stage of issue resolution is this?
o: Closure
Analysis
Identification
Resolution
Risk & Issue Management.w: Formally recording and recognising the issue is the identification stage, which begins the resolution process.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Unlike an issue, what defining feature does a risk always carry on a project?
o: A requirement for immediate corrective action now
A guaranteed negative effect on the budget
An effect that has already been felt by the team
A degree of uncertainty about whether it will occur
Risk & Issue Management.w: A risk always carries uncertainty about whether it will occur, unlike an issue which has already happened.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A stakeholder raises a formal complaint during a project review meeting. Which process is used to handle this?
o: Scope management
Risk identification
Configuration management
Issue management
Risk & Issue Management.w: A complaint is a current concern that has arisen, so it is captured and addressed through the issue management process.

Risk & Issue Management.q: In quantitative risk analysis, which technique might a team use to simulate many possible risk outcomes?
o: The Delphi technique
MoSCoW prioritisation
An Ishikawa diagram
Monte Carlo simulation
Risk & Issue Management.w: Monte Carlo simulation is a quantitative technique that models many scenarios to estimate the range of likely outcomes.

Risk & Issue Management.q: During a project review, the sponsor asks for an overview of the project's current risks and how each is being managed. Which document should the project manager present?
o: The business case
The product breakdown structure
The project schedule
The risk register
Risk & Issue Management.w: The risk register is the central record of identified risks, their assessed severity, planned responses and current status, making it the correct document for reviewing how risks are being managed.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A supplier-capacity risk has been successfully dealt with through earlier delivery. What should the project manager do next?
o: Close the risk and record its outcome in the register
Leave the risk open in case the problem returns later
Remove the supplier from the project altogether
Escalate the risk to the project sponsor for a decision
Risk & Issue Management.w: Once a risk has been resolved it should be closed and its outcome documented to keep the register accurate.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which of the following is NOT typically part of the issue management process?
o: Monitoring progress until the issue is resolved and then closed
Assigning a named owner to take responsibility for the issue
Scoring the probability and impact of the issue before it occurs
Recording the issue within a formal issue register or log
Risk & Issue Management.w: Scoring probability and impact belongs to risk management; an issue has already occurred, so it is logged, owned, resolved and closed.

Risk & Issue Management.q: When should a project risk normally be formally closed?
o: At the very start of the project's initiation stage
When it is no longer relevant or has been fully addressed
Only after the post-project review has taken place
As soon as it has first been identified by the team
Risk & Issue Management.w: A risk is closed once it no longer poses a threat or opportunity, whether through response or expiry.

Risk & Issue Management.q: At the closure stage of the risk management process, what does a team typically do with a risk that can no longer occur?
o: Formally close it and capture any lessons learned
Transfer it to an external supplier under contract
Escalate it to the programme board for a decision
Reassess its probability and impact scores
Risk & Issue Management.w: At closure a risk that can no longer occur is formally closed and any lessons are recorded for future use.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A lead engineer resigns unexpectedly and work on their deliverables has now stopped. In project terms, this is best classified as what?
o: A dependency
A risk
An issue
An assumption
Risk & Issue Management.w: An event that has actually happened and is now affecting delivery is an issue, not a risk, which is only a possible future event.

Risk & Issue Management.q: How does effective issue management benefit a project?
o: It helps maintain control and minimise disruption to delivery
It removes the need for a formal change control process
It guarantees that every deliverable will meet its specification
It eliminates all remaining risks from the project entirely
Risk & Issue Management.w: By recording and resolving problems promptly, issue management reduces their impact and helps keep the project under control.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A new appraisal system must be handed to HR within six weeks. What best distinguishes this project from HR's business-as-usual work?
o: The HR department holds greater control over the project budget
The project has a defined end date and delivers a unique output
The project exists to support HR's routine daily operations
The project is concerned only with engaging its stakeholders
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A project delivers a one-off output within defined constraints and then closes, whereas HR's ongoing work is repeatable business-as-usual.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Why might an organisation choose to manage several related projects together as a programme rather than entirely separately?
o: To achieve coordinated benefits that the individual projects could not deliver alone
To remove the need for any individual project to have its own objectives
To guarantee that each project finishes strictly within its own isolated budget
To convert temporary project work into permanent operational business activity
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A programme coordinates related projects so that combined, aligned benefits are realised that separate projects could not deliver individually.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which of the following best summarises the key purpose of project management?
o: To take the place of business-as-usual activities
To help organisations deliver change and achieve specific objectives
To increase permanent headcount in operational areas
To standardise routine reporting across all departments
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Project management enables organisations to deliver change and meet specific time, cost and quality objectives.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A city-centre event project faces growing scrutiny over its impact on local air quality and pollution. Which PESTLE category does this most relate to?
o: Technological
Environmental
Political
Legal
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Pollution, air quality and sustainability concerns fall under the environmental category of PESTLE.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A new team member asks how the discipline of project management should best be defined in practice.
o: The steady supervision of recurring departmental duties within fixed annual budgets
The organising of resources purely to reduce day-to-day operational running costs
The application of knowledge, tools and techniques to deliver objectives within agreed constraints
The prioritising of competing initiatives to reflect the organisation's changing strategy
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Project management applies knowledge, tools and techniques to deliver objectives within the constraints of time, cost and quality; the distractors describe operations and portfolio activity.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Keeping a logistics project aligned to the sponsor's strategic vision is best described as an example of what?
o: One of the fundamental purposes of project management
A post-project review conducted after handover
A portfolio management responsibility above the project
A quality assurance activity carried out independently
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Ensuring the project stays aligned to organisational strategy and the sponsor's objectives is a core purpose of project management.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A charity is running a time-limited fundraising campaign. Why is managing it using project management principles appropriate?
o: Because the campaign forms part of routine operations
Because fundraising is a continuous, repeatable task
Because project management suits one-off, goal-focused initiatives
Because the campaign has no defined end point
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Project management is designed for temporary initiatives with clear objectives and a defined end, which fits the campaign.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A new CEO cancels two projects, starts three, and groups related initiatives into one programme. Which type of management is being applied?
o: Programme assurance
Change control
Portfolio management
Operational leadership
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Prioritising, terminating and initiating initiatives across the organisation to reflect strategy is portfolio management.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A sponsor is concerned that high inflation and rising interest rates could affect a capital investment project. Which PESTLE category applies?
o: Legal
Technological
Economic
Environmental
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Inflation and interest rates are economic factors, which directly influence a project's cost and viability.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A PMO balances resource allocation and risk exposure across a suite of unrelated IT and marketing projects. What is being demonstrated?
o: Operational management
Programme governance
Portfolio management
Project assurance
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Balancing investment, resources and risk across unrelated projects to serve organisational strategy is portfolio management.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: When explaining project management to stakeholders unfamiliar with the discipline, which description would be the most accurate to give?
o: The application of processes and skills to deliver a project's objectives
The routine oversight of established services to keep them running smoothly
The selection of investments to balance the organisation's limited resources
The coordination of several related projects to achieve one strategic change
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Project management is the application of processes and skills to deliver the project's objectives; the remaining options describe operations, programme and portfolio management respectively.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A project is defined as being undertaken to achieve planned objectives. In what terms are these objectives usually expressed?
o: Outputs, outcomes or benefits
Routine, repeated daily tasks
Departments, functions or teams
Profits, dividends or returns
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Planned objectives on a project are defined in terms of outputs, outcomes or benefits, distinguishing a project from operations, programmes and portfolios.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Why do organisations apply project management to unique, time-limited pieces of work?
o: To ensure the work continues indefinitely as part of routine operations
To guarantee that the work encounters no risks or unexpected events
To achieve the defined objectives within agreed time, cost and quality constraints
To keep the project team occupied until a permanent role becomes available
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: The key purpose of project management is to achieve the project objectives within the agreed constraints, typically time, cost and quality.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Compared with business as usual, project work is generally characterised by higher levels of which factor?
o: Uncertainty, because the outputs are unique
Repetition, because the tasks are standardised
Stability, because the team is permanent
Predictability, because the work is routine
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Because projects deliver unique outputs, they carry greater uncertainty and risk than the routine, repeatable work of operations.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: During an overseas product launch, the team flags that new tax legislation has been enacted. Which PESTLE category does this relate to?
o: Technological
Sociological
Environmental
Legal
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: New legislation, including tax law, falls under the legal category of PESTLE, which covers the laws and regulations affecting a project.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A council forms a temporary team to build a new leisure centre, disbanding it once the centre opens. Which characteristic marks this as a project?
o: The output is identical to previous deliverables
The endeavour is transient with a defined end point
The team and funding are permanent and ongoing
The work repeats on a fixed monthly cycle
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A project is transient, having a defined beginning and end, after which the temporary organisation is disbanded.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Why is the temporary nature of a project important to the way it is managed?
o: It ensures defined objectives are delivered within a bounded time frame
It removes the need for any stakeholder involvement during delivery
It guarantees the team can immediately be reused on other work
It aligns all delivery activity strictly to the financial year
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Being time-bounded focuses the project on achieving its specific objectives within defined constraints rather than continuing indefinitely.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A sponsor asks what project management is fundamentally there to accomplish on their initiative. What is the best reply?
o: To guarantee the initiative faces no risks or changes whatsoever
To deliver the initiative's objectives successfully within the agreed constraints
To keep the initiative running indefinitely as a routine service
To maximise the number of tasks the team completes each week
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: The key purpose of project management is the successful delivery of the initiative's objectives within its agreed constraints.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A retailer plans to enter an unfamiliar overseas market. How would a PESTLE analysis help the project manager assess this move?
o: By revealing external influences in that market that could create risks or opportunities
By defining the acceptance criteria for the finished product
By allocating the project's work packages to named team members
By recording the internal costs of each project deliverable
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: PESTLE examines the external environment, exposing market-specific risks and opportunities the project must plan for.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Your project is one of eight coordinated under a wider business change programme. What is the role of programme management here?
o: To coordinate and align related projects for greater benefit
To focus only on your project's budget and schedule
To monitor health and safety across the organisation
To take over the duties of the individual project sponsors
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Programme management coordinates and aligns related projects so they contribute to wider, shared business benefits.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Midway through a busy period, a manager treats a unique system upgrade exactly like routine operations. Why is this approach likely to fail?
o: Routine operations demand far more governance than projects
The upgrade's uniqueness and finite scope need project management
The upgrade cannot involve any of the operational staff
Operations and projects require exactly the same controls
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A unique, time-bounded upgrade requires project management disciplines, which differ from the steady controls used for business as usual.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which of the following is most characteristic of business-as-usual rather than of project work?
o: Producing a unique output using temporarily assigned resources
Delivering a defined scope within a fixed time frame
Delivering repetitive tasks and services on a continuous basis
Following a phased life cycle to achieve set objectives
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Business-as-usual maintains ongoing, repeatable services and functions, unlike the unique, time-bounded outputs of a project.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A new data protection regulation takes effect during your design phase. Which analysis would help you understand its implications for the project?
o: A lessons-learned report
PESTLE analysis
A RAID log
Monte Carlo simulation
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: PESTLE assesses how external legal and political factors, such as new regulation, may affect the project.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A project manager reviews economic, legal and environmental trends affecting a new facility. What is the purpose of examining these together?
o: To confirm the internal budget allocation for the facility
To build a rounded picture of external influences on the project
To assign responsibilities to the facility's construction team
To measure the quality of the facility's finished components
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Considering these factors collectively, as in PESTLE, gives a rounded view of the external environment shaping the project.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Several related projects are managed together to improve customer service and maximise value. What are they collectively part of?
o: A portfolio
A business case
A programme
A risk register
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A programme is a group of related projects managed in a coordinated way to deliver benefits not available from managing them individually.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A team reviews trends in renewable-energy legislation to see how they could shape a new facility's design. Which tool are they most likely using?
o: SWOT analysis
PESTLE analysis
MoSCoW prioritisation
Cost-benefit analysis
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: PESTLE analysis identifies and assesses external factors, such as legislation, that could influence project outcomes.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Within the project, programme and portfolio hierarchy, which level is most directly concerned with aligning investment to organisational strategy?
o: Portfolio management
Work package management
Programme management
Project management
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Portfolio management is the level most directly focused on aligning the organisation's investment in projects and programmes with its strategy.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which of the following is most likely to be a portfolio management responsibility?
o: Selecting the right mix of projects to align with strategy
Ensuring two related projects are delivered in sync
Monitoring an individual project's risk register
Defining the detailed scope for a single project
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Portfolio management ensures the right projects and programmes are chosen and prioritised to meet strategic goals.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A manager claims that project management is simply 'getting the work done'. Which correction is the most accurate?
o: It is the informal delegation of tasks to whoever happens to have spare capacity
It is the day-to-day running of a settled service once it has been established
It is the ongoing ranking of investments to match the organisation's overall strategy
It is the planned application of processes and skills to achieve defined objectives
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Project management is a planned, structured application of processes and skills to defined objectives, not informal task allocation, operations or portfolio prioritisation.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: An operations manager notes their team's output rarely changes month to month. How does this contrast with a project team's work?
o: A project team also produces unchanging monthly output
A project team has no need to manage any resources
A project team operates without any start or end date
A project team works towards a defined, finite objective
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A project pursues a defined objective within a finite timeframe, unlike the steady, continuous output of operations.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A complex product must be delivered by combined IT and engineering teams. Which action best demonstrates project management?
o: Applying methods and tools to plan, execute and control delivery
Hiring additional administrative staff for routine services
Documenting every staff role across the whole organisation
Processing staff annual leave requests through a central team
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Applying structured methods, processes and tools to plan and control the delivery is the essence of project management.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A project manager wants to anticipate how the wider environment might influence a new venture. Which analysis best serves this purpose?
o: A responsibility assignment matrix mapping tasks to team roles
A PESTLE analysis of political, economic, social and other external factors
A work breakdown structure decomposing the project's deliverables
A risk register listing only internal delivery threats
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: PESTLE is used to scan the external environment, whereas the other tools address internal work, roles or logged threats.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which of the following is not part of managing a project?
o: Identifying and managing project risks
Resolving issues that arise during delivery
Continuously delivering an ongoing business function
Communicating with project stakeholders
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Project management concerns temporary, defined outputs; the continuous delivery of a business function is business-as-usual, not project work.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: An organisation groups related projects under one change initiative and separately reviews all initiatives for strategic fit. Which two disciplines are described?
o: Programme management then project management
Portfolio management then programme management
Project management then programme management
Programme management then portfolio management
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Grouping related projects to deliver a shared change is programme management; reviewing the whole collection for strategic fit is portfolio management.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which statement best defines project management as understood within the APM Body of Knowledge?
o: The routine monitoring of daily operational activities within a permanent department
The application of processes, methods and knowledge to achieve defined project objectives
The forecasting of resource requirements across the whole organisation each year
The assignment of repetitive tasks to staff within ongoing business functions
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Project management is the application of processes, methods, knowledge, skills and experience to achieve the project objectives within agreed constraints.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Why might a project manager carry out a PESTLE analysis during the initiation of a project?
o: To identify external factors that could influence the project
To map out the internal work breakdown structure
To set the payment schedule agreed with contractors
To evaluate the team's internal communication styles
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: PESTLE analysis is used to identify external, macro-environmental factors that may affect the project.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Within the wider hierarchy of managing change, which statement best defines what 'programme management' actually involves?
o: The management of a single temporary endeavour to produce one defined output
The coordinated management of related projects to deliver benefits not achievable separately
The routine supervision of continuing operational services and business functions
The selection of all organisational investments to reflect strategic priorities
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Programme management coordinates related projects to deliver benefits beyond what individual projects could achieve alone; the distractors describe a single project, portfolio management and operations.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which of the following best explains the value of carrying out a PESTLE analysis at the start of a large project?
o: It helps anticipate external influences on the project's success
It defines the individual responsibilities within the team
It identifies the project's key delivery milestones
It estimates the cost baseline used for procurement
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: PESTLE surfaces external threats and enablers early, helping the project anticipate factors beyond its direct control.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: What is the key distinction between a programme and a portfolio?
o: A programme coordinates related projects; a portfolio oversees all projects and programmes
A programme contains only unrelated projects, while a portfolio does not
A programme is aligned to strategy, whereas a portfolio is not
A portfolio is always smaller in scale than a programme
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A programme manages a set of related projects, while a portfolio spans the organisation's entire collection of projects and programmes.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: What is the primary purpose of project management within an organisation?
o: To take over the responsibilities of programme management
To standardise every routine operational procedure in use
To provide a controlled framework for delivering unique objectives
To remove the need for any risk and issue management
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Project management exists to provide structure, control and clarity so that defined, unique objectives are delivered.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: According to the APM, a project is best understood as a unique, transient endeavour undertaken primarily to achieve which of the following?
o: Balanced returns from a managed collection of investments
Steady outputs delivered through repeatable routine tasks
Planned objectives that bring about beneficial change
Coordinated benefits realised across several linked projects
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A project is a unique, transient endeavour undertaken to achieve planned objectives, defined in terms of outputs, outcomes or benefits.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Why does describing a project as 'transient' matter when defining what a project actually is?
o: It confirms the work will always exceed its planned budget
It signals the work has a defined start and finish
It shows the work will never involve any external suppliers
It guarantees the work produces identical repeated outputs
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Transience means a project has a defined beginning and end, unlike the continuous nature of operational business-as-usual work.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: When an organisation talks about 'portfolio management', which statement best captures what that discipline is concerned with?
o: The coordination of routine business activities to sustain steady operational performance
The selection, prioritisation and control of projects and programmes to meet strategic goals
The delivery of a group of related projects to achieve a single change outcome
The day-to-day control of one project's scope, cost, schedule and quality
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Portfolio management selects, prioritises and controls the organisation's projects and programmes to align them with strategy; the others describe a programme, a single project and operations.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which of the following is not a characteristic of a project?
o: An objective to deliver a unique output
A permanent team structure that continues indefinitely
A temporary nature, disbanding once objectives are met
A defined start point and a defined end point
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Projects are staffed by temporary teams assembled for the objective and disbanded on completion, so a permanent structure is not a project characteristic.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between project, programme and portfolio management?
o: Programme management replaces portfolio management in smaller organisations
Projects are managed independently of any portfolio or programme structure
Portfolio management provides strategic alignment, while programmes coordinate related change
There is no meaningful overlap between the three disciplines
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Portfolio management aligns all projects and programmes to strategy, while programmes coordinate related change and projects deliver defined outputs.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: The board reviews every current project across IT, finance and HR to reallocate funding by business priority. What process is this?
o: Configuration management
Programme planning
Change control
Portfolio management
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Portfolio management provides strategic oversight, prioritisation and resource balancing across all of an organisation's initiatives.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: On a rural community project, high unemployment and low digital literacy threaten delivery. These are examples of which PESTLE factor?
o: Technological
Environmental
Political
Sociological
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Demographic and social conditions such as unemployment and literacy are sociological factors that affect adoption and delivery.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A retailer runs related projects for online ordering, a mobile app and supply-chain automation. What ensures they are aligned for maximum benefit?
o: Programme management
Quality assurance
Change control
Portfolio management
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Programme management coordinates related projects so their combined benefit exceeds what each project could achieve alone.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which outcome would a project manager most reasonably expect from completing a PESTLE analysis?
o: A complete list of the project's internal stakeholders
A signed-off configuration baseline for all deliverables
A finalised critical path for the project schedule
A clearer view of the external context influencing the project
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: PESTLE produces an understanding of the external context; the other outputs come from scheduling, configuration and stakeholder work.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A risk on a healthcare project is patient resistance to digital appointment systems. Which PESTLE category does this best fit?
o: Sociological
Economic
Technological
Legal
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Public attitudes and cultural acceptance of change fall under the sociological category of PESTLE.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A charity plans a major national campaign. Why might its project manager use PESTLE rather than rely on internal information alone?
o: Because it records lessons learned from earlier campaigns
Because it sets out the quality tolerances for each deliverable
Because it surfaces external forces that internal planning would otherwise overlook
Because it decomposes the campaign into manageable work packages
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: PESTLE looks beyond the organisation, revealing external factors that internally focused planning tends to miss.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A manager lists features of project work to contrast it with business as usual. Which feature genuinely applies only to projects?
o: Continuing indefinitely with no planned closure
Being run by a permanent operational department
Delivering a steady, repeatable stream of outputs
Being temporary, with a defined start and end
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A project is temporary, with a defined start and end, whereas business as usual is repetitive and ongoing.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A finance team updates spreadsheets and processes invoices every day. How should this work most appropriately be classified?
o: Business-as-usual, because it involves regular, repeatable tasks
Business-as-usual, because it has a sponsor and a budget
A project, because it is constrained by time and cost
A project, because it is carried out by a skilled team
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Regular, repeatable work that maintains an ongoing service is business-as-usual, not a project.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A project board wants assurance that a new initiative will meet its aims without exceeding budget or deadline. Which discipline directly serves this purpose?
o: Project management, which delivers objectives within agreed constraints
Business-as-usual management, which sustains ongoing repeatable services
Facilities management, which maintains the organisation's physical assets
Operational supervision, which oversees continuous daily production
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Delivering objectives within the agreed constraints of time and cost is the defining purpose of project management.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A company produces a one-off prototype for a client using a new design method. How is this effort correctly classified?
o: Business-as-usual, because it involves routine manufacturing
A project, because it is a unique activity with defined outcomes
A project, because it forms part of regular production
Business-as-usual, because the client places orders frequently
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Creating a unique prototype with defined outputs is a time-bounded, one-off endeavour, which makes it a project.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A director reviews the organisation's entire collection of projects and programmes to decide which to fund, pause or stop. Which discipline is this?
o: Programme management
Portfolio management
Project management
Operational management
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Selecting, prioritising and controlling the whole collection of projects and programmes for strategic value is portfolio management.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which of the following activities most accurately represents what project management involves when delivering a project's objectives?
o: Delivering identical outputs repeatedly to satisfy steady and predictable customer demand
Planning, monitoring and controlling all aspects of a project to meet its objectives
Directing a coordinated set of projects to realise combined organisational benefits
Selecting which proposed initiatives should receive investment in each financial year
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Project management plans, monitors and controls all aspects of a project to achieve its objectives; the others describe business as usual, programme and portfolio management.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A bank runs daily transaction processing and, separately, a one-off move to new premises. Which statement about these two activities is correct?
o: The processing is operations; the move is a project
The processing is a project; the move is operations
Both are business as usual because both are essential
Both are projects because both consume resources
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Repetitive daily processing is business as usual, whereas the unique, time-bounded office move is a project.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A change initiative coordinates a new system, revised processes and staff training so that together they transform customer service. What is this?
o: Benefits realisation management
Portfolio management
Project management
Programme management
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Coordinating related projects so that combined they deliver a shared transformation is programme management.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which of the following scenarios best illustrates work that would be classified as a project?
o: Answering routine user queries on a support helpdesk each day
Processing the organisation's payroll at the end of every month
Maintaining a client's existing software system throughout the year
Implementing a new customer relationship management system over six months
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A time-bounded initiative delivering a unique output, such as a new CRM system, is a project; the others are ongoing, repeatable business-as-usual tasks.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Suppliers across time zones face delays because responsibilities are unclear. Which core purpose of project management is being undermined?
o: Establishing a clear framework of control and governance
Removing the need for stakeholder input entirely
Delivering the final product without any change
Minimising all administrative overhead on the project
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A key purpose of project management is to provide clear control and governance, including defined roles and responsibilities for decision-making.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A learner is confused between a programme and a portfolio. Which statement correctly distinguishes one from the other?
o: A portfolio delivers a single output, whereas a programme balances strategic investment
A portfolio's projects need not be related, whereas a programme's projects share a common objective
A portfolio always contains related projects, whereas a programme contains only unrelated ones
A portfolio is temporary, whereas a programme continues indefinitely as business as usual
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A programme's projects share a common objective, while a portfolio groups projects and programmes that need not be related, selected to meet strategic goals.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A colleague asks you to complete the sentence 'project management is the application of...' as accurately as possible.
o: ...processes, methods, knowledge and skills to achieve the project objectives
...standard operating procedures to sustain continuous business services
...financial controls to maximise the return from routine operations
...governance rules to coordinate a portfolio of unrelated investments
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: The recognised definition is the application of processes, methods, knowledge and skills to achieve the project objectives; the distractors describe operational and portfolio work.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which single feature is most fundamental to something being classed as a project rather than another type of organised work?
o: It is unique, producing outputs not delivered before
It generates a recurring, predictable stream of income
It continues indefinitely without a planned end point
It is managed by a permanently established department
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Uniqueness is a defining characteristic of a project; each project delivers something not produced in exactly that way before.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A colleague argues that assembling the same standard kitchen unit for the thousandth time is a project. Why is this description incorrect?
o: The task is too small to require any planning
The task is not managed by a project sponsor
The task carries no financial cost to complete
The task is repetitive and lacks any uniqueness
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Repetitive, routine work lacks the uniqueness that characterises a project and is better classed as business as usual.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A project manager is preparing to advise the board whether to launch a new venture. Why include a PESTLE analysis?
o: To show the external factors that could shape or threaten the venture's success
To allocate individual work packages to named members of the team
To confirm the internal reporting lines within the project's governance
To record the detailed costs of each deliverable in the budget
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: PESTLE reveals the external factors that could shape or threaten success, informing the launch decision.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which statement most accurately expresses the difference between a project and business-as-usual?
o: Business-as-usual has a defined end point, while projects continue indefinitely
Projects are delivered by a permanent team, while business-as-usual is not
Projects deliver defined change, while business-as-usual sustains current operations
Business-as-usual delivers unique outputs, while projects avoid any change
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Projects create change and specific deliverables, whereas business-as-usual keeps existing services running.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A manager selects and prioritises all of an organisation's projects to align with strategy and balance resources. What are they managing?
o: A single workstream
A portfolio
A programme
A delivery team
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Portfolio management selects and prioritises projects and programmes across the organisation to meet its strategic objectives.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A sponsor wants ongoing visibility of progress and risk on a six-month IT upgrade. Which function of project management supports this?
o: Providing structured monitoring and control of delivery
Shifting the project's focus towards routine operations
Reducing the frequency of staff performance reviews
Allocating additional resources to business operations
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Structured monitoring, reporting and control of progress and risk are central functions of project management.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which of the following statements best describes what is meant by a 'project'?
o: A temporary endeavour undertaken to deliver a defined and unique output
An ongoing operation undertaken to sustain routine business functions
A continuous process undertaken to provide day-to-day customer support
A permanent department established to deliver repeatable services
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A project is a unique, transient endeavour with a defined beginning and end, undertaken to deliver specified objectives.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A firm keeps starting change initiatives that overrun and drift from their aims. Introducing project management would primarily help by:
o: converting the initiatives into permanent operational functions
eliminating the possibility of any future change being requested
increasing the number of deliverables produced each month
controlling the work so objectives are met within agreed constraints
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Project management brings control and structure so that objectives are delivered within agreed constraints rather than drifting.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A project is undertaken to deliver an output. How is that output most accurately described?
o: A permanent departmental responsibility
A sustained operational service function
A defined product, service or result
An adaptable ongoing support mechanism
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: APM describes a project's output as a defined product, service or result achieved within agreed constraints.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: How is the purpose of project management best distinguished from simply completing tasks?
o: It assigns tasks randomly and reviews the results only at closure
It focuses only on producing outputs, ignoring objectives and constraints
It coordinates work purposefully to meet objectives within agreed limits
It concentrates solely on cost, disregarding time and quality entirely
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Project management purposefully coordinates work to meet objectives within agreed constraints, going beyond merely finishing individual tasks.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: You are delivering a new company intranet. Which of the following actions best reflects a project management activity?
o: Developing a risk register to manage delivery uncertainty
Running day-to-day maintenance on the existing intranet
Forwarding supplier invoices on to the procurement team
Producing the weekly staff timesheets for the HR team
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Actively managing delivery risks is part of the structured, controlled approach that characterises project management.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which of the following is a feature of business as usual that a project does not typically share?
o: It is undertaken to deliver a defined change
It is delivered by a temporary organisation
It continues on a steady, repeatable basis
It is disbanded once its objectives are met
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Business as usual is steady-state and repeatable, whereas a project is temporary and disbands once its objectives are achieved.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: During an induction session, how would you best explain to a trainee what the term 'project management' means?
o: The application of processes, methods, skills and knowledge to achieve specific project objectives
The continuous administration of repetitive tasks to sustain everyday business performance
The grouping of related projects so that benefits are delivered beyond individual efforts
The ongoing balancing of an organisation's investments against its available resources
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Project management is defined as the application of processes, methods, skills, knowledge and experience to achieve the project's objectives; the other options describe operations, programme and portfolio management.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A general election is called midway through a public infrastructure project. Why would a PESTLE analysis be helpful in this situation?
o: It defines the contractual dispute resolution process
It identifies how political change could affect project governance
It calculates the project's critical path more precisely
It improves the breakdown of the technical design tasks
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: PESTLE helps the project manager assess political factors, such as changes in leadership or policy, that may affect the project.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: What does project management chiefly enable an organisation to do that ad hoc working does not?
o: Guarantee that every stakeholder will be satisfied with the outcome
Continue the same activities indefinitely with no completion point
Deliver defined objectives in a controlled way within set constraints
Avoid ever having to make trade-offs between competing constraints
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: The purpose of project management is the controlled delivery of defined objectives within agreed constraints, not the avoidance of trade-offs.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: How do project management, programme management and portfolio management typically relate to one another within an organisation?
o: Programmes and portfolios are simply alternative names for particularly large projects
Portfolios sit within programmes, which in turn sit within individual projects
Projects sit within programmes, and both sit within portfolios aligned to strategy
Projects, programmes and portfolios are independent and never interact with each other
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Projects can form part of programmes, and projects and programmes together make up portfolios that are aligned to organisational strategy.

Leadership.q: How can a project leader who consistently models the standards and behaviours they expect influence their team?
o: It transfers leadership responsibility to the team
It guarantees that no conflict will ever arise
It sets a clear example that encourages similar behaviour and effort
It removes the need for any team ground rules
Leadership.w: Leading by example sets the standard others follow, encouraging the behaviour and effort that support performance.

Leadership.q: Which of the following is a common challenge when building a project team?
o: Ensuring that every member has an identical working style
Relying on communication being clear from the first day
Balancing team members' roles, personalities and availability
Removing every difference in members' skills and experience
Leadership.w: Forming a cohesive team requires balancing individuals' roles, personalities, skills and availability.

Leadership.q: A team leader gives regular, specific and constructive feedback to team members. What effect is this most likely to have?
o: It reduces the leader's own accountability for the outcome
It removes the need for any recognition or reward
It helps members improve and sustains strong performance
It fixes the project's deployment baseline permanently
Leadership.w: Regular constructive feedback helps team members learn and adjust, sustaining and improving their performance.

Leadership.q: A project manager wants to anticipate how their new team's behaviour will change as it matures. Which model is most relevant?
o: Belbin's team roles
A PESTLE analysis
A responsibility assignment matrix
Tuckman's stages of team development
Leadership.w: Tuckman's model describes forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning, helping anticipate how a team develops over time.

Leadership.q: A team leader coaches members to build the skills their roles require. How does this most likely influence performance?
o: It removes the need to plan the project schedule
It makes the team dependent on external suppliers
It shifts accountability for the benefits to operations
It strengthens capability and confidence, improving future output
Leadership.w: Coaching develops skills and confidence, raising the team's capability and its future performance.

Leadership.q: What distinguishes genuine leadership from merely instructing a team to comply?
o: It relies on enforcing rules so people obey through instruction
It concentrates on producing detailed progress reports
It focuses on allocating resources evenly across all tasks
It motivates people to commit willingly towards shared goals
Leadership.w: Leadership motivates people to commit willingly to shared goals, rather than securing mere compliance through instruction.

Leadership.q: In Belbin's model, which team role is most associated with exploring opportunities outside the team and developing external contacts?
o: Resource Investigator
Coordinator
Implementer
Team Worker
Leadership.w: The Resource Investigator is an outgoing networker who explores opportunities and brings in ideas and contacts from outside the team.

Leadership.q: A project leader uses team feedback to improve work processes and decision-making. What effect is this likely to have?
o: It weakens the leader's authority over the team
It enhances team ownership and improves performance
It increases conflict between team members
It undermines the project's governance arrangements
Leadership.w: Involving the team in shaping decisions creates a sense of ownership that improves engagement and output.

Leadership.q: A project manager applies Tuckman and Belbin, but a colleague expects them to remove all team problems. What is the correct view?
o: The models guide team development but do not guarantee a problem-free team
The models ensure the team never reaches the storming stage
The models fix the project's budget and schedule automatically
The models make leadership of the team unnecessary
Leadership.w: The models guide team development and role balance but do not guarantee a problem-free team; leadership is still required.

Leadership.q: What challenge might a project manager face when leading a team spread across multiple geographic locations?
o: Standardising tools that are already uniform everywhere
Reducing over-involvement from the team
Reconciling differing cultures and communication styles
Coping with excessive face-to-face interaction
Leadership.w: Differences in culture and communication style can cause misunderstanding and tension, requiring the leadership approach to be tailored.

Leadership.q: A team member consistently struggles with their workload. How can the leader best influence performance positively?
o: Ignore the issue in order to protect team morale
Remove the member from the team immediately
Provide support, coaching or mentoring to the member
Publicly highlight the member's poor performance
Leadership.w: Effective leaders support struggling team members to build their capability and confidence rather than penalising them.

Leadership.q: Members of a team with mixed experience are in conflict over task ownership. Which leadership challenge does this represent?
o: Slow approval cycles within governance
Inadequate quality assurance activity
Undefined roles and unclear expectations
Poor negotiation during procurement
Leadership.w: Conflict over ownership usually signals unclear roles, and it is the leader's task to clarify expectations and responsibilities.

Leadership.q: Which leadership behaviour is most likely to improve team commitment and output?
o: Avoiding all feedback in order to prevent conflict
Withholding key information to retain control
Setting unrealistic targets to push performance
Encouraging collaboration, openness and shared decision-making
Leadership.w: Inclusive leadership builds trust and a sense of ownership, leading to stronger commitment and better results.

Leadership.q: A previously effective team shows falling enthusiasm and less clarity of purpose. To which earlier Tuckman stage is it most likely reverting?
o: Adjourning
Forming
Norming
Storming
Leadership.w: Teams can slip back to norming when motivation or shared clarity declines, requiring the leader to re-establish focus.

Leadership.q: A newly formed team works entirely remotely and rarely meets in person. Which leadership challenge is most likely to arise?
o: Building rapport and trust without regular face-to-face contact
Preventing the team from using any digital tools
Ensuring members never communicate outside meetings
Guaranteeing that no member needs any direction
Leadership.w: Remote working makes building rapport and trust harder without the regular face-to-face contact that fosters it.

Leadership.q: A team member regularly offers original, unorthodox ideas and creative solutions during workshops. Which Belbin role best describes them?
o: Completer Finisher
Team Worker
Plant
Shaper
Leadership.w: The Plant is the creative thinker who generates novel ideas and imaginative solutions to the team's problems.

Leadership.q: How does leadership differ from management within a project environment?
o: Leadership focuses on scheduling, while management inspires the team
Leadership sets the vision and direction, while management ensures delivery
Leadership handles procurement, while management handles risk
Leadership and management are effectively identical in project delivery
Leadership.w: Leadership provides vision and inspires others, whereas management concentrates on planning, control and execution.

Leadership.q: A team member regularly supports colleagues, smooths over disagreements and helps keep the group harmonious. Which Belbin role best fits?
o: Specialist
Shaper
Coordinator
Team Worker
Leadership.w: The Team Worker is supportive and diplomatic, helping to maintain cohesion and ease friction within the team.

Leadership.q: Why can leading a team drawn from several different departments be challenging for a project manager?
o: Members may have divided loyalties and competing priorities
Members always share identical objectives and priorities
Members never require any form of communication
Members automatically report only to the project manager
Leadership.w: Cross-functional members often answer to home managers too, creating divided loyalties and competing priorities.

Leadership.q: One manager plans and controls the work; another energises and directs the people. Which is chiefly exercising leadership?
o: The manager who plans and controls the work
The manager who energises and directs the people
Both equally, because leadership simply means administration
Neither, since the two activities are identical
Leadership.w: Leadership is about energising and directing people towards a vision, whereas planning and controlling the work is management.

Leadership.q: A project team has begun openly disagreeing as members assert their opinions and challenge each other's roles. Which Tuckman stage is this?
o: Forming
Storming
Norming
Performing
Leadership.w: Storming is characterised by conflict as members assert their views and challenge roles and leadership.

Leadership.q: A leader creates an environment where team members feel trusted and encouraged to share ideas. What is this most likely to improve?
o: Team performance and innovation
The quality of the risk register
The accuracy of the project budget
The logistics of the project location
Leadership.w: Trust and inclusion encourage collaboration and allow teams to perform at their best.

Leadership.q: A project leader is described as providing 'direction'. What does this element of leadership involve?
o: Setting a clear vision and guiding the team towards shared objectives
Logging every risk that could affect the project outcome
Approving invoices submitted by the project's suppliers
Updating the configuration status of controlled items
Leadership.w: Providing direction is the leadership function of setting a vision and guiding the team towards shared objectives.

Leadership.q: Understanding that a team is at Tuckman's storming stage, how should a project manager use this insight?
o: By disbanding the team and starting again
By helping resolve conflict and clarifying roles and goals
By stepping back entirely and giving no direction
By assuming the team is fully mature and self-managing
Leadership.w: At the storming stage, conflict emerges, so the leader should facilitate resolution and clarify roles and objectives.

Leadership.q: How can appropriately delegating authority and trusting team members influence a project team's performance?
o: It always slows delivery because decisions take longer
It can increase ownership and motivation, improving output
It removes the leader's responsibility for the results
It prevents team members from developing new skills
Leadership.w: Appropriate delegation builds ownership and motivation, which tends to improve the team's output.

Leadership.q: Why is effective leadership important to team performance within a project environment?
o: It motivates the team and supports collaboration towards shared goals
It guarantees that project risk will be completely eliminated
It removes the need for the team to hold any meetings
It ensures that all project contracts are signed on time
Leadership.w: Leadership sets direction and motivates and aligns individuals so that the team works collaboratively towards the project’s shared goals.
