Leadership.q: Which of the following best defines leadership in a project context?
o: Recording risks and issues in the relevant registers
Enforcing compliance with procurement procedures
Monitoring the budget and updating the schedule
Providing vision, motivation and direction to the team
Leadership.w: Leadership is about inspiring and guiding people towards achieving the project's objectives, rather than administering controls.

Leadership.q: Which action by a team leader is most likely to boost performance during project execution?
o: Ignoring team conflicts to keep focus on delivery
Setting unrealistic deadlines to create a sense of urgency
Assigning every complex task to one individual
Coaching team members and providing development opportunities
Leadership.w: Coaching and development raise capability and motivation, which directly improves team performance.

Leadership.q: Members drawn from several departments are struggling with unclear communication and low trust. Which challenge does this illustrate?
o: Difficulties with procurement planning
Cross-functional team dynamics
Work breakdown structure confusion
Disengagement of the project sponsor
Leadership.w: Cross-functional teams frequently face communication and cohesion challenges arising from differing priorities and norms.

Leadership.q: A project team has reached the adjourning stage of Tuckman's model. Which leadership action is most appropriate?
o: Introduce fresh team norms and ground rules
Increase the workload to sustain performance
Recognise the team's achievements and support the transition
Drive the team straight into a new forming phase
Leadership.w: Adjourning marks disbandment, so the leader should acknowledge contributions and help members transition smoothly.

Leadership.q: How can a project team leader positively influence the performance of their team?
o: By withholding feedback in order to avoid any conflict
By micromanaging tasks and limiting the team's autonomy
By setting clear goals and recognising individual contributions
By delegating all responsibility to external suppliers
Leadership.w: Clear goals and genuine recognition improve motivation and alignment, which raises team performance.

Leadership.q: Two experienced specialists on a project team repeatedly clash over how the work should be done. What leadership challenge is this?
o: Managing interpersonal conflict between strong team members
Ensuring every member holds an identical opinion
Removing the need for any communication between members
Guaranteeing that no member ever contributes an idea
Leadership.w: Reconciling conflict between strong individuals is a genuine leadership challenge when developing a team.

Leadership.q: How does setting clear and achievable objectives for team members influence their performance?
o: It transfers accountability for delivery entirely to the team
It guarantees that no risks will affect their work
It gives them focus and a shared sense of direction, improving performance
It removes any need for the leader to monitor progress
Leadership.w: Clear, achievable objectives focus effort and give direction, which lifts individual and team performance.

Leadership.q: A project team includes members who only work part-time on the project. Which leadership challenge does this most likely create?
o: They will always prioritise the project above all other work
Their limited availability may conflict with their other duties
They will never need any direction from the project manager
They automatically remove all risk from the project
Leadership.w: Part-time members split their time, so availability clashes with their other duties are a common challenge.

Leadership.q: Which factor most commonly makes it difficult to build trust within a newly assembled project team?
o: Members already know each other's strengths perfectly
Members are unfamiliar with one another's ways of working
Members have no individual roles to fulfil
Members have a long shared history of working together
Leadership.w: In a new team, members are unfamiliar with each other's styles, so trust takes time to establish.

Leadership.q: A project manager regularly shares the vision, encourages initiative and supports team learning. Which leadership quality is being demonstrated?
o: Inspirational leadership that aligns the team
Purely reactive decision-making
Detailed cost and budget management
A command-and-control leadership style
Leadership.w: Inspirational leaders energise and align their teams around a shared sense of purpose.

Leadership.q: How does active listening help a project leader to improve team performance?
o: It slows down necessary project decision-making
It builds trust and allows issues to be addressed early
It removes the need for any formal reporting
It promotes a culture of blame within the team
Leadership.w: Active listening creates a safe environment where concerns can be raised and resolved before they escalate.

Leadership.q: Why might a project manager use models such as Belbin and Tuckman when developing a team?
o: To calculate the project's overall budget
To understand team roles and development stages and adapt their approach
To replace the need for a project schedule
To decide the project's procurement strategy
Leadership.w: Such models help the manager understand behavioural roles and development stages, so leadership can be adapted to support the team.

Leadership.q: A project manager finds the team has no Monitor Evaluator among its Belbin roles. Which risk is this most likely to create?
o: A shortage of new and creative ideas
Too great a reliance on outside stakeholders
Excessive attention to minor details
Weaker critical analysis and poorer decision-making
Leadership.w: The Monitor Evaluator supplies objective, analytical judgement; without one the team may reach poorly considered decisions.

Leadership.q: A newly formed project team is polite but hesitant and unsure of its direction. According to Tuckman's model, what should the leader mainly do?
o: Encourage members to work independently straight away
Avoid setting expectations to see how the team develops
Step back and let the team organise itself immediately
Provide clear direction and define the team's goals and roles
Leadership.w: In the forming stage the team looks to the leader for direction and structure to build its early confidence.

Leadership.q: In Belbin's model, which team role is most focused on turning ideas and plans into practical, workable actions?
o: Implementer
Resource Investigator
Plant
Monitor Evaluator
Leadership.w: The Implementer is disciplined and reliable, converting concepts and plans into organised, practical action.

Leadership.q: Which aspect of a team does Belbin's model primarily help a project manager to understand?
o: The reporting lines shown in an organisational breakdown structure
The balance of behavioural roles within the team
The order in which risks should be addressed
The stages a team moves through as it matures
Leadership.w: Belbin's model describes behavioural team roles, helping the manager build a balanced and effective team.

Leadership.q: A project team has reached the performing stage of Tuckman's model. Which leadership approach is most appropriate at this point?
o: Reassign the work frequently to keep the team stimulated
Revisit the ground rules and reset the team's agreed norms
Provide firm direction and closely define every role and task
Delegate and allow autonomy while monitoring for emerging issues
Leadership.w: A performing team is capable and self-managing, so the leader can delegate and facilitate rather than direct closely.

Leadership.q: What challenge might a project manager face when trying to build motivation in a high-pressure delivery environment?
o: The team being consistently underloaded with work
Stress and burnout reducing morale and engagement
Receiving too much interest from stakeholders
Spending excessive time on detailed planning
Leadership.w: Sustained pressure can lead to burnout, which the project manager must manage to keep the team effective and motivated.

Leadership.q: How does adapting leadership style to the team's needs and maturity help influence its performance?
o: It provides the right level of support and direction to keep the team effective
It removes the requirement to set any objectives
It ensures the team never needs feedback again
It hands day-to-day control to the project sponsor
Leadership.w: Adapting style to the team's maturity gives the appropriate balance of support and direction, sustaining effective performance.

Leadership.q: A team leader recognises a member's contribution during a sprint review. What effect is this most likely to have?
o: It boosts morale and encourages continued high performance
It delays the delivery of future sprints
It demotivates the remainder of the team
It reduces collaboration across the team
Leadership.w: Recognition reinforces positive behaviour and lifts morale, which can drive further high performance.

Leadership.q: Beyond simply issuing orders, effective project leadership is best characterised by which behaviour?
o: Focusing solely on the project's budget and schedule
Issuing detailed instructions and requiring strict compliance
Enabling and empowering people to contribute their best towards the goal
Avoiding contact with the team to remain impartial
Leadership.w: Leadership enables and empowers people to contribute their best, going beyond merely issuing orders.

Leadership.q: In Belbin's team role model, which role is most concerned with meeting deadlines and checking work thoroughly for errors?
o: Resource Investigator
Completer Finisher
Plant
Coordinator
Leadership.w: The Completer Finisher is conscientious and detail-focused, ensuring work is finished thoroughly and on time.

Leadership.q: A project manager brings in an expert to supply in-depth knowledge the team currently lacks. Which Belbin role does this describe?
o: Specialist
Shaper
Team Worker
Coordinator
Leadership.w: The Specialist provides deep, focused expertise in a specific area that the rest of the team does not possess.

Leadership.q: How can a leader who addresses conflict within the team promptly and fairly influence performance?
o: It guarantees that the project will meet its budget
It removes the need to hold any team meetings
It transfers responsibility for morale to the sponsor
It restores focus and cooperation, protecting performance
Leadership.w: Handling conflict promptly and fairly restores cooperation and focus, protecting the team's performance.

Leadership.q: In Tuckman's model of team development, which statement best describes what happens during the norming stage?
o: Members are newly brought together and remain cautious and reliant on the leader
Members work together seamlessly and need very little direction from the leader
Members begin to trust one another, settle into their roles and agree ways of working
Members openly challenge one another as roles and priorities are contested
Leadership.w: During norming, early conflict subsides, trust develops and the team agrees shared norms and ways of working.

Leadership.q: Two strong personalities in a project team are repeatedly in conflict. Which Tuckman stage does this reflect, and how should the leader respond?
o: Storming; help resolve it through open, respectful discussion
Forming; avoid any confrontation between them
Norming; increase their workload to distract them
Performing; reassign both members elsewhere
Leadership.w: Conflict as roles are asserted is typical of storming; the leader should facilitate open resolution rather than suppress it.

Leadership.q: A team member habitually questions assumptions and weighs the options logically before decisions are made. Which Belbin role does this suggest?
o: Shaper
Monitor Evaluator
Coordinator
Implementer
Leadership.w: The Monitor Evaluator is a logical, impartial thinker who analyses options and offers balanced judgement.

Leadership.q: Which behaviour is most closely associated with strong project leadership?
o: Providing a clear vision and empowering others to deliver
Focusing only on completing technical tasks personally
Delaying every decision until all data is fully confirmed
Micromanaging each individual task within the team
Leadership.w: Effective leaders set direction and empower others to deliver while keeping the team focused on the overall goals.

Leadership.q: How can a leader who communicates a clear and compelling vision of the goal influence team performance?
o: It guarantees the project will finish ahead of its schedule
It reduces the clarity of individual responsibilities within the team
It removes the need to communicate progress to stakeholders
It can raise motivation and a sense of purpose, improving performance
Leadership.w: A clear, compelling vision gives the team purpose and motivation, which tends to improve its performance.

Leadership.q: What is the result of a leader clearly aligning team tasks with the overall project objectives?
o: Increased scope creep across the project
Reduced accountability within the team
Less involvement from key stakeholders
Greater focus and improved team performance
Leadership.w: When people understand the purpose of their work, motivation and focus increase, improving results.

Leadership.q: You take charge of a project team whose members have not worked together before. What should your leadership focus be in the early stages?
o: Concentrate solely on technical delivery
Clarify roles, responsibilities and shared expectations
Let the team manage itself from the very start
Offer performance-based incentives before any work begins
Leadership.w: An unfamiliar team needs clear direction and agreed expectations to form a cohesive structure and work effectively.

Leadership.q: Which of the following is most likely to make it harder for a project manager to develop team cohesion?
o: Frequent changes in team membership
Consistent leadership behaviour over time
Early engagement in team development
Shared values and common goals
Leadership.w: Frequent membership changes disrupt trust and progress through the team's development stages, making cohesion harder to build.

Leadership.q: A project leader actively removes obstacles and provides the resources their team needs. How does this influence performance?
o: It transfers the project's risks onto the team members
It replaces the need for a project management plan
It reduces the sponsor's interest in the project
It enables the team to work more effectively and maintain momentum
Leadership.w: Clearing obstacles and supplying resources lets the team work without interruption, supporting effective performance.

Leadership.q: What is a key leadership challenge when managing a newly formed project team?
o: Resolving undefined roles and responsibilities
Delivering specialist technical training
Drafting the legal contracts for suppliers
Avoiding any emotional engagement with the team
Leadership.w: Early in a project, roles are often ambiguous, and the leader must clarify them to prevent confusion and inefficiency.

Leadership.q: A team member generates many ideas but often loses focus on follow-through. Which Belbin team role does this behaviour most closely reflect?
o: Completer Finisher
Plant
Implementer
Monitor Evaluator
Leadership.w: In Belbin's model the Plant is creative and idea-driven but may neglect the practical follow-up needed to complete work.

Leadership.q: Which stage of Tuckman's model best describes a mature team that delivers effectively and needs little supervision?
o: Forming
Performing
Storming
Norming
Leadership.w: In the performing stage the team is capable, self-directing and works efficiently towards its shared goals.

Leadership.q: A project leader encourages open dialogue, recognises effort and adapts their approach to the team's needs. What are they demonstrating?
o: Risk-based contingency planning
A purely authoritarian leadership style
Situational leadership that supports performance
Transactional management of the team
Leadership.w: Situational leaders adapt their behaviour to the maturity and context of the team, which supports its development and performance.

Leadership.q: How can frequently changing project priorities pose a leadership challenge when managing a team?
o: They automatically improve the team's confidence
They simplify communication with stakeholders
They can cause confusion and resistance if not communicated clearly
They remove the need for any scope reviews
Leadership.w: Shifting priorities can disrupt momentum and buy-in, so strong leadership and clear communication are needed to realign the team.

Leadership.q: Using Belbin, a manager finds the team has no one focused on checking work for errors. Which action does the model suggest?
o: Move the team to Tuckman's adjourning stage
Add or develop a Completer Finisher role in the team
Escalate the whole project to the sponsor immediately
Abandon the use of any team development model
Leadership.w: Belbin's Completer Finisher focuses on accuracy and checking work, so filling that gap balances the team.

Leadership.q: Partway through a project the team resolves its own disagreements and no longer needs frequent check-ins. Which Tuckman stage is this?
o: Performing
Norming
Forming
Storming
Leadership.w: A performing team is mature and self-regulating, working effectively with minimal supervision from the leader.

Leadership.q: A high-performing team member frequently dominates discussions. Which team leadership challenge does this represent?
o: Improving weak procurement planning
Balancing assertiveness with inclusive collaboration
Correcting a failure in change control
Managing ineffective benefits realisation
Leadership.w: The leader must value strong contributors while encouraging balanced participation to maintain team harmony.

Leadership.q: In a project, leadership is most closely concerned with which of the following?
o: Establishing direction and motivating people to achieve shared goals
Aggregating the project's costs into reporting categories
Recording and controlling changes to the scope baseline
Inspecting deliverables to confirm they meet their requirements
Leadership.w: Leadership is chiefly about establishing direction and motivating people towards shared goals, unlike technical control activities.

Leadership.q: A project manager has no direct line-management authority over team members borrowed from other functions. Why is this a challenge?
o: Influence must be relied upon because formal authority is limited
The project no longer requires any leadership at all
The members will automatically ignore their home managers
The team can now be instructed without any negotiation
Leadership.w: With limited formal authority, the project manager must lead through influence rather than instruction.

Leadership.q: A manager unites the team around a shared goal and motivates them to commit to it. Which capability are they chiefly demonstrating?
o: Procurement
Scheduling
Assurance
Leadership
Leadership.w: Uniting a team around a goal and motivating commitment is a demonstration of leadership.

Leadership.q: A new member joins a project team midway through, tension rises and productivity dips. What should the project leader do?
o: Return to team-building activity to rebuild cohesion
Give the new member only isolated tasks to do
Ignore it and expect the team to settle itself
Remove the new member from the team at once
Leadership.w: Adding a member can cause the team to regress, so the leader should revisit norming activities to restore cohesion.

Leadership.q: In what way does unclear authority within a project team present a leadership challenge?
o: It can cause delays and disputes over who makes decisions
It increases the speed of every decision that is made
It removes the need for a project sponsor
It boosts accountability throughout the whole team
Leadership.w: Unclear authority creates confusion and hesitation over decision-making, reducing efficiency and eroding trust.

Scope Management.q: A project logs each deliverable, tracks its versions and controls access to it. Which discipline does this describe?
o: Quality assurance
Change control
Benefits management
Configuration management
Scope Management.w: Identifying, versioning and controlling deliverables is configuration management.

Scope Management.q: A project manager creates an organisational breakdown structure (OBS). What is the main purpose of this tool?
o: To record the project's detailed work breakdown structure
To show the reporting relationships and lines of authority
To define the project's risks and their planned responses
To set out the methods used to communicate with stakeholders
Scope Management.w: An OBS sets out the project's organisational hierarchy, showing roles, reporting relationships and lines of authority.

Scope Management.q: A team both authorises a requested change and then updates the version record of the affected deliverable. Which two disciplines have they used?
o: Configuration management only
Quality assurance, then benefits management
Change control only
Change control, then configuration management
Scope Management.w: Authorising the change is change control; updating the deliverable's version record is configuration management.

Scope Management.q: What is the primary purpose of change control within project scope management?
o: To adjust the project's budget in line with the latest forecasts
To allow changes to proceed without approval to maintain momentum
To develop the initial scope statement at the start of the project
To assess and then approve or reject proposed changes to scope
Scope Management.w: Change control is the formal process for assessing proposed changes and deciding whether to approve or reject them before implementation.

Scope Management.q: After a change, the team confirms that the new deliverable matches the approved configuration. Which activity is this?
o: Configuration planning
Status accounting
Verification audit
Configuration identification
Scope Management.w: Verification and audit confirm that items conform to their approved configuration and that changes were made correctly.

Scope Management.q: A project manager uses a responsibility assignment matrix (RAM). What is the key benefit of using this tool?
o: It tracks the financial cost incurred against each project phase
It allocates the packages of work to their related deliverables
It shows who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed
It breaks the project schedule down into its individual tasks
Scope Management.w: A RAM, often using RACI, maps who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed for each task, giving clear role accountability.

Scope Management.q: Which statement best describes how scope is managed differently in linear and iterative projects?
o: Linear projects fix scope early, whereas iterative projects adapt it over time
Linear projects define scope late, whereas iterative projects define it early
Both linear and iterative projects fix their scope only at project closure
Iterative projects rely on strict change control, whereas linear projects stay flexible
Scope Management.w: Linear projects establish scope early in the life cycle, whereas iterative projects refine it throughout delivery.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following best describes how a cost breakdown structure (CBS) supports effective budget control on a project?
o: By setting out the project's overall decision-making structure
By showing the cost associated with each part of the project
By categorising the project's scope into functional units
By assigning named individuals to each of the project tasks
Scope Management.w: By attributing costs to each project element, the CBS lets the project manager monitor and control spending against the budget.

Scope Management.q: How does configuration identification differ from status accounting within the configuration management process?
o: Identification defines and references the items; status accounting records their state and history
Identification records change history; status accounting assigns each item a reference
Both assign references, but only one audits the schedule
Both record change history, but only one plans the budget
Scope Management.w: Identification defines and labels the configuration items, whereas status accounting maintains the ongoing record of their status and changes.

Scope Management.q: Why must a project's baseline be updated once an approved change has been implemented?
o: So that performance is measured against the current, agreed configuration
So that the change avoids needing any authorisation
So that the original change request can be permanently deleted
So that no further changes can ever be requested
Scope Management.w: The baseline is updated so future performance is measured against the current, agreed configuration reflecting the change.

Scope Management.q: A developer implements a software change from an informal request, and it later proves incompatible with existing modules. Which process breakdown occurred?
o: Stakeholder mapping was not kept properly up to date
Change control was bypassed and configuration was not enforced
Quality control was applied too heavily to the work
Risk escalation was skipped during the delivery phase
Scope Management.w: The change was not authorised through change control and was not verified or integrated through configuration management, so both controls failed.

Scope Management.q: A product breakdown structure sets out the main product, its subassemblies and its components. Why is this useful to the project manager?
o: It identifies which work packages are behind schedule
It clarifies exactly what the project must deliver
It shows who is responsible for each delivery
It allocates team members to each activity
Scope Management.w: The PBS defines and visualises all elements of the final product, clarifying exactly what the project must deliver.

Scope Management.q: A team has implemented a change, but its effects on cost and schedule were never recorded. Which change control step was most likely omitted?
o: Approval by the project sponsor
Impact assessment
Configuration verification audit
Change request logging
Scope Management.w: Impact assessment identifies the cost, time, quality and risk effects of a change and must precede approval and implementation.

Scope Management.q: Once a change has been implemented, what is a key final step in the change control process?
o: Monitor the impact and confirm alignment with project objectives
Notify the members of the wider supply chain
Archive all unused change request forms immediately
Submit the change again for a further round of approval
Scope Management.w: A post-implementation review confirms the change has delivered the intended benefit and remains aligned with the project's objectives without adverse side effects.

Scope Management.q: How does starting scope definition with a product breakdown structure help ensure completeness?
o: It confirms who will approve changes to the schedule
It fixes the project budget before any products are known
It ensures all required deliverables are identified before the work is planned
It removes the need to produce a work breakdown structure
Scope Management.w: Identifying all deliverables in the PBS first ensures the work needed to create them can be planned completely, reducing missed scope.

Scope Management.q: In configuration management, what does the term 'configuration item' typically refer to?
o: A stakeholder's preferred method of receiving communication
A deliverable or document that is placed under version control
A resource that has been assigned across several tasks
A task that lies on the project's overall critical path
Scope Management.w: A configuration item is any product, deliverable or document that is identified and controlled through the configuration management process.

Scope Management.q: A diagram breaks a new aircraft into fuselage, wings and avionics, then into their sub-parts. Which structure is this?
o: Cost breakdown structure
Organisational breakdown structure
Product breakdown structure
Work breakdown structure
Scope Management.w: A product breakdown structure decomposes the final output into its major products and their component parts.

Scope Management.q: A supplier requests a change to a component because of a manufacturing constraint, so the project manager raises a change request. Which process decides whether the change is accepted?
o: Change control
Scheduling optimisation
Risk escalation
Scope definition
Scope Management.w: Change control is the formal process used to evaluate a change request and decide whether the change to scope should be accepted.

Scope Management.q: Two teams run the same product, one linearly and one iteratively. What difference in scope management should be expected?
o: The linear team changes scope daily; the iterative team never alters it
Neither team applies any control over scope changes
The linear team fixes scope early; the iterative team reprioritises it each cycle
Both teams leave scope entirely undefined until handover
Scope Management.w: Linear fixes scope early, while iterative reprioritises it repeatedly as the solution develops.

Scope Management.q: In a linear project with scope locked at the concept phase, a client requests a significant change during delivery. How is this typically handled?
o: It is implemented without review to avoid delay
It is added straight into the next delivery sprint
It is deferred until the benefits realisation phase
It is assessed through a formal change control process
Scope Management.w: Linear projects manage changes to a fixed scope through a formal change control process to maintain control of the project.

Scope Management.q: A chart divides a project into 'design', 'build' and 'test', each split into smaller work packages. Which structure is this?
o: Product breakdown structure
Cost breakdown structure
Responsibility assignment matrix
Work breakdown structure
Scope Management.w: A work breakdown structure decomposes the total work of a project into progressively smaller, manageable work packages.

Scope Management.q: A senior stakeholder questions whether recent product updates were properly authorised. Which combination of processes evidences both approval and controlled implementation?
o: Change control and configuration management
Scheduling and stakeholder management
Benefits management and procurement
Risk management and issue tracking
Scope Management.w: Change control provides the record of approval, while configuration management shows the change was applied and tracked correctly.

Scope Management.q: A team identifies all the key deliverables that must be placed under version control. Which configuration management activity is this?
o: Verification audit
Configuration planning
Configuration identification
Status accounting
Scope Management.w: Configuration identification determines which items are to be controlled and labels them so they can be managed.

Scope Management.q: What must happen before a change can be applied to a project's baseline?
o: Declaration of a change freeze across the project
Renegotiation of the relevant supplier contract
Deletion of the affected configuration item
Formal approval through the change control process
Scope Management.w: No change should be applied to a baseline until it has been formally assessed and approved through change control.

Scope Management.q: Which configuration management activity ensures that only approved changes are made to configuration items?
o: Configuration planning
Configuration identification
Status accounting
Configuration control
Scope Management.w: Configuration control ensures that changes to controlled items follow the correct review and approval process before being made.

Scope Management.q: Which sequence best represents the typical flow of a change control process?
o: Approve, escalate, configure, then define
Assess, approve, implement, then review
Implement, review, approve, then log
Reject, implement, report, then close
Scope Management.w: A change is first assessed for impact, then formally approved, implemented in a controlled way, and finally reviewed to confirm the outcome.

Scope Management.q: How do change control and configuration management jointly relate to a project's baseline?
o: Neither of the two processes has any bearing on the project's baseline
Both freeze the baseline permanently so that it can never be altered
Configuration management authorises baseline changes; change control archives the previous plan
Change control authorises amendments to the baseline; configuration management records the updated, controlled baseline
Scope Management.w: Change control governs whether the baseline may be amended; configuration management maintains the record of the controlled, updated baseline.

Scope Management.q: A configuration management plan is produced during initiation. What does this plan typically include?
o: A list of the approved external procurement providers
Roles, responsibilities, item tracking methods and audit schedules
The benefits realisation strategy for the whole project
A detailed cost breakdown of each individual task
Scope Management.w: The configuration plan defines the framework for managing items, including who is responsible, how items are tracked, and when audits occur.

Scope Management.q: Which stage directly follows the approval of a change in a typical change control process?
o: Log the original change request
Assess the change's impact
Implement the change and update the baseline
Reject the change request
Scope Management.w: Once authorised, the change is implemented and the affected baseline and records are updated to reflect it.

Scope Management.q: Why is scope in a linear project usually captured in a detailed baseline agreed before delivery starts?
o: So that stakeholders need not be consulted during planning
So that the team can alter deliverables freely without any record
So that scope can be decided only after the product is built
So that any later change can be measured against an agreed, approved reference
Scope Management.w: A fixed scope baseline gives an agreed reference so later changes can be assessed and controlled against it.

Scope Management.q: Uncontrolled additions to the agreed work are steadily expanding a project beyond its plan. Which discipline is intended to prevent this?
o: Resource management
Quality management
Scope management
Risk management
Scope Management.w: Controlling additions to the agreed work, and so preventing scope creep, is a core purpose of scope management.

Scope Management.q: How does a responsibility assignment matrix (RAM) help to reduce duplication of effort on a project?
o: By ranking the project's activities in their order of criticality
By defining the communication channels between the stakeholders
By assigning each member of the team to a specific budget code
By clarifying who is responsible and accountable for each task
Scope Management.w: By assigning clear responsibility and accountability, the RAM prevents overlap and confusion about who should do each task.

Scope Management.q: A project board rejects a change after assessment shows high cost for limited benefit. What does this demonstrate about change control?
o: It speeds up delivery through early implementation
It removes the need for any stakeholder input
It ensures that only beneficial changes are implemented
It supports uncontrolled changes to the project scope
Scope Management.w: Change control applies formal evaluation so the project is protected from changes that are unnecessary or harmful to its objectives.

Scope Management.q: Once a work breakdown structure is complete, which subsequent planning activity does it most directly enable?
o: Selecting the project's governance board
Approving the project's business case
Realising the project's long-term benefits
Estimating and scheduling the identified work packages
Scope Management.w: The WBS defines manageable work packages that can then be estimated, scheduled and assigned for control.

Scope Management.q: Team members are unsure who is accountable for each work package, causing duplicated effort. Which tool should the project manager use?
o: A cost breakdown structure
A responsibility assignment matrix
A risk breakdown structure
A critical path network
Scope Management.w: A RAM clarifies who is responsible and accountable for each work package, reducing gaps and duplication.

Scope Management.q: At which point in the change control process is a change formally accepted or rejected?
o: Before the change request is logged
At the authorisation stage, after the impact has been assessed
Only after the change has already been implemented
During the project's closure phase exclusively
Scope Management.w: A change is formally accepted or rejected at the authorisation (decision) stage, once its impact has been assessed.

Scope Management.q: A colleague asks you to complete the sentence 'scope management is the process of...' using correct terminology.
o: ...reporting progress regularly to the project's various stakeholders
...allocating the people and equipment needed for the project's activities
...identifying and mitigating the threats that could affect the project
...defining, controlling and delivering the required work of the project
Scope Management.w: Scope management is the process of defining, controlling and delivering the required work; the distractors describe resource, risk and communication activities.

Scope Management.q: An agile team adapts its backlog regularly throughout delivery. What does this indicate about scope management on the project?
o: Scope is left undefined until testing begins
Scope is adapted continuously as the project evolves
Scope is fixed and unchanged after the concept phase
Scope is fully defined at the start and then locked
Scope Management.w: Regular backlog refinement reflects iterative scope management, in which scope adapts to evolving priorities and feedback.

Scope Management.q: A team lists activities like 'write code' and 'run tests' but never identifies the deliverables these produce. Which structure is missing?
o: An organisational breakdown structure
A cost breakdown structure
A responsibility assignment matrix
A product breakdown structure
Scope Management.w: The product breakdown structure identifies the deliverables; without it the team risks planning work without confirming what it must produce.

Scope Management.q: A team uses a product breakdown structure (PBS) to represent the end product. What is its primary purpose in scope management?
o: To allocate costs to individual project activities
To estimate the overall schedule for the project
To define the deliverables that make up the final product
To assign team members to each project task
Scope Management.w: A PBS breaks the end product down hierarchically to define the deliverables that make up the final product.

Scope Management.q: A responsibility assignment matrix is typically created by combining which two structures?
o: The work breakdown structure and the organisational breakdown structure
The product breakdown structure and the benefits map
The communication plan and the procurement strategy
The cost breakdown structure and the risk register
Scope Management.w: A RAM maps the work packages of the WBS against the people or teams in the OBS to assign responsibilities.

Scope Management.q: Which configuration management activity maintains records of each item's current state and its history of changes?
o: Status accounting
Configuration planning
Verification audit
Identification
Scope Management.w: Status accounting keeps the records showing the current status and change history of each configuration item.

Scope Management.q: Why might a project manager create a product breakdown structure before a work breakdown structure?
o: To create a baseline budget for the project
To determine the cost of the individual tasks first
To assign team members to their roles early on
To establish a shared understanding of the product to be delivered
Scope Management.w: The PBS clarifies the deliverables required, giving a shared understanding of the product so that the WBS can be built around it.

Scope Management.q: In which phase of a typical linear life cycle is the project scope first defined and documented?
o: The delivery phase
The handover phase
The concept phase
The benefits realisation phase
Scope Management.w: The concept phase establishes the early definition of scope as part of the initial planning of the project.

Scope Management.q: How does a cost breakdown structure (CBS) help a project manager with tracking project costs?
o: By allocating a named team member to each individual task
By linking a cost to each element of the project's scope
By listing the decision gates set throughout the project
By recording the lessons learned from earlier projects
Scope Management.w: The CBS links costs to defined elements of scope, allowing the project manager to track actual spending against the budget.

Scope Management.q: What is the purpose of configuration verification within the configuration management process?
o: To review supplier invoices submitted during the delivery phase
To redefine the project budget once the baseline has been agreed
To approve the protocols used for stakeholder communication
To confirm that configuration items match their approved specifications
Scope Management.w: Verification and audit confirm that configuration items conform to their approved specification and that records accurately reflect their status.

Scope Management.q: Why must configuration management and change control operate together on a project?
o: To assign the members of the team to their delivery roles
To allow the project to eliminate the use of baselines
To ensure changes are properly evaluated, approved and implemented
To remove the need for any formal documentation of change
Scope Management.w: Change control evaluates and approves changes, while configuration management ensures they are consistently applied and documented.

Scope Management.q: A proposed change is rejected because it would create inconsistencies with existing components. Which process supported this decision?
o: Risk assessment
Schedule management
Quality assurance
Configuration management
Scope Management.w: Configuration management maintains the integrity and consistency of the product, so it can identify a change that would conflict with existing items.

Scope Management.q: When a project team lists what is 'in scope' and 'out of scope', which discipline are they applying?
o: Scope management
Risk management
Quality management
Procurement management
Scope Management.w: Defining what is in and out of scope sets the boundaries of the project's work, which is a core part of scope management.

Scope Management.q: A stakeholder asks whether the latest test script represents the most current version. Which configuration activity provides the answer?
o: Configuration identification
Status accounting
Verification audit
Configuration planning
Scope Management.w: Status accounting records the version history, current status and location of each controlled item, allowing such questions to be answered.

Scope Management.q: How do change control and configuration management together protect the integrity of a project's deliverables?
o: One trains the users; the other reviews the benefits realised
One ensures changes are properly authorised; the other keeps items consistent and correctly versioned
One identifies risks; the other transfers them to a supplier
One fixes the budget; the other sets the delivery schedule
Scope Management.w: Change control ensures only authorised changes proceed, while configuration management keeps deliverables consistent and correctly versioned.

Scope Management.q: What is the role of configuration management once a scope change has been formally approved?
o: To carry out the approval of the original change request
To redefine the project's chosen life cycle for delivery
To ensure the approved change is applied and documented correctly
To communicate the approved change out to the stakeholders
Scope Management.w: After change control approves a change, configuration management ensures it is implemented, recorded and reflected in the controlled products.

Scope Management.q: A learner confuses scope management with schedule management. Which statement correctly explains how the two disciplines differ?
o: Scope management sequences the work, while schedule management defines what is required
Scope management controls cost, while schedule management controls quality
Both are simply identical processes operating under two different names
Scope management defines the work required, while schedule management sequences it in time
Scope Management.w: Scope management defines what work is required, whereas schedule management arranges that work in time; they are distinct disciplines.

Scope Management.q: In the context of scope management, how is 'change control' best defined?
o: The process for levelling resources across the project schedule
The process for closing risks once they no longer apply
The process for formally requesting, assessing and approving changes to scope
The process for identifying and recording all project stakeholders
Scope Management.w: Change control is the process by which changes to scope are formally requested, evaluated and authorised.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following best describes the role of a change control board on a project?
o: A group authorised to review and approve or reject scope changes
An external panel appointed to audit the project's accounts
A working group responsible for the project's external marketing
A team that decides on the project's team-building activities
Scope Management.w: A change control board is the body with the authority to evaluate change requests and decide whether to approve or reject them.

Scope Management.q: At the start of a project a team decides the naming conventions, tools and responsibilities for managing controlled items. Which configuration management activity is this?
o: Verification audit
Configuration planning
Identification
Status accounting
Scope Management.w: Configuration planning establishes how items will be managed, including conventions, tools and responsibilities.

Scope Management.q: A project team uses the RACI model to assign responsibilities. Which type of tool are they using?
o: An organisational breakdown structure
A work breakdown structure
A responsibility assignment matrix
A product breakdown structure
Scope Management.w: RACI (responsible, accountable, consulted, informed) is a common form of responsibility assignment matrix used to clarify roles.

Scope Management.q: A project sets up a version-controlled folder with controlled access for all configuration items. Which activity does this address?
o: Configuration identification
Status accounting
Verification audit
Configuration control
Scope Management.w: Configuration control includes the procedures that govern controlled access and the storage of approved item versions.

Scope Management.q: A stakeholder submits a formal request to alter a key deliverable. What is the first step in the change control process?
o: Escalate the matter straight to the project board
Implement the requested change to the deliverable immediately
Log the change request and assess its likely impact
Update the configuration baseline before any review
Scope Management.w: The first stage of change control is to log the request and assess its impact on time, cost, quality and risk before any decision.

Scope Management.q: If change control operated without any configuration management, what problem would most likely arise?
o: The project would be unable to identify any of its stakeholders
Approved changes might be made without the resulting versions being recorded or traceable
No change could ever be authorised because there would be no approval route
The business case could not be written before delivery began
Scope Management.w: Without configuration management, authorised changes would not be recorded, so version control and traceability of items would be lost.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following best describes the relationship between a PBS and a WBS?
o: The PBS defines the deliverables and the WBS defines the work to create them
The PBS defines the risks and the WBS defines the risk responses
The PBS sets the budget and the WBS sets the time limits
The PBS defines the costs and the WBS defines the people involved
Scope Management.w: The PBS identifies the product's deliverables, while the WBS defines the work needed to produce those deliverables.

Scope Management.q: How does configuration management help to maintain the integrity of project deliverables?
o: By automatically approving every change that stakeholders request
By removing change restrictions so the team can work more flexibly
By ensuring changes to deliverables are reviewed, approved and documented
By allocating individual team members to specific project tasks
Scope Management.w: Configuration management provides formal control over deliverables so that any change is identified, controlled and recorded, keeping items consistent with requirements.

Scope Management.q: How does the timing of change control differ from that of configuration management on a project?
o: Change control acts when a change is requested, whereas configuration management runs continuously to keep records current
Change control runs continuously, whereas configuration management acts only at project closure
Both operate only once, during the concept phase, and then stop
Both operate only after the outputs have been handed over to operations
Scope Management.w: Change control is triggered by each change request, while configuration management is an ongoing activity keeping item records up to date.

Scope Management.q: A project manager must define 'configuration management' for a new starter. Which description is correct?
o: The technical and administrative control of a project's deliverables and their versions
The formal process for requesting and approving changes to scope
The identification and engagement of the project's stakeholders
The evening out of resource demand across the schedule
Scope Management.w: Configuration management is the technical and administrative control of deliverables, their status and their versions.

Scope Management.q: Why is a post-implementation review an essential part of the change control process?
o: To ensure the change was recorded within the supplier contract
To validate that all stakeholders were formally consulted first
To confirm the change achieved its intended outcomes without adverse effects
To determine the payment terms owed to the supplier
Scope Management.w: The review confirms the change was effective and has not introduced new problems in other areas of the project.

Scope Management.q: A change board has approved a deliverable change. Which process now ensures the new version is recorded and the old one withdrawn?
o: Benefits management
Configuration management
Risk management
Change control
Scope Management.w: Once a change is authorised, configuration management records the new version and controls withdrawal of the superseded one.

Scope Management.q: Testing reveals a flaw and the team wants to modify a deliverable. Which process ensures the change is formally evaluated and approved?
o: Risk assessment
Benefits management
Change control
Schedule control
Scope Management.w: Change control ensures any alteration to scope or a deliverable is formally reviewed and authorised before it is implemented.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following best defines configuration management in the context of a project?
o: Measuring the project's performance against its agreed baselines
Planning the allocation of resources across the packages of work
Estimating the level of budget reserve the project should hold
Identifying, controlling and tracking the project's products and their changes
Scope Management.w: Configuration management is the technical and administrative activity of identifying, controlling, accounting for and verifying a project's products throughout their life.

Scope Management.q: A linear project fixes all deliverables before work starts, while an iterative project adapts them over time. What does this show about scope management?
o: Iterative projects carry out no planning before delivery
Linear projects are inherently less reliable than iterative ones
Iterative projects manage scope incrementally as understanding grows
Iterative projects fail to define their scope at all
Scope Management.w: Iterative projects manage scope in increments, refining it as understanding of the requirements improves.

Scope Management.q: Midway through a project a client requests several enhancements to the agreed product. What should the project manager do first?
o: Add the changes to the next iteration in order to save time
Submit a formal change request for the change to be reviewed
Update the work breakdown structure and proceed with the changes
Amend the entries in the configuration log to reflect the changes
Scope Management.w: The first step is to raise a change request so the change can be logged and its impact assessed before any implementation.

Scope Management.q: A project manager derives the work breakdown structure directly from the product breakdown structure. What benefit does this bring?
o: It removes the need for any change control process
It ensures the planned work aligns with the required deliverables
It fixes the responsibilities of each team member
It guarantees the project finishes ahead of schedule
Scope Management.w: Deriving the WBS from the PBS ensures the work planned maps directly to the deliverables required, reducing the chance of missed scope.

Scope Management.q: A team switches from a linear to an iterative approach. What should they expect to change about scope management?
o: Scope will now be locked permanently at the start
Scope will be decided solely by the project sponsor
Scope will now be reviewed and adjusted each cycle
Scope will no longer need any prioritisation
Scope Management.w: Moving to iterative delivery means scope is reviewed and reprioritised in each cycle rather than fixed once.

Scope Management.q: When is a responsibility assignment matrix (RAM) most useful during a project?
o: When defining the project's overall scope and its schedule
When conducting the project's lessons learned review at closure
When assigning clear ownership of deliverables and decision-making
When establishing the communication channels with stakeholders
Scope Management.w: The RAM is most valuable when ownership and accountability for deliverables and decisions must be made explicit.

Scope Management.q: An auditor physically checks delivered products against the configuration records to confirm they match. Which activity is this?
o: Verification audit
Status accounting
Configuration identification
Configuration planning
Scope Management.w: A verification audit confirms that the recorded configuration matches the actual products, checking the records are accurate.

Scope Management.q: An agile team reviews scope at the start of each sprint and updates priorities from user feedback. How does this reflect iterative scope management?
o: The deliverables are set upfront and reviewed only monthly
The product evolves through ongoing review and stakeholder input
The team proceeds without defining any scope at all
The scope is fixed at the start and is never revisited
Scope Management.w: In iterative projects the scope evolves as work progresses, guided by continual review and stakeholder feedback.

Scope Management.q: A linear project finalised its scope during the concept phase. What is the likely consequence when new requirements emerge during delivery?
o: The change will be managed through strict change control
The scope will be re-planned freely at every stage
The change will be absorbed into the work automatically
The team will simply reprioritise its next sprint
Scope Management.w: Linear projects fix scope early, so new requirements arising later are handled through a formal, strictly controlled change process.

Scope Management.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between change control and configuration management?
o: They are the same process operating under two different names
Change control governs whether changes happen; configuration management maintains records of items and versions
Configuration management authorises changes; change control audits the schedule
Both processes apply only after the project has been formally closed
Scope Management.w: Change control decides on changes while configuration management keeps the record of controlled items and their versions; the two are complementary.

Scope Management.q: Why does a linear life cycle generally require tighter scope control than an iterative one?
o: Because it welcomes unlimited change at any point in delivery
Because it has no defined deliverables that need protecting
Because its baseline is fixed early, so change disrupts the plan
Because scope is only ever agreed after delivery has ended
Scope Management.w: A linear baseline is set early, so uncontrolled change threatens the plan and demands rigorous control.

Scope Management.q: In a linear project, when is the scope of work normally fixed?
o: Early on, and then controlled through formal change control
Only after the product has been handed over
Continuously throughout each delivery cycle
At the very end, once all work is complete
Scope Management.w: Linear projects define scope early and thereafter manage any changes through formal change control.

Scope Management.q: What does version control help to ensure within the configuration management process?
o: That outdated documents are clearly identified and replaced
That the project's tasks are placed in the correct sequence
That the project's procurement rules are properly followed
That the entries in the risk register are correctly prioritised
Scope Management.w: Version control ensures that only the latest approved versions of documents and products are in use, and older versions are withdrawn.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following best explains the distinction between change control and configuration management?
o: Change control evaluates proposed changes, and configuration management ensures approved changes are correctly implemented
Change control tracks scheduling milestones, and configuration management carries out product testing
Change control plans the use of resources, and configuration management defines the project team's roles
Change control manages procurement, and configuration management handles the project's budget reporting
Scope Management.w: Change control is the gatekeeper that assesses and approves changes; configuration management ensures approved changes are applied and maintained.

Scope Management.q: A developer implements a change to a deliverable before it has been reviewed or authorised. Which stage of the change control process has been omitted?
o: Post-implementation review
Benefits review
Configuration audit
Impact assessment
Scope Management.w: Impact assessment evaluates the effect of a proposed change on time, cost, quality and risk before it can be approved and implemented.

Scope Management.q: A project manager notices discrepancies between the latest deliverable and the configuration baseline. Which process should be reviewed first?
o: Procurement management
Scheduling control
Communication planning
Configuration management
Scope Management.w: Configuration management keeps deliverables aligned with the current approved baseline, so it should be reviewed when discrepancies appear.

Scope Management.q: Why are both change control and configuration management needed together in scope management?
o: To evaluate and approve changes and then maintain them in the outputs
To prevent any changes at all from being made to the project
To provide the project's budget approval and procurement sign-off
To handle only the external modifications made to contracts
Scope Management.w: Change control evaluates and approves changes, while configuration management ensures those approved changes are correctly applied and maintained.

Scope Management.q: An audit confirms that versioning rules were followed and only approved changes were made. What does this outcome confirm?
o: That all of the planned benefits have been realised
That the stakeholder requirements have changed
That the agreed project baseline has since changed
That configuration control and verification were effective
Scope Management.w: A satisfactory audit demonstrates that changes were properly controlled and that items conform to their approved configuration.

Scope Management.q: Why is it important to carry out regular configuration audits during a project?
o: To ensure that all project work is completed ahead of schedule
To confirm that only authorised changes have been implemented and recorded
To speed up the procurement processes used by the project
To reduce the number of team members the project requires
Scope Management.w: Configuration audits verify that only authorised changes have been made and that the deliverables and records match the approved configuration.

Scope Management.q: A project manager wants to show how the project's work is distributed across the organisation's departments and teams. Which tool suits this?
o: A cost breakdown structure
A responsibility assignment matrix
A product breakdown structure
An organisational breakdown structure
Scope Management.w: An OBS structures the project's people resources into the organisational units responsible for the work.

Scope Management.q: A client requests an urgent change to a critical deliverable. What should the project manager do first?
o: Implement the change straight away to meet expectations
Include the change within the next routine progress report
Email the project team and proceed with it immediately
Raise and assess a change request through the formal procedure
Scope Management.w: Every change, however urgent, is raised and assessed through the formal change control procedure so its impact is understood before any decision.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following is not normally an activity within the configuration management process?
o: Status accounting
Configuration procurement
Configuration identification
Configuration planning
Scope Management.w: Procurement is not part of configuration management; the recognised activities include planning, identification, control, status accounting and verification.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following best explains how a product breakdown structure supports scope definition?
o: It lists all stakeholders and their communication preferences
It defines the product deliverables in a structured hierarchy
It records the planned and actual cost of each activity
It organises the reporting structure of the project team
Scope Management.w: The PBS sets out the product's deliverables in a structured hierarchy, giving a clear understanding of the required scope.

Scope Management.q: A deliverable is altered without going through the change control process. What is the most likely outcome?
o: More efficient approval of the change by the control board
Reduced cost and improved satisfaction among stakeholders
Stronger compliance with the project's quality standards
Increased risk of scope creep and unplanned rework
Scope Management.w: Unauthorised changes bypass assessment of their impact, leading to scope creep, misalignment with the baseline and likely rework.

Scope Management.q: A work breakdown structure contains items such as 'code user interface' and 'test module'. What does this structure help to define?
o: The procurement process for the external suppliers
The financial framework underpinning the project
The structure of the client's own organisation
The work required to produce each project deliverable
Scope Management.w: The WBS breaks the scope into the work required to complete each deliverable, expressed as manageable work packages.

Scope Management.q: When comparing the two, which pairing correctly matches each structure to what it represents?
o: PBS = responsibilities; WBS = risks
PBS = activities; WBS = products
PBS = deliverables; WBS = the work to create them
PBS = costs; WBS = timescales
Scope Management.w: A PBS represents the deliverables (products), whereas a WBS represents the work required to create those deliverables.

Scope Management.q: A team implemented a change straight after it was requested, without evaluating its effect on cost, time and quality. Which stage was skipped?
o: Closing the completed project
Impact assessment of the proposed change
Implementing the approved change
Logging the initial change request
Scope Management.w: Implementing straight after the request skipped the impact assessment stage, where effects on cost, time and quality are evaluated before a decision.

Scope Management.q: Which process ensures that a project delivers only the work required to meet its objectives?
o: Cost management
Change control
Stakeholder management
Scope management
Scope Management.w: Scope management defines and controls the work included in the project so that it delivers only what is necessary to meet its objectives.

Scope Management.q: A configuration audit finds that several different versions of the same document are in active use. Which activity has failed?
o: Configuration identification
Configuration control
Verification audit
Configuration planning
Scope Management.w: Configuration control should prevent unauthorised or duplicate versions from being released and used across the project.

Scope Management.q: Which characteristic of scope management is more typical of iterative than linear projects?
o: A single formal acceptance of scope at project handover
A detailed scope baseline agreed once and rarely altered
Complete avoidance of stakeholder involvement in scope
Flexibility to adjust deliverables in response to regular feedback
Scope Management.w: Iterative scope management is characterised by flexibility to adjust deliverables as feedback arrives.

Scope Management.q: Which document typically captures the details of a proposed scope change before it is formally reviewed?
o: Change request form
Stakeholder matrix
Configuration item log
Communication plan
Scope Management.w: A change request form initiates the process, recording the proposed change and its rationale so it can be assessed and a decision made.

Scope Management.q: At its lowest level, what does a work breakdown structure typically break the work down into?
o: High-level phases only, without further detail
Individual products and their raw materials
Work packages that can be assigned, estimated and controlled
Departments responsible for the project
Scope Management.w: A WBS decomposes work to the level of manageable work packages that can be assigned, estimated, scheduled and controlled.

Scope Management.q: What is the primary focus of configuration management within scope management?
o: Selecting the most suitable procurement route
Estimating the total cost of each work package
Approving or rejecting individual requests for change
Maintaining the integrity and consistency of the project's products
Scope Management.w: Configuration management maintains the integrity and consistency of the project's products and their versions.

Scope Management.q: What is the main difference between a product breakdown structure and a work breakdown structure?
o: The PBS shows the deliverables and the WBS shows the work to create them
The PBS sets the deadlines and the WBS sets the budgets
The PBS shows the work and the WBS shows the associated costs
The PBS supports communication and the WBS supports risk management
Scope Management.w: The PBS defines what the project must produce, while the WBS defines the work needed to produce those deliverables.

Scope Management.q: How does an organisational breakdown structure (OBS) contribute to the successful delivery of a project?
o: It defines the sequence in which project activities will be performed
It sets out the risk responses required to address external threats
It assigns costs to each of the project’s deliverables and work packages
It clarifies reporting relationships and lines of management control within the project
Scope Management.w: An OBS depicts the project’s reporting lines and accountabilities, supporting governance and management control of the work.

Scope Management.q: Which term describes the process that ensures every alteration to scope is evaluated before it is accepted or rejected?
o: Change control
Stakeholder analysis
Resource smoothing
Configuration management
Scope Management.w: Change control ensures each proposed alteration to scope is assessed before a decision is made.

Scope Management.q: A senior stakeholder wants to understand how reporting will work across the project's several teams. Which structure should the project manager refer them to?
o: The product breakdown structure (PBS)
The organisational breakdown structure (OBS)
The work breakdown structure (WBS)
The cost breakdown structure (CBS)
Scope Management.w: The OBS shows reporting lines and how roles fit within the project's organisation, which is exactly what the stakeholder is asking about.

Scope Management.q: Why is a cost breakdown structure (CBS) usually derived from the work breakdown structure (WBS) on a project?
o: Because the WBS identifies the work that then needs to be costed
Because the CBS defines the thresholds for approving scope change
Because the WBS controls how stakeholders are communicated with
Because the CBS sets the reporting line for each work package
Scope Management.w: The WBS defines the work to be done, and the CBS attributes cost estimates to those components, so the two structures align.

Scope Management.q: Before delivery, a sponsor and team use a product breakdown structure to agree exactly what will be produced. What does this most help avoid?
o: Misunderstandings about which deliverables are in scope
The need to schedule any of the work
The requirement to assign any responsibilities
The production of a project management plan
Scope Management.w: Agreeing the deliverables via a PBS creates a shared understanding of scope, reducing later disputes about what is in or out.

Scope Management.q: A project manager wants to organise estimated costs into a hierarchy of categories for budgeting. Which structure suits this?
o: A product breakdown structure
A responsibility assignment matrix
A cost breakdown structure
An organisational breakdown structure
Scope Management.w: A cost breakdown structure organises project costs into a hierarchy of categories, supporting budgeting and cost control.

Scope Management.q: What does configuration management rely on to determine whether a proposed update can be safely implemented?
o: Approval given through the change control process
The project's overall work breakdown structure
The procedures used for escalating project risks
The project's stakeholder map and analysis
Scope Management.w: Configuration management only applies changes that have first been formally assessed and approved through change control.

Scope Management.q: A work breakdown structure is being developed for a software deployment project. What level of detail should it provide?
o: A breakdown of all the work packages needed to complete the deliverables
The roles and responsibilities of each team member
Only the financial costs linked to each task
Only the task names together with their durations
Scope Management.w: The WBS should decompose the total scope into smaller, manageable work packages that capture all the work required.

Scope Management.q: Why is effective scope management essential to the success of a project?
o: It removes the need for any configuration management on the project
It ensures the project will always be delivered within its budget
It guarantees that every project risk will be completely eliminated
It defines and controls what the project will and will not deliver
Scope Management.w: Scope management establishes and controls the boundaries of the work, helping to prevent scope creep and ensuring the agreed outputs are delivered.

Scope Management.q: Why is change control generally less rigid in an iterative life cycle?
o: Because iterative projects avoid producing any documentation
Because scope is expected to evolve throughout delivery
Because testing takes place only at project closure
Because the project budget is fixed from the outset
Scope Management.w: Iterative life cycles anticipate that scope will be refined continuously, so change is handled more flexibly than in linear projects.

Scope Management.q: A sponsor wants the flexibility to refine requirements as user needs emerge. Which life cycle is better suited, and why?
o: Linear, because it freezes the scope right from the start
Iterative, because it removes the need for any planning
Iterative, because it supports evolving scope through continuous feedback
Linear, because it copes best with high levels of uncertainty
Scope Management.w: An iterative life cycle is designed to accommodate changing requirements, allowing scope to evolve through continuous feedback.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following statements best describes the function of an organisational breakdown structure (OBS)?
o: It sets out the required packages of work in a hierarchy
It assigns a specific cost to each member of the team
It shows the structure of roles and reporting within the project
It defines the sequence in which tasks are to be delivered
Scope Management.w: An OBS is a hierarchical view of how the project is organised, showing roles and who reports to whom.

Scope Management.q: In a RACI responsibility assignment matrix, what does designating a person as 'accountable' for a task signify?
o: They are ultimately answerable for the task's completion, though others may do the work
They physically carry out every element of the task themselves
They are merely kept informed once the task has been completed
They are consulted for an opinion but hold no further involvement
Scope Management.w: In RACI, the accountable person is ultimately answerable for the task, even though responsible parties may perform the work.

Scope Management.q: A linear project treats a scope change as an exception requiring formal approval. Why does this differ from an iterative approach?
o: Because iterative projects fix all requirements upfront
Because linear projects have no defined scope at all
Because iterative projects never allow any scope changes
Because iterative projects expect scope to evolve cycle by cycle
Scope Management.w: Iterative delivery anticipates evolving scope, so change is routine rather than an exception.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following correctly lists the main activities of a typical configuration management process?
o: Initiation, planning, execution, monitoring and closure
Planning, identification, control, status accounting and verification audit
Concept, definition, deployment, transition and benefits
Identification, analysis, response, review and closure
Scope Management.w: A typical configuration management process comprises planning, identification, control, status accounting and verification audit.

Scope Management.q: In an iterative project, which mechanism is most commonly used to manage what gets built next?
o: A locked scope baseline signed at initiation
A fixed work breakdown never revisited after concept
A prioritised, evolving backlog reviewed each cycle
A single change request covering the whole project
Scope Management.w: Iterative scope is managed through a prioritised backlog that is reviewed and reordered each cycle.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is developing a cost breakdown structure (CBS) for a project. What is the main purpose of this structure?
o: To record the issues and lessons learned during delivery
To break the deliverables down into manageable packages of work
To set out the reporting lines that exist between team members
To identify and track the costs of the project's individual components
Scope Management.w: A CBS breaks the project's costs down against its components, giving the project manager a structured basis for budgeting and cost control.

Scope Management.q: A team uses a work breakdown structure to define tasks and a product breakdown structure to define deliverables. What is a key benefit of using both?
o: They remove the need to maintain a stakeholder register
They reduce the need for a procurement process
They provide a legal framework for engaging suppliers
They link the work required to the outputs that are expected
Scope Management.w: Using both structures ensures the planned work is directly connected to the agreed outputs the project must deliver.

Scope Management.q: During the change control process, what is the main purpose of the impact assessment stage?
o: To implement the change as quickly as possible
To understand the effect on time, cost, scope and quality before deciding
To remove the change from the register permanently
To close any related issues automatically
Scope Management.w: Impact assessment evaluates the consequences on time, cost, scope and quality so an informed authorisation decision can be made.

Scope Management.q: When defining scope management for a project, which of the following best describes what it is chiefly concerned with?
o: The behavioural roles adopted by the individual members of the team
The methods and channels used to communicate with the stakeholders
The totality of outputs, outcomes and work required by the project
The tolerances that are applied to the project's cost estimates
Scope Management.w: Scope covers the totality of the outputs, outcomes and work required; managing it means defining and controlling that whole.

Scope Management.q: Why does the combined use of change control and configuration management help prevent unauthorised versions of a deliverable?
o: Changes are implemented immediately and reviewed only at project closure
Only approved changes are made, and every resulting version is recorded and traceable
Approval authority is delegated to whoever raises the change request
Version records replace the need to assess the impact of any change
Scope Management.w: Together they ensure changes are authorised before implementation and that every version is controlled and traceable, preventing uncontrolled copies.

Scope Management.q: A configuration log records the current status of each controlled item. Which configuration management activity does this represent?
o: Status accounting
Configuration control
Configuration identification
Configuration planning
Scope Management.w: Status accounting keeps a traceable record of the status of every configuration item and the changes made to it.

Scope Management.q: How does configuration management support the change control process when a request is being assessed?
o: By identifying which configuration items the proposed change would affect
By deciding whether the change should be approved or rejected
By selecting the supplier who will implement the change
By setting the overall budget available for changes
