Scope Management.w: Configuration records show which items a change would affect, informing the impact assessment that supports the change control decision.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following is true of a responsibility assignment matrix (RAM)?
o: It defines the physical components of the final product
It determines the order of the project's activities
It links organisational roles to the project's tasks
It sets the level of influence held by each stakeholder
Scope Management.w: A RAM matches roles from the OBS to the tasks in the WBS, ensuring each activity has clearly assigned responsibility.

Scope Management.q: Scope management is often said to have two core activities. Which pair best describes them?
o: Defining the required work, then controlling changes to it
Estimating the budget, then reporting the actual spend
Identifying the risks, then assigning owners to each
Scheduling the work, then levelling the resources across it
Scope Management.w: Scope management first defines the work required and then controls changes to it; the distractors describe scheduling, cost and risk activities.

Scope Management.q: Which process ensures that changes to scope are formally approved so they do not adversely affect quality or budget?
o: Risk escalation
Resource allocation
Team briefing
Change control
Scope Management.w: Change control assesses, authorises and integrates proposed changes so the impact on quality, cost and time is controlled.

Scope Management.q: How does an organisational breakdown structure (OBS) support role clarity within a project team?
o: By setting out the project's configuration control procedures
By identifying the deliverables that the project must produce
By showing how responsibilities are distributed through the organisation
By detailing the project's individual financial cost centres
Scope Management.w: The OBS clarifies who holds responsibility and who reports to whom, improving transparency of roles across the team.

Scope Management.q: During testing a stakeholder suggests altering the interface, and the team updates the prototype without formal approval. What risk does this pose?
o: It reduces the project's reliance on captured lessons learned
It improves team morale but delays the realisation of benefits
It helps the team to finalise the configuration log early
It may cause scope creep and misalignment with the baseline
Scope Management.w: Changing a product without change control means the impact is not assessed, risking scope creep and divergence from the agreed baseline.

Scope Management.q: During configuration management, which activity assigns a unique reference to each item so that it can be tracked individually?
o: Status accounting
Verification audit
Identification
Configuration control
Scope Management.w: Identification defines the configuration items and gives each a unique reference so it can be tracked throughout the project.

Scope Management.q: Midway through delivery a client requests several enhancements to the agreed product. What should the project manager do first?
o: Add the changes into the next stage of work in order to save time
Amend the configuration records directly to reflect the new requirements
Update the work breakdown structure and begin the changes straight away
Submit a formal change request so the impact can be assessed and reviewed
Scope Management.w: Under change control, a formal change request must be raised and its impact assessed and approved before any change is implemented.

Scope Management.q: A change request has just been logged on a project. What is the next stage in a typical change control process?
o: Update the risk register and take no further action
Assess the impact of the proposed change
Immediately implement the change to save time
Close the project's business case
Scope Management.w: After a change is logged, its impact on time, cost, scope and quality is assessed before any decision to authorise it.

Scope Management.q: An IT team delivers in two-week sprints, and the client requests changes after each review. What does this indicate about scope?
o: Scope is tightly fixed at the beginning of the project
Scope is determined only at the close of the project
Scope is evolving continuously through collaboration
Scope is restricted to the original deliverables only
Scope Management.w: This is iterative scope management, in which requirements evolve through continuous collaboration, review and feedback.

Scope Management.q: A review finds a project failed to deliver key elements because scope was poorly controlled. Which process should have prevented this?
o: Scope management
Resource scheduling
Communication planning
Risk analysis
Scope Management.w: Scope management ensures that all required deliverables are identified, defined and controlled throughout the project.

Scope Management.q: A client requests a change to a configured product, and it must be assessed and approved before work begins. Which process provides this formal evaluation?
o: Stakeholder engagement
Risk management
Change control
Scope definition
Scope Management.w: Change control provides the formal route for assessing and approving or rejecting a change before it affects any configuration items.

Scope Management.q: A cost breakdown structure (CBS) most directly supports which of the following financial activities on a project?
o: Setting out the responsibilities held by each stakeholder
Assigning individual tasks to named members of the team
Estimating, budgeting and monitoring the project's costs
Monitoring the project's risks and its open issues
Scope Management.w: A CBS provides a structured breakdown of cost that underpins estimating, budgeting and ongoing cost monitoring for control.

Scope Management.q: How is scope typically handled in an iterative project compared with a linear one?
o: It is defined only after delivery finishes
It is frozen at the outset and never revisited
It is set by suppliers rather than the project team
It is refined progressively as each iteration is reviewed
Scope Management.w: Iterative scope is refined cycle by cycle in response to review and feedback, unlike a fixed linear baseline.

Scope Management.q: While reviewing the configuration log, a project support officer finds two conflicting versions of a technical specification. Which configuration process has most likely failed?
o: Resource levelling
Risk mitigation
Benefits tracking
Version control
Scope Management.w: Version control ensures a single current, approved version is in use, so conflicting versions point to a failure of this control.

Scope Management.q: Which statement correctly matches a breakdown tool to its use?
o: The RAM aggregates all project costs into reportable categories
The OBS lists the risks that could affect project delivery
The CBS structures project costs, while the OBS structures the teams
The CBS assigns responsibilities for each project work package
Scope Management.w: The CBS organises costs and the OBS organises the people resources, each serving a distinct planning purpose.

Scope Management.q: A sponsor asks for proof that recent product updates match the approved changes. Which configuration management records should be provided?
o: The version history and the configuration log
The stakeholder matrix and the project's RAID log
The updated work and organisational breakdown structures
The lessons learned report and the project audit plan
Scope Management.w: Version histories and the configuration log evidence that approved changes were tracked and correctly implemented in the product.

Scope Management.q: How do change control and configuration management typically work together when a change is proposed?
o: Configuration management approves the change and change control disposes of old items
Both processes independently decide whether the change should proceed
Change control authorises the change and configuration management records the resulting versions
Change control tracks version history while configuration management judges the request
Scope Management.w: Change control decides whether a change is authorised; configuration management then records and controls the versions that result.

Scope Management.q: How do a product breakdown structure and a work breakdown structure support scope definition when used together?
o: They set out the project's risks and outstanding issues
They identify the communication channels and reporting lines
They link the deliverables to the work required to produce them
They record the financial transactions made for the stakeholders
Scope Management.w: Together the PBS and WBS connect what must be delivered to the work required to deliver it, giving a complete view of scope.

Scope Management.q: Which configuration management activity defines how items will be controlled and versioned throughout a project?
o: Configuration planning
Configuration identification
Status accounting
Verification audit
Scope Management.w: Configuration planning sets out the framework, roles and procedures for how configuration items will be managed across the project.

Scope Management.q: Which of the following is a characteristic of scope management in a linear project?
o: Frequent reprioritisation of user stories each cycle
Continuous negotiation of scope with the stakeholders
Formal control of changes once the initial scope is defined
Dynamic delivery of requirements as they evolve
Scope Management.w: Linear projects define scope early and rely on formal change control to evaluate and manage any changes thereafter.

Scope Management.q: A developer works from an outdated version of a requirements document. Which configuration management activity has failed?
o: Verification audit
Status accounting
Configuration identification
Configuration planning
Scope Management.w: Status accounting maintains and communicates the current status of items; when it fails, out-of-date versions are used in error.

Communication.q: What is a disadvantage of using physical noticeboards for communication on a project?
o: They provide real-time chat features for participants
They rely on people being present in person to see updates
They can be edited and updated remotely with ease
They automatically create a backup of their content
Communication.w: Physical noticeboards are static and only reach those who can access them in person.

Communication.q: Under the communication plan, status updates are issued every Monday by 10 a.m. What does this help the project manager achieve?
o: Freedom from attending project governance meetings
Predictable updates that build stakeholder confidence
Automatic generation of procurement requests
The removal of any need to produce progress reports
Communication.w: Predictable, scheduled updates keep stakeholders informed and build confidence in how the project is being controlled.

Communication.q: Which of the following statements best defines communication in the context of a project?
o: The process of completing and filing project documentation
A control activity used only during the planning phase
The exchange of information between people to reach shared understanding
The transfer of technical data solely to the project sponsor
Communication.w: Communication in projects is the exchange of information to achieve shared understanding and alignment among those involved.

Communication.q: What is a major risk of using unstructured methods such as instant messaging for decisions?
o: They ensure the team complies with governance requirements
They leave no audit trail to trace how decisions were made
They improve the clarity of the project's agreed scope
They enforce formal stakeholder approval of every decision
Communication.w: Informal chats often bypass documentation, making it difficult to trace how and why decisions were taken.

Communication.q: Which of the following is a potential drawback of virtual communication methods?
o: They provide the same rich body-language cues as meeting in person
They remove every difficulty associated with differing time zones
They always ensure the confidentiality of shared information
They can suffer technical problems and reduced personal connection
Communication.w: Virtual tools can create barriers through technical limitations and weaker non-verbal engagement.

Communication.q: What is a recognised disadvantage of physical, paper-based communication on a project?
o: It promotes instant feedback between the sender and the recipient
It is ideally suited to sending urgent updates at short notice
It is difficult to update and distribute quickly when things change
It is the most secure communication option in every situation
Communication.w: Paper-based communication is slow to amend and circulate, which is a disadvantage in a fast-changing project environment.

Communication.q: What is a major benefit of using virtual communication tools on a project?
o: They guarantee strong cohesion among all team members
They prevent technical problems from disrupting the project
They enable collaboration across different locations and time zones
They remove the need to engage with project stakeholders
Communication.w: Virtual communication allows geographically dispersed teams to collaborate effectively regardless of location.

Communication.q: Why can virtual tools such as shared whiteboards be advantageous for collaborative planning?
o: They remove the need to keep any project documentation
They are inherently more secure than meeting in person
They prevent disagreement between the project's stakeholders
They allow asynchronous contributions from remote participants
Communication.w: Shared online tools support collaboration even when participants are not all available at the same time.

Communication.q: What is a key limitation of using email as a communication method?
o: It is the most suitable channel for urgent decision-making
It is not actually a written form of communication
It lacks tone and non-verbal cues, so it can be misread
It always ensures an immediate two-way exchange of views
Communication.w: Emails can be misinterpreted because they carry no tone of voice or body language.

Communication.q: External stakeholders report that they are not receiving relevant project information. Which document should the project manager review first?
o: The risk register's list of threats and their owners
The quality plan's checklists and acceptance criteria
The communication plan's stakeholder list and distribution schedule
The benefits register's expected outcomes and measures
Communication.w: The communication plan defines who should receive which information and when, so its stakeholder mapping and schedule are the first thing to check.

Communication.q: A project manager must brief forty stakeholders in different offices within an hour. Which method offers the strongest advantage here?
o: A virtual broadcast or video conference to all of them
A handwritten memo pinned to each noticeboard
A printed newsletter posted to each office
A one-to-one face-to-face meeting with each person
Communication.w: A virtual broadcast reaches many dispersed stakeholders simultaneously and quickly, its key advantage over the alternatives.

Communication.q: Before delivering a major milestone presentation, why would a project manager consult the communication plan?
o: To review the supplier's procurement performance
To approve an outstanding change request to scope
To confirm the audience, delivery method and timing of the update
To reassess the risk thresholds and escalation triggers
Communication.w: The communication plan defines the who, what, how and when of key information sharing, so it confirms how the milestone update should be delivered.

Communication.q: Why can face-to-face communication be less effective in certain project delivery environments?
o: It provides too much written documentation for the team
It can be impractical for dispersed teams or tight schedules
It excludes body language from the exchange of information
It removes the need to consider cultural sensitivities
Communication.w: For geographically dispersed or fast-moving projects, arranging in-person meetings can be costly and time-consuming.

Communication.q: How does a communication plan help ensure stakeholders receive consistent information even when different team members send updates?
o: It requires the project manager personally to send every single message
It replaces the need for a project schedule during delivery
It prevents team members from ever contacting stakeholders directly
It defines the agreed messages, channels and timing that everyone follows
Communication.w: By defining agreed messages, channels and timing, the plan keeps information consistent regardless of which team member issues it.

Communication.q: A plan lists the executive board against a monthly summary report. Which attribute of the communication is this defining?
o: The frequency
The medium
The audience
The sender
Communication.w: Naming the executive board as the group to receive the report defines the audience for that communication.

Communication.q: What is a risk of stakeholders relying solely on written communication such as reports?
o: Reports are the ideal channel for resolving emotional conflict
Reports encourage immediate two-way dialogue between parties
Reports may be misinterpreted or ignored without discussion
Reports remove all ambiguity as soon as they are issued
Communication.w: Written reports can be overlooked or misunderstood, particularly where there is no chance to seek clarification.

Communication.q: A project holds a face-to-face kick-off meeting with key stakeholders. What is a genuine advantage of this approach?
o: It removes the need for any later follow-up communication
It lowers the travel and venue costs for the project
It speeds up the project's procurement decisions
It helps build trust and stronger relationships early on
Communication.w: Face-to-face interaction helps build relationships, trust and alignment at the start of a project.

Communication.q: A communication plan entry reads: 'monthly, by email'. Which two attributes of the communication does this define?
o: Frequency and medium
Audience and purpose
Sender and audience
Purpose and frequency
Communication.w: 'Monthly' defines the frequency of the communication and 'by email' defines its medium.

Communication.q: Halfway through a critical online review, the connection repeatedly drops out. Which disadvantage of virtual communication does this show?
o: It always takes far longer than a face-to-face meeting
It leaves no possibility of recording the session
It depends on reliable technology and stable connectivity
It can never involve more than two participants
Communication.w: Virtual communication depends on reliable technology and connectivity; technical failures can disrupt or degrade the exchange.

Communication.q: Which communication method best allows immediate two-way feedback and interpretation of tone and body language?
o: Posting to a shared online drive
Holding a face-to-face meeting
Distributing a printed newsletter
Exchanging threads of email
Communication.w: Face-to-face communication is the richest method, providing direct dialogue and non-verbal cues.

Communication.q: What is a benefit of using instant-messaging platforms within a project team?
o: They support fast, informal exchanges that aid quick decisions
They remove the need for the team to hold any meetings
They create a formal, legally binding record of decisions
They eliminate the difficulties caused by differing time zones
Communication.w: Instant messaging enables rapid, informal collaboration, which is useful for fast-moving issues.

Communication.q: Which of the following would a communication plan typically specify about each message?
o: The exact cost of producing each report
The project's detailed technical specification
The intended audience for the message
The supplier's contractual penalties
Communication.w: A communication plan defines who each message is for, alongside its content, method, frequency and responsibility.

Communication.q: Which of the following is most likely to support effective communication on a project?
o: Delaying all project updates until the project reaches closure
Engaging stakeholders and delivering consistent, timely messages
Changing the communication approach at frequent intervals
Giving the delivery team only verbal instructions
Communication.w: Effective communication depends on engaging stakeholders and sharing consistent, timely information.

Communication.q: A communication plan records why each message is sent, such as 'to maintain sponsor confidence'. Which attribute is this?
o: The purpose of the communication
The frequency of the communication
The medium of the communication
The recipient of the communication
Communication.w: Recording the reason a message is sent defines its purpose within the communication plan.

Communication.q: A key decision made verbally in a corridor is later disputed because nobody wrote it down. Which drawback of informal verbal communication is shown?
o: It reaches too many recipients at once
It is too slow for urgent matters
It often leaves no permanent record
It relies entirely on stable technology
Communication.w: Informal verbal communication frequently leaves no documented record, making agreements hard to confirm later.

Communication.q: On a project, what distinguishes genuine communication from merely transmitting information to a group of recipients?
o: The seniority of the person sending the message
The volume of information contained in the message
The choice of digital rather than printed channels
The receiver's feedback confirming the message is understood
Communication.w: Feedback that confirms the message has been understood turns one-way transmission into genuine, effective communication.

Communication.q: Which of the following would you least expect to find within a project communication plan?
o: The format and frequency of routine status reports
A record of decisions already taken on the project
The preferred communication channel for each stakeholder
The individuals responsible for issuing project updates
Communication.w: A communication plan is a forward-looking tool; a record of decisions already taken belongs in a separate decision log.

Communication.q: A project manager is drafting a communication plan. Which content should it include to ensure messages reach the right people?
o: The organisational charts of unrelated internal departments
The licence terms of the software used on the project
Stakeholders, methods, frequency and communication responsibilities
The catering preferences for the project's regular meetings
Communication.w: A communication plan sets out who receives information, how and when it is shared, and who is responsible for sharing it.

Communication.q: A stakeholder does not receive project updates because of a gap in the communication plan. What was most likely left out?
o: The earned value baseline agreed for the project
The storage location of the archived project data
The stakeholder's preferred method and required frequency
The project's formal change control process
Communication.w: A communication plan specifies who receives what information, when and how, so omitting these details can create gaps.

Communication.q: What is a common disadvantage of relying on face-to-face communication in a project?
o: It can incur higher costs through travel and scheduling
It is too formal to be used in iterative environments
It limits the opportunities for participants to give feedback
It reduces the level of trust between team members
Communication.w: Although effective for building trust, face-to-face communication can be costly and time-consuming to arrange.

Communication.q: A communication model describes a sender, a message, a medium and a receiver. Which further element makes it effective?
o: A more senior sender issuing the message
A longer, more detailed written message
Feedback confirming the message has been understood
A larger distribution list for the message
Communication.w: Feedback closes the loop between sender and receiver, confirming shared understanding and making communication effective.

Communication.q: Specifying that updates will be shared 'via video call' in a communication plan defines which attribute?
o: The frequency of the update
The owner of the update
The medium of the update
The audience of the update
Communication.w: Stating the channel, such as a video call, defines the medium or method of communication within the plan.

Communication.q: A team uses a RACI matrix and a stakeholder register to inform its communication plan. What benefit does this bring?
o: Roles and responsibilities are reflected in tailored communication
The overall project schedule is noticeably shortened
Procurement is then able to proceed without any oversight
The need to carry out risk assessments is removed
Communication.w: Drawing on a RACI matrix and stakeholder register ensures each communication is directed to the right person in the most appropriate way.

Communication.q: How does a communication plan help a project manager direct communication effort where it is most needed?
o: By fixing the project scope so that no updates are required
By removing the need to report progress to the sponsor at all
By requiring every stakeholder to receive identical daily updates
By matching the type and frequency of information to each audience's needs
Communication.w: The plan matches information type and frequency to each audience, so the project manager focuses communication effort where it is most needed.

Communication.q: What advantage does a physical display board in a shared site office offer a co-located project team?
o: It captures the tone and body language of the author
It provides a searchable digital archive of all the messages
It provides constant, at-a-glance visibility of key information to everyone present
It automatically notifies remote members of every update
Communication.w: A physical display gives everyone in the shared space continuous, at-a-glance access to key project information.

Communication.q: Why is face-to-face communication often the most suitable method for delivering sensitive or difficult news to a stakeholder?
o: It allows tone, empathy and immediate reassurance to be conveyed in person
It creates a permanent written record of exactly what was said
It reaches large, geographically dispersed audiences at the lowest cost
It removes the need to follow the conversation up afterwards
Communication.w: Face-to-face communication conveys tone and body language and allows immediate, empathetic two-way response, suiting sensitive messages.

Communication.q: A contract must be signed and kept as lasting evidence of what both parties agreed. Which method best suits this?
o: A brief telephone call
A live video conference
A physical, printed document
An instant-messaging chat
Communication.w: A physical, printed document provides a durable, signable record, an advantage where formal evidence of agreement is required.

Communication.q: What is a common issue with relying solely on virtual communication platforms?
o: They are vulnerable to internet outages or system failures
They remove the need for any project documentation
They function without issue in every geographic region
They require no training for people to use them
Communication.w: Poor connectivity or system failures can disrupt communication entirely when it depends only on virtual platforms.

Communication.q: Why does having an agreed communication plan actually save the project manager effort during the delivery of a project?
o: It automatically resolves all of the disagreements between stakeholders
It removes the need to maintain a detailed underlying schedule
It eliminates every one of the project's risks well in advance
Communication decisions are agreed once rather than repeated each time
Communication.w: With communications agreed in advance, the project manager avoids reconsidering who, what, when and how for each message, saving effort.

Communication.q: What is regarded as the primary objective of communication within a project?
o: To remove the need for formal project documentation
To ensure that all identified project risks are mitigated
To support shared understanding among the project's stakeholders
To reduce the total number of meetings that are held
Communication.w: The purpose of communication is to ensure that everyone involved understands the relevant information and expectations.

Communication.q: What advantage does video conferencing offer when compared with a voice-only call?
o: It removes the possibility of any technical problems arising
It is more formal and removes the need for a meeting agenda
It guarantees that no message can ever be misinterpreted
It conveys visual cues such as facial expressions and gestures
Communication.w: Video adds non-verbal context to a conversation, helping to clarify tone and intent.

Communication.q: What is a key benefit of summarising a verbal discussion in a follow-up email?
o: It guarantees the eventual success of the whole project
It removes the need for the original discussion to take place
It removes every possibility of the message being misread
It provides a record of what was agreed and the next steps
Communication.w: A written summary creates a record and reinforces shared understanding of what was agreed verbally.

Communication.q: Two departments received different updates and the sponsor asks why. How does the communication plan help the project manager respond?
o: It requires every department to receive identical content
It prevents the two departments from working together
It removes the manager's need to answer such questions
It records how communications were tailored and the reasons why
Communication.w: The plan documents who receives which information and why, allowing variations in the communication approach to be justified.

Communication.q: What is a benefit of using email for communication on a project?
o: It is always a fully secure and completely private channel
It provides a written trail that can be referred to later
It functions without any need for an internet connection
It removes the need to hold project meetings altogether
Communication.w: Email creates an auditable written record that is easy to store and refer back to throughout the project.

Communication.q: A manager defines communication as sending a message from sender to receiver 'with feedback'. Why is the feedback element important?
o: It confirms the receiver has received and understood the message
It formally records the message within the communication plan
It sets out the agreed scope for the project's deliverables
It introduces the technical terminology the team will use
Communication.w: Feedback confirms that the message has been received and understood, which is central to effective communication.

Communication.q: Which advantage does a recorded virtual meeting offer that a face-to-face meeting usually does not?
o: It removes any possibility of a technical failure
It guarantees immediate emotional reassurance to all
It can be replayed later by those who could not attend
It always conveys body language much more clearly
Communication.w: A recorded virtual meeting can be stored and replayed, giving absent members access to the discussion later.

Communication.q: What is a limitation of virtual communication methods when engaging project stakeholders?
o: It always guarantees full understanding of the message
It allows the physical handover of deliverables in person
It supports the same rich non-verbal cues as being present
It can reduce emotional connection and weaken rapport
Communication.w: Virtual settings can hinder relationship-building because of reduced physical presence and informal interaction.

Communication.q: Which of the following is most likely to be included in a project communication plan?
o: A list of the sponsors of previous, unrelated projects
Escalation routes for unresolved communication issues
The individual salaries of the project team members
The technical hardware specifications of the deliverables
Communication.w: A communication plan commonly sets out how communication issues are escalated if they cannot be resolved.

Communication.q: In a fast-paced project with several stakeholder groups, what benefit does a communication plan provide?
o: It removes the need to carry out any risk management
It maps who needs what, keeping communication relevant and manageable
It guarantees that all communication happens in real time
It automatically prevents any changes to project scope
Communication.w: A good plan helps the project manager manage the volume and relevance of communication across diverse stakeholder groups.

Communication.q: Which of the following is the weakest description of communication in a project setting?
o: A process aimed at building shared understanding
An exchange of information involving feedback
A two-way flow between sender and receiver
A one-off transmission that needs no confirmation
Communication.w: Communication requires feedback and shared understanding, so a one-way transmission needing no confirmation is the weakest description.

Communication.q: A project posts updates only on a physical noticeboard, and remote staff never see them. Which disadvantage of this method does this reveal?
o: It reaches only those physically present
It provides no permanent written record
It is far too fast for considered messages
It prevents any interpretation of tone
Communication.w: Physical, paper-based communication only reaches people at the location, excluding remote or dispersed stakeholders.

Communication.q: What benefit does a communication plan provide when conflict arises from misunderstood expectations?
o: It provides an agreed record of communication responsibilities
It guarantees that every team member is satisfied
It delays resolving the matter until project closure
It removes the need to involve stakeholders at all
Communication.w: Documented communication methods and responsibilities reduce ambiguity and provide a reference point that supports conflict resolution.

Communication.q: A project manager lists each recipient, message, channel and timing in a communication plan. Which further detail should be added?
o: The detailed critical path of the schedule
Who is responsible for issuing each communication
The project's complete cost breakdown
The full risk register scoring
Communication.w: A communication plan should also record who is responsible for issuing each communication, alongside recipient, message, channel and timing.

Communication.q: What is an advantage of using physical, paper-based communication in certain project environments?
o: It prevents any form of miscommunication from occurring
It gives a tangible, lasting record that does not depend on technology
It is always the quickest way to distribute project information
It guarantees that recipients will actually read the information
Communication.w: Physical communication provides a reliable, permanent record in environments where technology access is limited.

Communication.q: A communication plan helps the project manager manage stakeholder expectations during delivery mainly because it does which of the following?
o: It fixes the scope so that no further changes can ever occur
It sets out clearly what will be communicated, to whom and how often
It guarantees that all stakeholders will actively support the project
It removes the need to record any of the project's risks
Communication.w: By defining what is communicated, to whom and how frequently, the plan sets consistent expectations and reduces surprises for stakeholders.

Communication.q: What is a key benefit of a communication plan to the project manager?
o: It prevents any conflict from arising within the team
It ensures consistent, structured messaging reaches the right people
It guarantees that the project will be delivered successfully
It removes the need to maintain any project documentation
Communication.w: A communication plan helps deliver the right message, to the right people, at the right time in a consistent format.

Communication.q: Two team members carried out a task differently after a briefing because neither confirmed what was meant. Which aspect of communication failed?
o: There was no feedback to confirm shared understanding
The message was too short to be archived
The message was sent to too many recipients
The wrong communication medium was chosen
Communication.w: Without feedback to confirm shared understanding, the message was interpreted differently, so the communication was not effective.

Communication.q: How does a communication plan help to reduce misunderstandings on a project?
o: By reducing the amount of stakeholder engagement needed
By clarifying who communicates what, when and how
By transferring all communication tasks to suppliers
By restricting the team to informal conversations only
Communication.w: Clear responsibilities and defined channels support accurate, consistent communication throughout the project.

Communication.q: For a quick decision needing input from team members across three time zones, which method offers the greatest advantage?
o: A physical noticeboard in the site office
A single face-to-face meeting at head office
A virtual meeting or video conference
A printed memo posted to each location
Communication.w: Virtual methods connect geographically dispersed members quickly and cheaply, without the time and cost of bringing everyone together in person.

Communication.q: How does a communication plan help when several stakeholder groups with differing needs are involved?
o: It allows senior leadership to be left out of all updates
It restricts every communication to a single email channel
It requires the same message to be sent to every group
It lets the manager tailor messages to each audience's needs and influence
Communication.w: Communication plans support stakeholder-specific approaches, improving the relevance and effectiveness of engagement.

Communication.q: What does a well-structured communication plan help a project team to ensure during delivery?
o: That the right people receive the right information at the right time
That only face-to-face meetings are used throughout the project
That all identified project risks are resolved automatically
That every project meeting is cancelled to save time and cost
Communication.w: A communication plan sets out who needs what information, when and how, so the right people are kept informed at the right time.

Communication.q: Which communication method is most effective for detailed discussions that need clarification and negotiation?
o: Holding a face-to-face meeting
Issuing a monthly written status report
Sending a one-way recorded video message
Circulating a general group email
Communication.w: Face-to-face meetings allow complex points to be discussed and clarified immediately through two-way dialogue.

Communication.q: Beyond audience, method and frequency, which further detail strengthens a communication plan?
o: The colour scheme used in every report
The supplier's internal reporting lines
The daily attendance of every team member
A means of gathering feedback from recipients
Communication.w: Including a feedback mechanism ensures communication is two-way, confirming messages are received and understood.

Communication.q: What is a downside of relying too heavily on informal verbal communication?
o: It guarantees that information is always communicated accurately
Agreements may go undocumented and be misunderstood later
It removes the need for any defined escalation routes
It substantially increases the volume of project documentation
Communication.w: Informal verbal communication relies on memory, so agreements can be forgotten or misunderstood unless confirmed in writing.

Communication.q: What is a benefit of using several different communication methods on a project?
o: It removes the need to plan communication in advance
It reliably leads to information overload for stakeholders
It allows the project manager to reduce stakeholder engagement
Stakeholders receive information in the format that best suits them
Communication.w: Tailoring the method to each stakeholder's needs increases the likelihood that information is received and understood.

Communication.q: Why is effective communication considered critical to success within a project environment?
o: It removes the need for any project documentation to be produced
It allows the project manager to avoid engaging with stakeholders
It enables collaboration and alignment between the project’s stakeholders
It ensures all decisions are made solely by the project sponsor
Communication.w: Effective communication keeps stakeholders informed and aligned, enabling collaboration and supporting project success.

Communication.q: How can virtual meetings benefit a project team spread across different countries?
o: They reduce clarity by removing the body language of participants
They remove the need to keep any written record of decisions
They allow real-time collaboration between teams in different locations
They delay project updates because of the technology involved
Communication.w: Virtual communication lets geographically dispersed teams collaborate in real time without the delay and cost of travel.

Communication.q: Why is a communication plan especially valuable during stakeholder turnover or project handover?
o: It removes the need for any formal handover activity
It records prior communications, expectations and channels used
It allows new stakeholders to disregard past agreements
It prevents any future misunderstanding from ever occurring
Communication.w: A documented plan helps new stakeholders quickly understand the communication structures and the context of what has gone before.

Communication.q: How does having a documented communication plan give the project manager a consistent basis for project communications?
o: It records who receives what information, how and when, so messages stay consistent
It guarantees the project will be delivered comfortably within its budget
It removes the need to identify the project's stakeholders at all
It transfers responsibility for delivery across to the stakeholders
Communication.w: The plan records who receives what, how and when, giving the project manager a consistent, agreed basis for all communications.

Communication.q: Beyond simply sending information, what must effective project communication achieve between the parties involved?
o: A shared understanding confirmed through feedback between sender and receiver
The largest possible volume of messages distributed to everyone
A permanent written record stored for audit purposes only
A one-way flow of instructions requiring no response
Communication.w: Effective communication achieves shared understanding, confirmed through feedback between sender and receiver, not merely the sending of information.

Communication.q: In which situation is a physical, printed communication method likely to be most beneficial?
o: When real-time collaborative editing is required
When rapid decisions must be reached within the team
When stakeholders are remote and rely on mobile devices
When working with non-digital audiences or in technology-restricted settings
Communication.w: Printed documents ensure accessibility where technology access is unreliable or absent.

Communication.q: Which of the following is a recognised disadvantage of video conferencing in projects?
o: Prolonged calls can cause fatigue and reduced concentration
It cannot be recorded for those unable to attend
It is always more effective than meeting in person
It guarantees that every participant contributes equally
Communication.w: Extended video calls can cause fatigue, which reduces attention and engagement.

Communication.q: A dispersed team relies on email for a complex negotiation, which drags on for days. Which disadvantage of email does this illustrate?
o: It provides an instant, written audit trail
It reaches large numbers of recipients at once
It automatically records the sender and time
It handles nuanced, back-and-forth discussion poorly
Communication.w: Email is asynchronous and text-based, making it poorly suited to nuanced, real-time negotiation that benefits from immediate two-way dialogue.

Communication.q: What is a risk of overusing group email threads on a project?
o: They always deliver clear and unambiguous decisions
They can overwhelm recipients and dilute the key messages
They reduce the amount of information that is shared
They create an instant and reliable feedback loop
Communication.w: Excessive group emails can cause important information to be overlooked and reduce overall clarity.

Communication.q: A colleague expects the communication plan to contain the project's full risk scores. Why is this misplaced?
o: Risk scores must replace the audience details in the plan
Risk scores belong in the risk register, not the communication plan
Risk scores are the sole content of a communication plan
Risk scores are never recorded anywhere on a project
Communication.w: Risk scores belong in the risk register; a communication plan records audience, method, frequency and responsibility.

Communication.q: A new stakeholder joins mid-delivery and the project manager uses the communication plan to brief them. Which benefit does this demonstrate?
o: A reduction in the number of technical defects found
Faster processing of change requests through governance
Improved oversight of supplier procurement activities
Consistent onboarding of stakeholders into established communications
Communication.w: The communication plan ensures new stakeholders quickly receive timely, relevant information and understand existing communication arrangements.

Communication.q: A communication plan states that weekly status reports go to the steering group, issued by the project coordinator. Which attributes does this define?
o: The audience, method, frequency and responsibility for the information
The probability, impact and response owner for a risk
The severity, priority and closure date for an issue
The supplier, contract value and delivery date for procurement
Communication.w: It specifies what is communicated, to whom, how often and by whom, all of which are standard contents of a communication plan.

Communication.q: Which disadvantage is most closely linked to communicating solely through written reports?
o: They cannot be stored or referred back to
They offer no opportunity for immediate feedback
They always reach the wrong recipients
They depend on continuous internet access
Communication.w: Written reports are one-way and asynchronous, offering no immediate opportunity to clarify or give feedback, so misunderstandings can persist.

Communication.q: Which of the following is a key advantage of face-to-face communication on a project?
o: It removes any need for written follow-up or documentation
It reduces the travel and scheduling costs for the team
It permits immediate feedback and the reading of body language
It guarantees that stakeholders will agree with the message
Communication.w: Face-to-face communication conveys non-verbal cues and allows misunderstandings to be clarified immediately.

Communication.q: What is a limitation of relying on phone calls as the main communication method?
o: Calls always provide detailed visual aids for the discussion
Calls remove every risk of a message being misinterpreted
Calls may not be recorded or documented easily
Calls are always the best fit for project governance
Communication.w: Unless recorded or followed up in writing, phone calls can leave no official record of what was said.

Communication.q: What is the benefit to the project manager of defining a communication frequency within the plan?
o: It ensures updates are delivered regularly and predictably
It guarantees that suppliers will meet their commitments
It allows decisions to be taken without any discussion
It removes the need to keep any project documentation
Communication.w: Scheduled updates create consistency and reduce ambiguity, helping to build stakeholder trust.

Communication.q: Which of the following best describes the typical contents of a project communication plan?
o: The system defects, their severity and current resolution status
The supplier contracts, payment terms and procurement schedule
The project's risks, their probabilities and planned responses
Stakeholders, communication methods, frequency and responsibilities
Communication.w: A communication plan sets out who needs information, how and how often it will be provided, and who is responsible for providing it.

Communication.q: Naming the person accountable for issuing each project report is which part of a communication plan?
o: The responsibility, or sender, for the communication
The frequency of the communication
The medium of the communication
The purpose of the communication
Communication.w: Identifying who issues each message defines the responsibility, or sender, attribute of the communication plan.

Communication.q: In terms of stakeholder support, what benefit does a well-maintained communication plan bring to the project manager?
o: Well-informed stakeholders are more likely to remain engaged and supportive
Stakeholders no longer need to be consulted on any decisions
The project becomes exempt from its scheduled governance reviews
The project's approved budget is automatically increased in size
Communication.w: Timely, relevant communication keeps stakeholders informed and engaged, which helps sustain their support for the project.

Communication.q: Which statement best captures what the process of communication actually involves during project delivery?
o: Issuing instructions that require no response
A two-way process of conveying and confirming meaning
Recording information for audit purposes only
Broadcasting updates to as many people as possible
Communication.w: Communication is a two-way process of conveying information and confirming that its meaning has been received and understood.

Communication.q: Head office insists on face-to-face reviews, but the project team works across four countries. Which drawback does this most clearly expose?
o: It can only ever reach a single person at a time
It leaves no record whatsoever of any decisions taken
It is costly and impractical to gather everyone in one place
It removes all ability to read tone and body language
Communication.w: Face-to-face meetings require people to be co-located, which is costly and impractical for a geographically dispersed team.

Life Cycles.q: What principally happens during the transition phase of a typical linear project life cycle?
o: The high-level idea is assessed for viability and strategic fit
Detailed plans, schedules and budgets are produced and baselined
The main deliverables are designed, built and progressively tested
Outputs are handed over to users and the project is formally closed
Life Cycles.w: In the transition phase the outputs are handed over into use and the project is closed down.

Life Cycles.q: Within a single iteration of an iterative life cycle, which set of activities is typically carried out?
o: Closure and disbanding of the entire project team
Procurement of all materials with no further planning needed
A one-off concept phase followed by permanent operations
Planning, building and reviewing an increment of the solution
Life Cycles.w: Each iteration repeats a compact set of plan-build-review activities to produce an increment.

Life Cycles.q: Within a hybrid approach, which work is best suited to the iterative element of the life cycle?
o: Fixed infrastructure that must be installed in a strict, unchanging order
Regulatory documentation that cannot be altered once it is approved
Foundational elements whose design is settled before delivery begins
Evolving features that benefit from repeated user feedback and refinement
Life Cycles.w: The iterative element suits uncertain, evolving requirements that improve through successive cycles of feedback and refinement.

Life Cycles.q: A colleague asks what 'hybrid life cycle' means. Which explanation is correct?
o: Delivering the entire project through a single fixed sequence of phases
Running the same iterative cycle continuously until funding is exhausted
Handing the project between two organisations at the halfway point
Blending linear and iterative approaches within one project's delivery
Life Cycles.w: A hybrid life cycle blends linear and iterative methods so each part of the work uses the most suitable approach.

Life Cycles.q: Infrastructure must be delivered in a fixed sequence, while software features are released in cycles based on user feedback. Which life cycle is being used?
o: Iterative
Extended
Hybrid
Linear
Life Cycles.w: A hybrid life cycle combines a linear approach for predictable work with an iterative approach for work that benefits from feedback.

Life Cycles.q: What is the main purpose of the closure phase in a typical linear project life cycle?
o: Designing and building the deliverables
Reviewing performance and capturing lessons learned
Approving the project business case
Training the operational end users
Life Cycles.w: Closure reviews project performance, captures lessons learned and hands over responsibility for realising the remaining benefits.

Life Cycles.q: What is the defining feature of the way phases are arranged in a linear project life cycle?
o: Phases can be reordered freely according to team preference
Each phase is largely completed before the next one begins
All phases run in parallel from the very start of the project
Phases repeat in short cycles until the customer is satisfied
Life Cycles.w: A linear life cycle runs its phases sequentially, with each substantially finished before the next starts.

Life Cycles.q: How does a hybrid life cycle mainly differ from a purely iterative life cycle?
o: A hybrid abandons all upfront planning in favour of continuous change
A hybrid is always shorter and cheaper than an iterative approach
A hybrid never gathers stakeholder feedback during delivery
A hybrid keeps predefined linear phases for part of the work, unlike a fully iterative approach
Life Cycles.w: Unlike a purely iterative life cycle, a hybrid retains fixed linear phases for the parts of the work that are stable.

Life Cycles.q: Which situation is the strongest reason for a project to adopt a hybrid life cycle?
o: Some parts are predictable while others need flexibility
All requirements are fixed and fully understood
The product is simple, small and repetitive
The customer has minimal involvement in delivery
Life Cycles.w: Hybrid life cycles are chosen when some components need firm, predictive control while others benefit from adaptive delivery.

Life Cycles.q: Compared with a standard linear life cycle, what does an extended life cycle mainly change?
o: It shortens the concept phase so that the delivery phase can start much sooner
It lengthens the timeline after delivery to realise benefits and, later, dispose of the asset
It repeats the delivery phase in short cycles until stakeholders are satisfied
It merges the definition and delivery phases into a single continuous phase
Life Cycles.w: The extended life cycle chiefly adds time after delivery, continuing through benefits realisation to the eventual disposal of the asset.

Life Cycles.q: Which feature most clearly distinguishes an iterative life cycle from a linear one in terms of its phases?
o: Its phases are repeated to develop the solution incrementally
Its phases are always carried out by external suppliers
Its phases are performed strictly once in a fixed order
Its phases exclude any form of review or feedback
Life Cycles.w: The defining difference is repetition of phases to build the solution incrementally rather than a single pass.

Life Cycles.q: In an iterative project life cycle, what typically happens at the end of each development iteration?
o: The final product is signed off and the project closes
Stakeholder feedback is gathered to shape later iterations
All remaining risks are transferred to suppliers
The business case is rewritten from scratch
Life Cycles.w: Each iteration ends with a review that gathers stakeholder feedback, informing and adapting the next iteration.

Life Cycles.q: In project management, what is the primary purpose of adopting an extended project life cycle?
o: To shorten the overall delivery timescale
To reduce resource usage during development
To manage post-project benefits and performance
To avoid further stakeholder engagement
Life Cycles.w: The extended life cycle continues beyond handover to ensure benefits are realised and performance is monitored over time.

Life Cycles.q: A team completes a cycle of planning, building and reviewing, then begins the same activities again. Which life cycle does this reflect?
o: A linear life cycle
An extended life cycle
An iterative life cycle
A hybrid life cycle
Life Cycles.w: Repeating the same set of activities over successive cycles is the defining feature of an iterative life cycle.

Life Cycles.q: Which sequence correctly orders the deliverable focus across a linear life cycle?
o: Handover first, then build, then definition, then the concept
A working product, then plans, then an idea, then handover
An idea, then detailed plans, then the build, then handover
Plans, then the concept, then handover, then the build
Life Cycles.w: The linear life cycle progresses from concept (idea), to definition (plans), to deployment (build), to transition (handover).

Life Cycles.q: In a typical iterative life cycle, why are development activities repeated rather than completed only once?
o: To progressively evolve and improve the product through successive cycles
To fix the full scope and budget before any work starts
To avoid producing any documentation until the final release
To remove the need for stakeholder involvement during delivery
Life Cycles.w: Repetition lets the product evolve incrementally, incorporating feedback with each cycle.

Life Cycles.q: In an extended project life cycle, what typically triggers the final termination or disposal phase?
o: The delivery phase producing the project's outputs
The delivered asset reaching the end of its useful life
The very first benefit being realised in operation
The business case first being approved by the sponsor
Life Cycles.w: The termination or disposal phase begins once the asset has reached the end of its useful life and its benefits are exhausted.

Life Cycles.q: What is the main benefit of extending a project life cycle to include a benefits realisation phase?
o: It fixes the delivery budget more tightly before any work is allowed to begin
It confirms that the intended benefits are actually achieved once the outputs are in use
It allows the requirements to be changed freely throughout the delivery phase
It reduces the number of governance decision gates the project must pass through
Life Cycles.w: Adding a benefits realisation phase lets the organisation confirm the forecast benefits are delivered in operational use.

Life Cycles.q: In a typical linear project life cycle, at which phase are the detailed schedule, budget and project management plan normally finalised?
o: Definition
Concept
Development
Handover
Life Cycles.w: The definition phase is where the detailed plans, schedule and budget are developed and baselined before delivery begins.

Life Cycles.q: Infrastructure is delivered using a linear model while customer-facing features are developed and adjusted during delivery. What is this model called?
o: Extended
Agile
Hybrid
Waterfall
Life Cycles.w: Mixing sequential and iterative components within one project is the defining characteristic of a hybrid life cycle.

Life Cycles.q: In an iterative life cycle, what is typically produced at the end of each cycle of work?
o: A partial or improved increment of the overall solution
The final, fully complete product ready for closure
A fixed baseline that can never afterwards be revised
A complete business case covering the whole programme
Life Cycles.w: Each iteration delivers an increment that adds to or improves the evolving solution.

Life Cycles.q: In an iterative life cycle, what term is commonly used for the short, time-boxed development cycles the team works in?
o: Milestones
Gateways
Phases
Sprints
Life Cycles.w: Sprints are the short, time-boxed iterations used to deliver increments of the product in iterative and agile approaches.

Life Cycles.q: A linear project has delivered and installed new equipment and has trained the staff who will operate it. Which phase is being completed?
o: Definition
Handover and closure
Concept
Development
Life Cycles.w: Handover and closure is where the deliverables are transitioned to the users and the project is formally brought to an end.

Life Cycles.q: What is the main advantage of adopting a hybrid life cycle on a project with mixed requirements?
o: It removes the need for any change control because everything is planned upfront
It guarantees the project will finish earlier than a purely linear approach
It applies predictable planning where requirements are stable and flexibility where they evolve
It allows the team to avoid producing a deployment baseline at any stage
Life Cycles.w: The hybrid approach matches the method to the work, giving predictability to stable elements and adaptability to uncertain ones.

Life Cycles.q: Which of the following activities would appear within an extended life cycle but not within a standard one?
o: Producing the detailed project management plan
Reviewing whether forecast benefits have been realised in operational use
Defining the project's scope during the concept phase
Approving the deployment baseline before delivery begins
Life Cycles.w: Reviewing realised benefits after handover is characteristic of the extended life cycle, which continues beyond delivery of the outputs.

Life Cycles.q: During which phase of a typical linear life cycle is the initial idea first tested for feasibility and strategic fit?
o: Transition
Deployment
Concept
Definition
Life Cycles.w: The concept phase tests the initial idea for feasibility and strategic fit before detailed planning begins.

Life Cycles.q: Which characteristic best distinguishes a hybrid life cycle from other project life cycles?
o: It postpones all delivery until every requirement is agreed
It deliberately combines plan-driven and adaptive methods in one approach
It relies solely on adaptive methods with no fixed structure
It follows one rigid sequence with no scope for iteration
Life Cycles.w: The defining feature of a hybrid life cycle is its deliberate combination of plan-driven and adaptive methods within a single project.

Life Cycles.q: Midway through planning, a team realises part of the scope is fixed and part is unclear. Why might a hybrid life cycle suit them?
o: It ensures no changes will ever be requested during delivery
It combines predictable planning with adaptive delivery within one project
It replaces the need for a project manager to coordinate the work
It lets them skip defining any requirements until the very end
Life Cycles.w: A hybrid life cycle accommodates both fixed and evolving work by combining plan-driven and adaptive approaches in one project.

Life Cycles.q: An extended life cycle includes a final phase covering the safe retirement of the delivered asset at the end of its useful life. What is this phase called?
o: The concept and feasibility phase
The termination or disposal phase
The delivery and integration phase
The initiation and mobilisation phase
Life Cycles.w: The extended life cycle concludes with a termination or disposal phase, managing the retirement of the asset once its benefits are exhausted.

Life Cycles.q: Which activity is most characteristic of the concept phase within a typical linear project life cycle?
o: Defining the business need and justification for change
Completing the post-project benefit reviews
Allocating detailed work packages to the delivery team
Producing and signing off the final test results
Life Cycles.w: The concept phase articulates the need, high-level options and justification for the project before detailed planning begins.

Life Cycles.q: A team is building a new mobile app through short development cycles with regular end-user feedback. Which life cycle is most likely being used?
o: Extended
Hybrid
Iterative
Linear
Life Cycles.w: An iterative life cycle delivers in small increments and refines the product through repeated cycles of stakeholder feedback.

Life Cycles.q: A client wants a fixed upfront cost and schedule for deployment but also wants to evolve features after go-live. Which approach best fits?
o: Extended
Iterative
Hybrid
Linear
Life Cycles.w: A hybrid approach allows a predictable, planned deployment while retaining iterative flexibility to evolve features later.

Life Cycles.q: A construction firm pours foundations in a fixed sequence but develops the building's smart controls in short cycles. Which life cycle is this?
o: Linear life cycle
Iterative life cycle
Hybrid life cycle
Extended life cycle
Life Cycles.w: Combining a linear sequence for fixed work with iterative cycles for evolving elements within one project is a hybrid life cycle.

Life Cycles.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the phases of a typical linear project life cycle?
o: Deployment
Definition
Optimisation
Concept
Life Cycles.w: The four phases of a typical linear life cycle are concept, definition, deployment and transition; optimisation is not one of them.

Life Cycles.q: You are running a construction project with a linear life cycle and fully defined requirements. What is the correct sequence of phases?
o: Concept, Definition, Development, Handover and Closure
Concept, Definition, Deployment, Closure
Initiation, Development, Execution, Review
Concept, Feasibility, Deployment, Handover
Life Cycles.w: A typical APM linear life cycle runs through Concept, Definition, Development, and Handover and Closure.

Life Cycles.q: Which activity is most closely associated with the extended project life cycle?
o: Monitoring benefit delivery over time
Defining the work breakdown structure
Procuring the development resources
Identifying the initial user requirements
Life Cycles.w: The extended life cycle focuses on tracking benefit delivery, often long after the deliverables have been handed over.

Life Cycles.q: A sponsor wants the value of a new asset to be monitored for years after handover until it is retired. Which life cycle supports this?
o: Hybrid life cycle
Iterative life cycle
Extended life cycle
Linear life cycle
Life Cycles.w: Only the extended life cycle spans beyond delivery to include benefits realisation and eventual disposal, matching the sponsor's requirement.

Life Cycles.q: Which of the following statements best describes a typical hybrid project life cycle?
o: An adaptive model that uses only agile techniques
A combination of linear and iterative life cycle elements
An extended life cycle with additional benefit reviews
A series of fixed-scope deliveries with no overlap
Life Cycles.w: A hybrid life cycle blends predictive (linear) and adaptive (iterative) elements to suit the different parts of a project.

Life Cycles.q: How does an extended project life cycle differ from a hybrid life cycle?
o: Extended adds phases after handover, whereas hybrid blends linear and iterative approaches
Extended blends linear and iterative delivery, whereas hybrid adds operational phases
Both remove the closure phase, but extended repeats delivery in short sprints
Both fix scope at the outset, but hybrid allows benefits to be reviewed later
Life Cycles.w: An extended life cycle lengthens the timeline to cover benefits and disposal, while a hybrid life cycle combines linear and iterative delivery approaches.

Life Cycles.q: In which phase of a linear life cycle are the project's outputs actually built and tested?
o: Deployment
Definition
Transition
Concept
Life Cycles.w: The deployment phase is where the project management plan is executed and the outputs are created and tested.

Life Cycles.q: After delivering a new CRM system, the team must monitor its use and confirm the expected benefits are achieved. To which part of the life cycle does this belong?
o: The development phase
The definition phase
The extended life cycle
The concept phase
Life Cycles.w: Monitoring performance and realising benefits after handover are activities of the extended project life cycle.

Life Cycles.q: Compared with a typical linear life cycle, which additional phases does an extended life cycle usually include?
o: Concept and definition phases scheduled before delivery begins
Extra approval and procurement phases during the handover
Additional testing and integration phases within the delivery phase
Benefits realisation and eventual termination or disposal phases
Life Cycles.w: An extended life cycle adds phases for realising benefits in operation and for the eventual disposal or termination of the asset.

Life Cycles.q: By the end of the concept phase in a linear life cycle, what is normally produced?
o: A detailed configuration management status report
A signed acceptance certificate confirming benefits realised
An outline business case recommending whether to proceed
The fully tested product ready for operational handover
Life Cycles.w: The concept phase concludes with an outline business case that supports the decision on whether to continue into definition.

Life Cycles.q: Which statement best describes how the phases are arranged in a typical iterative project life cycle?
o: A fixed, once-only sequence of phases completed from start to finish
A set of activities repeated over successive cycles to refine the solution
A single design phase followed by permanent operational running
A series of unrelated phases carried out by separate organisations
Life Cycles.w: An iterative life cycle repeats a set of activities across successive cycles to develop the solution progressively.

Life Cycles.q: After closure, the sponsor commissions periodic reviews to check whether the expected return on investment is being achieved. What does this indicate?
o: That extended life cycle activities are underway
That the project has re-entered development
That the original scope was left incomplete
That a formal change request has been raised
Life Cycles.w: Post-closure benefit reviews to confirm long-term value are part of the extended project life cycle.

Life Cycles.q: Which statement best describes what is meant by an 'extended project life cycle'?
o: A life cycle repeated in short cycles until the customer finally accepts the product
A life cycle whose delivery phase is lengthened to allow for additional testing
A life cycle that adds benefits realisation and eventual asset disposal to the standard phases
A life cycle in which the concept and definition phases are merged into one
Life Cycles.w: An extended life cycle continues beyond output handover to include benefits realisation and, ultimately, the termination or disposal of the asset.

Life Cycles.q: In a hybrid life cycle, which type of work is typically handled through the linear, plan-driven element?
o: Features whose requirements are expected to change repeatedly during delivery
Stable components with well-defined, unlikely-to-change requirements
Any work the customer wishes to review after every short iteration
Experimental elements where the final solution is still unknown
Life Cycles.w: The linear element suits stable, well-understood work that can be fixed and planned in advance without frequent change.

Life Cycles.q: Which sequence best represents how work flows through a typical iterative project life cycle?
o: Repeated cycles of build and review until the product is complete
Concept, definition, delivery and handover performed once only
Delivery carried out entirely before any planning takes place
A one-off design followed immediately by closure
Life Cycles.w: Iterative work progresses through repeated build-and-review cycles until the solution is complete.

Life Cycles.q: Why might an organisation choose an iterative life cycle for a project with uncertain requirements?
o: Because it fixes all requirements permanently before delivery
Because repeating cycles allow requirements to be refined as understanding grows
Because it removes the need for any project reviews
Because it guarantees a lower overall cost than any alternative
Life Cycles.w: Iterative cycles let requirements be clarified and refined progressively, suiting projects where they are not fully known upfront.

Life Cycles.q: A delivery model of successive product iterations shaped by stakeholder input is best suited to what kind of requirements?
o: Fixed by contract and legally constrained
Simple, repetitive and well understood
Evolving, uncertain or likely to change
Stable and fully defined from the outset
Life Cycles.w: Iterative life cycles suit evolving or uncertain requirements because feedback between iterations allows the product to be refined.

Life Cycles.q: In a typical linear project life cycle, which phase immediately follows the concept phase?
o: Transition
Definition
Deployment
Operation
Life Cycles.w: A linear life cycle runs concept, definition, deployment then transition, so definition follows the concept phase.

Life Cycles.q: During a typical iterative life cycle, when is stakeholder feedback most commonly gathered?
o: Only before the first iteration begins
Never, because the scope is fixed at the outset
Only once, at the very end of the project
At the close of each iteration to shape later cycles
Life Cycles.w: Iterative delivery seeks feedback at the end of each cycle so subsequent iterations can respond to it.

Life Cycles.q: A document management system has been handed over to operations. Which activity would typically follow within the extended project life cycle?
o: Evaluating actual benefits against those forecast
Drafting the project initiation documentation
Holding the initial project kick-off workshop
Running performance tests on the old system
Life Cycles.w: Comparing benefits actually achieved against those forecast is a central activity of the extended life cycle.

Life Cycles.q: Which statement most accurately describes what a hybrid project life cycle brings together within a single project?
o: Two consecutive linear life cycles, each producing a separate final deliverable
A single linear sequence repeated so the team can refine the output twice
Continuous iterations throughout, with no predefined phases fixed in advance
Linear phases for stable, well-understood work alongside iterative cycles for evolving requirements
Life Cycles.w: A hybrid life cycle blends a plan-driven (linear) approach for defined work with an adaptive (iterative) approach for evolving elements within one project.

Life Cycles.q: In a linear life cycle, moving from the definition phase into the deployment phase typically requires what?
o: Completion of user training and formal handover to operations
Approval at a decision gate confirming plans are ready for delivery
The first sprint retrospective to reprioritise the backlog
Realisation of the benefits set out in the business case
Life Cycles.w: Phase boundaries in a linear life cycle are controlled by decision gates that authorise progression once plans are ready.

Life Cycles.q: Which statement best describes a core feature of an iterative project life cycle?
o: The full scope is fixed upfront and delivered in one release
Formal reviews are avoided throughout the delivery period
The product is released in increments with frequent reassessment
Benefits are only realised once the final delivery is complete
Life Cycles.w: Iterative life cycles release the product in successive increments, reassessing and adapting the plan after each one.

Quality.q: One product is basic but meets every requirement; another is elaborate but misses several. Which better demonstrates quality?
o: The elaborate product, because it offers more features
Neither, because quality cannot be compared between products
The basic product, because it conforms to its requirements
The elaborate product, because it clearly cost more to build
Quality.w: Quality is conformance to requirements, so the basic product that fully meets its requirements demonstrates quality.

Quality.q: Why might an organisation choose to conduct a project audit while the project is still being delivered?
o: To test the completed deliverables for technical faults
To confirm compliance and highlight improvements while action is still possible
To cancel the project before any more money is committed
To sign off the final benefits review with the sponsor
Quality.w: A mid-project audit can surface issues early, allowing corrective action to be taken while the project is still underway.

Quality.q: Which of the following is a typical output of the quality control process on a project?
o: Records of inspections and test results for the deliverables
The quality management plan produced for the whole project
The schedule of independent process audits to be carried out
The list of quality standards the project will adopt
Quality.w: Quality control produces inspection and test records for deliverables; the other items are outputs of quality planning or assurance.

Quality.q: A senior manager commissions a check on whether a project complies with corporate governance requirements. Which process is this?
o: Conducting a project audit
Planning the project's risk responses
Realising the project's benefits
Carrying out quality control
Quality.w: A project audit is the formal assessment of a project's compliance with governance, processes and policies.

Quality.q: Which statement best defines quality control in a project setting?
o: Training the team members in various quality methods
Planning how the required quality will be assured
Monitoring results to check they comply with standards
Identifying lessons learned from earlier quality issues
Quality.w: Quality control monitors and inspects project outputs to confirm they meet the specified requirements.

Quality.q: Which of the following best describes the role of decision gates within quality management?
o: They replace all other assurance activities
They confirm each phase meets its standards before progressing
They ensure only the final output is reviewed
They remove the need to engage with stakeholders
Quality.w: Decision gates support quality by confirming that the objectives and standards for a phase are met before progressing.

Quality.q: During delivery a team reviews whether its agreed working procedures are being applied consistently across all workstreams. Which process is this?
o: Quality control
Quality assurance
Change control
Benefits management
Quality.w: Reviewing whether agreed processes and procedures are being applied is a quality assurance activity.

Quality.q: How does quality control contribute to the successful delivery of a project?
o: By verifying that outputs meet defined standards before they are accepted
By ensuring that the plans align closely with the users’ needs
By selecting the most appropriate project delivery methodology
By communicating agreed changes to the project’s stakeholders
Quality.w: Quality control checks outputs against defined standards before acceptance, reducing rework and helping ensure deliverables are fit for purpose.

Quality.q: Why can two stakeholders usually agree on whether a deliverable has quality when its requirements are clear?
