o: Because quality is judged objectively against the agreed requirements
Because quality depends only on each person's individual taste
Because quality is decided solely by the deliverable's price
Because quality always means the highest specification possible
Quality.w: With clear requirements, quality can be judged objectively against them rather than by subjective opinion.

Quality.q: Following project handover, who is normally accountable for tracking whether the intended benefits are actually realised?
o: The project sponsor or designated benefits owner
The finance administrator who managed the budget
The lead supplier who provided the deliverables
The project manager who led the delivery work
Quality.w: Benefits are usually realised after the project has closed, so accountability passes to the sponsor or a designated benefits owner identified in the business case.

Quality.q: Which of the following is a common tool used to carry out quality assurance?
o: Product inspections of the deliverables
Change request logs for the project
Issue registers maintained by the team
Peer reviews of the processes used
Quality.w: Peer reviews of processes support quality assurance by verifying that agreed procedures are being applied.

Quality.q: After a prototype is built it undergoes several tests to confirm it meets the client's requirements; which process is this part of?
o: Risk management activity
Quality assurance of processes
Quality control of outputs
Change management activity
Quality.w: Quality control includes testing outputs to confirm they meet the required standards and client expectations.

Quality.q: A modest, low-cost component performs exactly as its specification demands. How should its quality be judged?
o: Poor, because it is inexpensive and simply designed
Good, because it meets its requirements and is fit for purpose
Poor, because it lacks additional premium features
Impossible to judge without knowing its market price
Quality.w: Because it meets its requirements and is fit for purpose, the component is of good quality regardless of cost.

Quality.q: A benefit review finds that only part of the forecast savings were achieved; what should the organisation do?
o: Analyse why the benefits were not fully realised
Treat the whole project as a complete failure
Cancel all future benefit reviews entirely
Ignore the results because the project has closed
Quality.w: The gap between expected and actual benefits should be analysed and captured as lessons learned for future projects.

Quality.q: What is a likely consequence of a project running no quality management at all?
o: Deliverables may fail to meet requirements and prove unfit for purpose
The project's scope becomes permanently fixed
All of the project's risks are automatically eliminated
Stakeholder communication is no longer required
Quality.w: Without quality management, deliverables risk failing requirements and being unfit for purpose.

Quality.q: Why is carrying out quality planning during the early stages of a project so important?
o: It guarantees the fastest possible project delivery
It removes the need to communicate with stakeholders
It reduces the budget the project will require
It defines how outputs will be verified against requirements
Quality.w: Quality planning establishes clear verification criteria, reducing rework and increasing confidence in delivery.

Quality.q: In a linear life cycle, a board reviews whether the project should move into its next phase; what is this review called?
o: A stakeholder review
A decision gate
A post-project review
A formal quality audit
Quality.w: A decision gate is a review point used to decide whether a project should proceed to the next phase.

Quality.q: A plan is being produced to set out how requirements will be confirmed throughout delivery; which process does this describe?
o: Quality control of outputs
Quality assurance of processes
Change control of the scope
Quality planning for the project
Quality.w: This is quality planning, which decides how quality will be measured and verified before work is carried out.

Quality.q: Quality planning is best described as which type of activity within quality management?
o: An activity concerned only with closing the project
A proactive activity that sets standards before delivery
A reactive activity carried out only after defects appear
An activity limited to auditing supplier processes
Quality.w: Quality planning is proactive, establishing the standards and approach to quality before delivery begins.

Quality.q: Which of the following best describes quality assurance within a project?
o: Identifying the risks that the project faces
Monitoring adherence to the quality processes used
Checking finished deliverables against the standards
Defining the acceptance criteria for outputs
Quality.w: Quality assurance ensures that the quality management processes are being followed and remain effective.

Quality.q: Why is it important that project outputs are fit for purpose?
o: To impress stakeholders during the project's review meetings
To shorten the overall duration of the project's activities
To meet quality objectives and deliver value to the customer
To reduce the planning resources needed by the project
Quality.w: Outputs that are fit for purpose satisfy the project's quality objectives and deliver the intended value to the customer.

Quality.q: A team specifies tolerances for the appearance, function and durability of a new product; which phase are they most likely in?
o: Quality planning for the product
Formal scope definition work
Stakeholder engagement activity
Quality control of the product
Quality.w: Defining tolerances and acceptance measures for deliverables is a key part of quality planning.

Quality.q: Which of the following is the range of outcomes a decision gate can authorise for a project?
o: Continue to the next phase, amend the plan, or stop the project
Only continue, since a gate can never stop a project
Only stop, since a gate cannot allow continuation
Reassign the entire project team to other work
Quality.w: A decision gate can decide to proceed, amend or stop, not merely authorise continuation.

Quality.q: A team assumes a 'quality' product must be the most expensive and feature-rich option. Why is this view mistaken?
o: Quality has no connection to the customer's stated needs
Quality requires deliberately exceeding every stated requirement
Quality is only ever judged by the project's total cost
Quality means meeting the agreed requirements, not maximising features
Quality.w: Quality is about meeting the agreed requirements and fitness for purpose, not about cost or maximising features.

Quality.q: Which statement best describes the purpose of quality management within a project?
o: To avoid the need for any configuration control
To provide contingency against time overruns
To remove every risk that the project might face
To ensure deliverables are reviewed against agreed criteria
Quality.w: Quality management ensures outputs are assessed against agreed standards and are suitable for their intended use.

Quality.q: Which of the following is NOT a purpose of quality assurance on a project?
o: Inspecting and correcting individual defective deliverables
Providing confidence that the processes can deliver the required quality
Checking that the agreed processes are being followed
Giving objective, independent evidence about how the work is done
Quality.w: Inspecting and correcting individual deliverables is quality control; assurance is process-focused and provides confidence.

Quality.q: A quality control check finds that several components fail to meet the specification; what should happen next?
o: Ignore the failures because most components passed
Adjust the original scope to match the output
Change the requirements to suit the output
Report the failure and decide on corrective action
Quality.w: Non-conformance found in quality control should be reported so that corrective action can be taken to meet the standard.

Quality.q: Why is a project audit usually carried out by people independent of the delivery team?
o: So the assessment of compliance with processes is objective and unbiased
So the delivery team can approve its own results
So the benefits can be measured long after handover
So the next phase is automatically authorised
Quality.w: Independence lets a project audit assess process compliance objectively, free from the delivery team's bias.

Quality.q: What is the main output produced by the quality planning process on a project?
o: A project closure report
A project risk register
A change control log
A quality management plan
Quality.w: The quality management plan sets out how quality will be defined, managed and verified throughout the project.

Quality.q: A project manager works with stakeholders to agree the quality requirements before delivery begins; which process is this?
o: Change control of the scope
Quality control of the outputs
Quality planning for the project
Progress reporting to sponsors
Quality.w: Quality planning identifies the quality requirements and determines how they will be met before execution begins.

Quality.q: Why is delivering far beyond the agreed requirements not necessarily a sign of quality?
o: Quality is measured solely by how much is delivered
Quality always improves whenever more features are added
Quality is unrelated to the requirements set for the deliverable
Quality is about meeting requirements, so over-delivery can waste resources
Quality.w: Since quality means conformance to requirements, delivering beyond them (gold plating) adds no quality and can waste resources.

Quality.q: Which of the following is a typical activity carried out during quality planning?
o: Identifying the residual risks remaining after responses are applied
Monitoring the changing attitudes of the project’s stakeholders
Defining the acceptance criteria that deliverables must meet
Approving the procurement contracts entered into by the project
Quality.w: Quality planning determines the standards and acceptance criteria that deliverables must meet and how quality will be achieved.

Quality.q: How does quality assurance differ from quality control in the delivery of a project?
o: Assurance checks that processes are followed, while control inspects the outputs
Assurance inspects the deliverables, while control defines the standards
Assurance applies only to iterative projects, while control applies to linear ones
Assurance happens after delivery, while control happens before planning begins
Quality.w: Quality assurance provides confidence that the correct processes are being followed, while quality control checks the resulting deliverables against standards.

Quality.q: A project manager describes a deliverable as being of 'high quality'. What does 'quality' mean in the context of a project?
o: That it meets the agreed requirements and is fit for purpose
That it was completed ahead of its planned schedule
That it includes more features than were originally specified
That it exceeds recognised industry standards for the sector
Quality.w: In APM terms, quality means the deliverable conforms to its agreed requirements and is fit for its intended purpose.

Quality.q: Which outcome would a well-run quality management approach be expected to deliver?
o: A guarantee that no risks will ever materialise
Deliverables that reliably conform to their specifications
A permanent freeze on the project's approved budget
An automatic increase in the size of the project team
Quality.w: Effective quality management produces deliverables that reliably conform to their specifications.

Quality.q: Which of the following statements most accurately captures the central focus of the quality planning process?
o: Identifying the quality criteria and the means to satisfy them
Measuring completed products against their specification
Reviewing whether agreed procedures are being applied
Escalating issues that exceed the manager's authority
Quality.w: Quality planning focuses on defining the quality criteria to be met and the methods and resources used to satisfy them.

Quality.q: What is meant by 'quality' in the context of a project?
o: Delivering outputs that meet the agreed requirements and are fit for purpose
Providing the most technically advanced solution available
Meeting customer expectations regardless of the agreed scope
Completing every task well ahead of its planned deadline
Quality.w: Quality is defined as meeting the specified requirements and ensuring the output is fit for its intended purpose.

Quality.q: A sponsor wants assurance that the methods being used are capable of producing acceptable outputs. Which activity provides this?
o: Quality control, by inspecting each finished item
Quality assurance, by evaluating whether processes are sound
Configuration management, by controlling document versions
Risk management, by logging threats to delivery
Quality.w: Quality assurance evaluates whether the processes are capable of delivering acceptable outputs, giving the sponsor confidence.

Quality.q: Why is quality assurance often carried out by people independent of the delivery team?
o: So that the delivery team is relieved of all quality responsibility
So that inspection of the final product can be skipped entirely
So that the schedule can be shortened by removing reviews
So that confidence in the processes is objective and unbiased
Quality.w: Independence gives quality assurance objectivity, providing unbiased confidence that processes are sound.

Quality.q: What is the main purpose of a decision gate within project governance?
o: To approve the contracts held with suppliers
To assess whether the project should continue
To carry out the lessons learned sessions
To delegate new work packages to the team
Quality.w: Decision gates provide control points where continuation of the project is reviewed against performance and objectives.

Quality.q: A post-project review finds that weak stakeholder engagement led to missed requirements; what should be done with this insight?
o: Ignore it because the project has now closed
Use it to place blame on the stakeholders
Delete it to protect the project's reputation
Document it as a lesson learned for future projects
Quality.w: Lessons learned should be captured and shared so that stakeholder engagement improves on future projects.

Quality.q: Quality management is best understood as an umbrella covering which combination of activities?
o: Estimating, scheduling and procurement
Quality planning, quality assurance and quality control
Identification, analysis and risk response
Concept, definition and handover
Quality.w: Quality management encompasses quality planning, quality assurance and quality control.

Quality.q: A team inspects completed deliverables to confirm they meet the agreed requirements; which process are they performing?
o: Quality planning of outputs
Quality control of outputs
Risk management activity
Stakeholder management work
Quality.w: Quality control involves inspecting and testing deliverables to verify they meet the agreed quality requirements.

Quality.q: After a challenging delivery, an organisation holds a structured session on what went well and what could improve; what is this?
o: A post-project review
A risk assessment
A quality control check
A cost benefit analysis
Quality.w: A post-project review allows the team and stakeholders to reflect on and learn from the project experience.

Quality.q: A project fails to meet its key success criteria at a gate review; what is the likely outcome?
o: New scope is added without any assessment
The project may be paused or stopped
The project budget is increased without review
The team proceeds automatically to the next stage
Quality.w: Decision gates allow the organisation to pause, redirect or stop a project based on its current performance and alignment.

Quality.q: Which review is specifically concerned with confirming whether the intended benefits have actually materialised?
o: A project audit
A decision gate
A benefit review
A post-project review
Quality.w: A benefit review checks whether the forecast benefits have actually been realised, usually after closure.

Quality.q: Before delivery begins, a project manager defines the standards the outputs must meet and how conformance will be checked. Which process is this?
o: Quality planning
Configuration management
Quality control
Quality assurance
Quality.w: Setting the required standards and how conformance will be checked, ahead of delivery, is quality planning.

Quality.q: At a decision gate review, who typically decides whether the project proceeds to the next phase?
o: An external team of auditors
The project manager acting alone
The governance board or sponsor
The project team collectively
Quality.w: Gate decisions are made by the governance board or sponsor to provide objective oversight and strategic alignment.

Quality.q: Against what standard should a project deliverable's quality ultimately be judged in practice?
o: The requirements and needs it was created to satisfy
The total budget that was spent on producing it
The number of premium features it happens to contain
Its ranking against rival products in the marketplace
Quality.w: Quality is judged against the requirements and needs the deliverable was created to satisfy, not cost or market position.

Quality.q: A quality assurance review shows that a key process is not being applied consistently; what should happen next?
o: The findings should be ignored by the team
The project should be closed down immediately
Corrective actions should be identified and implemented
The product should be delivered without change
Quality.w: Quality assurance identifies process shortfalls so that corrective actions can realign work with quality standards.

Quality.q: What is the primary purpose of quality control within a project?
o: To document the interests of the stakeholders
To confirm outputs conform to specifications through inspection
To produce a detailed and costed business case
To manage the contracts held with suppliers
Quality.w: Quality control verifies outputs through inspection, measurement and testing to confirm they meet requirements.

Quality.q: At what point during project delivery does the quality control process principally take place?
o: Only after the project has been formally closed down
When deliverables have been produced and can be inspected or tested
Before any work starts, when standards are being set
Continuously, by auditing the management processes in use
Quality.w: Quality control takes place once deliverables exist and can be inspected or tested against their requirements.

Quality.q: A project manager sets up processes to ensure the final product meets the agreed requirements. What is the main purpose of quality management?
o: To make the project's procurement arrangements simpler
To reduce the number of stakeholders involved in the project
To ensure outputs are delivered to a consistent and acceptable standard
To increase the overall speed at which the product is delivered
Quality.w: Quality management exists to ensure that project outputs consistently meet the agreed standards and are fit for purpose.

Quality.q: Which of the following would typically be discussed during a post-project review?
o: Lessons learned and performance against objectives
Plans for procuring brand new suppliers
Estimates for the costs of a new product
Detailed technical rework of the product
Quality.w: Post-project reviews cover overall performance, stakeholder feedback and lessons learned to inform future projects.

Quality.q: During quality planning, a team agrees to follow recognised industry standards to guide development; what does this represent?
o: Selecting the quality measures for the project
Avoiding risk by outsourcing the work
Assigning the procurement roles for the team
Reducing project cost through standardisation
Quality.w: Choosing standards during quality planning helps define the measures used to verify that deliverables meet requirements.

Quality.q: A project team is discussing whether their final product meets the definition of 'quality'. Which statement best defines quality?
o: Every project risk was successfully avoided during delivery
The final cost of the product came in below the initial budget
The deliverable includes as many additional features as possible
The output meets the defined requirements and serves its intended purpose
Quality.w: Quality means the deliverable satisfies its agreed specifications and is suitable for its intended use.

Quality.q: In a project, what is quality management fundamentally intended to ensure about the deliverables?
o: That they involve the fewest possible team members
That they are produced at the lowest possible cost
That they are fit for purpose and meet the agreed requirements
That they are delivered before the agreed schedule
Quality.w: Quality management ensures deliverables meet agreed requirements and are fit for purpose.

Quality.q: An audit is carried out to assess whether the project's quality procedures are being applied correctly; which process is this?
o: Project scheduling activity
Quality assurance of processes
Requirements gathering work
Risk assessment activity
Quality.w: Audits are a form of quality assurance used to confirm that established quality procedures are being followed.

Quality.q: A manager arranges a peer review of the team's process to confirm agreed procedures are being followed; what is this an example of?
o: Quality assurance of processes
Scope verification activity
Change control process
Quality control of outputs
Quality.w: Quality assurance confirms that project processes are being followed correctly so that quality outputs are produced.

Quality.q: Of quality planning, assurance and control, which is the only one performed on the finished or in-progress deliverables themselves?
o: Quality control
Quality assurance
Quality governance
Quality planning
Quality.w: Quality control is performed on the deliverables themselves through inspection and testing; planning and assurance act on standards and processes.

Quality.q: What best distinguishes a project audit from a post-project review carried out after closure?
o: Audits are informal discussions, whereas reviews are formal inspections
Audits apply only to iterative projects, whereas reviews apply to linear ones
Audits assess benefits, whereas reviews assess only the schedule
Audits check compliance and governance, whereas reviews capture performance and lessons
Quality.w: Audits examine whether the project complied with organisational processes and governance, while post-project reviews focus on results and lessons learned.

Quality.q: A construction project introduced quality procedures early and monitored them regularly; what benefit does this bring?
o: It removes the need to obtain stakeholder approval
It increases the likelihood that deliverables meet their specifications
It guarantees that no changes will occur during delivery
It reduces the amount of planning the team must do
Quality.w: Applying quality management consistently helps ensure deliverables meet agreed specifications and reduces the likelihood of rework.

Quality.q: A team defines, plans and controls its processes so that outputs satisfy customer expectations; what is the purpose of this?
o: To provide the cheapest possible product to the customer
To shorten the overall project life cycle
To ensure deliverables meet stakeholder-defined standards
To transfer quality responsibility across to the suppliers
Quality.w: The purpose of quality management is to define the agreed quality requirements and ensure they are met throughout the project.

Quality.q: A reviewer evaluates whether the design procedure in use will reliably yield acceptable results. Is this assurance or control?
o: Control, because it corrects a defect found in the product
Assurance, because it counts the number of finished items produced
Assurance, because it examines the process rather than a finished output
Control, because it inspects a completed deliverable against its specification
Quality.w: Examining whether a process will reliably yield acceptable results is quality assurance, which is process-focused.

Quality.q: A team regularly reviews the work completed so far, checking each output against its specification; which process is this?
o: Risk assessment activity
Resource optimisation activity
Communication planning work
Quality control of outputs
Quality.w: Quality control includes regular reviews and inspections to ensure deliverables meet their agreed specifications.

Quality.q: A team agrees, at the outset, the tolerances and acceptance criteria their deliverables must satisfy. This activity is an example of what?
o: Benefits management forecasting the project's value
Quality control checking against those criteria
Quality planning defining those criteria upfront
Quality assurance auditing the applied processes
Quality.w: Defining tolerances and acceptance criteria in advance is part of quality planning, which sets the requirements to be met.

Quality.q: Which activity is most closely associated with quality control on a project?
o: Defining the quality standards the project will need to meet
Inspecting completed deliverables against their agreed acceptance criteria
Planning how the quality assurance processes will be carried out
Conducting the post-project review once delivery is complete
Quality.w: Quality control inspects, tests or reviews completed deliverables against defined acceptance criteria to confirm they conform.

Quality.q: A project has quality procedures in place but never reviews whether the team follows them; what is missing?
o: Risk management activity
Scope management activity
Issue control activity
Quality assurance of processes
Quality.w: Without checks to verify process adherence, quality assurance is not being properly implemented.

Quality.q: A client asks what calling their deliverable 'quality' actually guarantees about it. What is the best answer?
o: That it conforms to its agreed requirements and is fit for its purpose
That it is the most advanced and expensive option available
That it includes every possible additional feature
That it was delivered faster than originally scheduled
Quality.w: Quality means conformance to agreed requirements and fitness for purpose, not maximum cost, features or speed.

Quality.q: Quality assurance is often described as 'process-focused'. What does this mean in practice?
o: It concentrates on ensuring the methods used can produce quality, rather than checking each output
It records risks and issues as they arise during delivery
It inspects every finished output and rejects those that fail
It focuses only on controlling the project's overall budget
Quality.w: Being process-focused, quality assurance ensures the methods used are capable of producing quality rather than inspecting each output.

Quality.q: Which statement best describes the purpose of carrying out a benefit review on a project?
o: An evaluation of whether the expected business benefits have been delivered
A report on the availability of the team once the project ends
A discussion of scope changes held with the project’s suppliers
An internal audit of the time-tracking systems used by staff
Quality.w: A benefits review assesses whether the anticipated benefits set out in the business case have actually been realised.

Quality.q: On a software project the team decides all deliverables must comply with a recognised standard; which aspect of quality planning is this?
o: Creating the change control procedures
Selecting the relevant quality standards
Defining the overall budget baseline
Documenting the lessons learned so far
Quality.w: Quality planning includes selecting the standards that will guide development and testing of deliverables.

Quality.q: Why does a project adopt quality management rather than relying on inspection alone?
o: To eliminate the need for any project documentation
To guarantee the project finishes ahead of schedule
To build quality in through planning, assurance and control
To remove the sponsor's involvement in the project
Quality.w: Quality management builds quality in through planning, assurance and control rather than depending on end inspection.

Quality.q: What does the quality planning process mainly set out to establish before delivery of a project begins?
o: The quality standards required and how they will be met
The defects found in completed deliverables
The market price of each project deliverable
The behavioural roles within the project team
Quality.w: Quality planning determines the relevant quality standards and requirements and defines how they will be achieved during the project.

Quality.q: Why are benefit reviews often carried out well after a project has finished?
o: To give the project team time to recover
To reduce the overall costs of the project
To allow benefits time to emerge and be measured
To avoid any pressure coming from the sponsors
Quality.w: Some benefits take time to materialise, so reviews after implementation assess whether those outcomes were achieved.

Quality.q: What is quality assurance primarily intended to prevent during the delivery of a project?
o: The need for any change requests to be raised during delivery
Disagreements arising between the project’s various stakeholders
Defects in deliverables, by ensuring the correct processes are followed
The approval of the project’s final outputs at each decision gate
Quality.w: By giving confidence that appropriate processes are being followed, quality assurance helps prevent defects arising in project deliverables.

Quality.q: What is the main purpose of holding a post-project review once delivery is complete?
o: To capture lessons learned and evaluate how the project performed
To gain approval for the final budget submitted by the project
To allocate the project’s resources to the next planned project
To assess the morale of the members of the project team
Quality.w: A post-project review evaluates performance and captures lessons learned so that future projects can benefit from the experience.

Quality.q: Why is it beneficial for a project to establish its quality management approach right at the start?
o: To ensure outputs meet requirements and are fit for purpose
To deliver the project in the shortest time possible
To transfer all quality responsibility across to the suppliers
To remove the need for any project documentation later
Quality.w: A quality management approach set from the outset helps ensure deliverables meet the required standards and are fit for purpose throughout the life cycle.

Quality.q: Which of the following techniques is most commonly used to carry out quality control?
o: A formal lessons learned report
Inspection and testing procedures
The work breakdown structure
Critical path analysis of tasks
Quality.w: Inspection and testing are key techniques in quality control, confirming that outputs meet requirements.

Quality.q: A client receives a product that looks impressive but fails to meet several contractual requirements. How would its quality be assessed?
o: It is high quality, because of its technical complexity
It is high quality, because it exceeded the client's expectations
It is low quality, because it does not meet the agreed requirements
It is acceptable quality, because the client was impressed by it
Quality.w: Quality is judged against the agreed requirements, so a product that fails to meet them is of low quality regardless of its appearance.

Quality.q: A sponsor asks how the project will make sure quality is managed, not just checked at the end. What is the best response?
o: Quality will only be inspected once the product is finished
Quality will be planned, assured and controlled throughout delivery
Quality will be measured solely by the final cost
Quality will be left entirely to the supplier to judge
Quality.w: Quality management spans planning, assurance and control throughout delivery, not just a final check.

Quality.q: Who should ideally take part in a post-project review to make it effective?
o: Key stakeholders, project team members and project leadership together
External consultants only, engaged specifically for the review
The finance department only, reviewing the project’s final costs
The project manager alone, without input from any other party
Quality.w: A broad group of those involved in the project should contribute so that the review provides a balanced and comprehensive evaluation.

Quality.q: A sponsor asks how the team ensures their processes consistently produce quality outputs; which process is most relevant?
o: Quality assurance of processes
Procurement planning work
Quality control of outputs
Stakeholder analysis activity
Quality.w: Quality assurance focuses on the processes used to ensure that quality outputs are consistently produced.

Quality.q: A deliverable performs exactly the job it was intended to do. In quality terms, this makes it what?
o: Fit for purpose, and therefore of good quality
Low grade, and therefore of poor quality
Over-specified, and therefore inherently wasteful
Non-conforming, and therefore automatically defective
Quality.w: A deliverable that does exactly the job intended is fit for purpose, which is the essence of quality.

Quality.q: Which of the following best defines 'quality planning' in the context of a project?
o: Controlling any slippage against the schedule
Determining how quality requirements will be defined and met
Documenting the risk responses that were chosen
Inspecting the finished deliverables to find defects
Quality.w: Quality planning determines the quality standards required and how they will be achieved across the project.

Quality.q: Which review focuses mainly on capturing lessons learned to improve future projects?
o: A benefit review
A post-project review
A decision gate
A configuration audit
Quality.w: A post-project review captures lessons learned so future projects can benefit from them.

Quality.q: A project manager wants confidence that both the process and the product will meet requirements. Which discipline provides this?
o: Benefits management
Quality management
Risk management
Configuration management
Quality.w: Quality management addresses both process and product, giving confidence that requirements will be met.

Quality.q: Quality control is often described as a 'detective' activity. What does carrying it out actually involve?
o: Inspecting and testing outputs to find any that do not meet requirements
Setting the quality standards and tolerances before the work begins
Auditing whether the correct processes are being followed consistently
Planning how quality will be managed across the whole project
Quality.w: Quality control is detective: it inspects and tests outputs to find non-conformances, unlike planning or assurance which are preventive.

Quality.q: At what point during a project should quality management activities be applied?
o: Only at the very end, once the product is finished
Only if a defect is reported by the customer
Only before any planning has begun
Throughout the life cycle, from planning through to delivery
Quality.w: Quality management runs throughout the life cycle, building quality in rather than checking only at the end.

Quality.q: What is the primary purpose of quality assurance within a project?
o: To ensure the processes used are effective and followed
To assign the available resources to tasks
To control and monitor the project budget
To inspect and test the final outputs
Quality.w: Quality assurance confirms that the quality processes used to produce deliverables are effective and being applied.

Quality.q: Which of the following outputs would typically result from the quality planning process?
o: A completed post-project review report
A quality plan defining standards and responsibilities
A signed contract with a chosen supplier
A register of risks and their owners
Quality.w: Quality planning produces a quality plan setting out the standards, methods and responsibilities for achieving quality.

Quality.q: A sponsor wants independent confirmation, during delivery, that governance and processes are being followed. Which mechanism serves this best?
o: A post-project review
A decision gate
A benefit review
A project audit
Quality.w: A project audit gives independent assurance that governance and processes are being applied correctly.

Quality.q: Before construction starts, a manager identifies standards, reviews specifications and outlines inspection procedures; which process is this?
o: Quality control of outputs
Quality assurance of processes
Quality planning for delivery
Issue management activity
Quality.w: Defining standards, requirements and inspection methods before execution is the essence of quality planning.

Quality.q: In quality management, which activity examines the product itself rather than the process that created it?
o: Quality control
Quality planning
Continuous improvement
Quality assurance
Quality.w: Quality control examines the product, that is the deliverable, whereas quality assurance examines the process used to create it.

Quality.q: A defect is discovered while the final product is being tested; which process is responsible for detecting it?
o: Change control process
Quality control of outputs
Risk management activity
Issue resolution activity
Quality.w: Quality control detects defects through the inspection and testing of deliverables.

Quality.q: A project audit examines whether the team followed agreed processes. What is the main purpose of carrying one out?
o: To assess adherence to agreed policies, procedures and governance
To assign blame to individuals for the project's problems
To plan the scope of work for the next project phase
To approve the final invoice submitted by the suppliers
Quality.w: A project audit checks whether project activities have complied with internal and external standards and governance requirements.

Quality.q: What does passing through successive decision gates help to confirm about a project during its life?
o: That it remains viable and justified before further resources are committed
That its scope can never again be altered
That all of its benefits have already been realised
That the delivery team has followed every process correctly
Quality.w: Decision gates repeatedly confirm the project remains viable and justified before more resources are committed.

Quality.q: How does the term 'quality' differ from the term 'grade' in a project context?
o: Grade measures conformance, while quality ranks features by luxury
Quality means a higher grade; the two terms are identical
Quality is meeting requirements; grade is a category of features
Quality always requires the most expensive materials available
Quality.w: Quality is conformance to requirements, while grade categorises features or characteristics; a low grade can still be high quality.

Quality.q: Which of the following is the most likely outcome of a project audit?
o: Recommendations to improve governance and process adherence
The immediate release of all the project's resources
A revised business case approved by the sponsor
A new procurement strategy for future contracts
Quality.w: Audits are intended to produce recommendations that strengthen process compliance and governance for the current or future projects.

Quality.q: A benefit review is scheduled some months after a project completes; what is its primary purpose?
o: To close down all of the procurement contracts
To assign new tasks to the former project team
To begin a fresh change control process
To determine whether planned benefits have been realised
Quality.w: Benefit reviews assess whether the expected outcomes and benefits have actually been delivered after implementation.

Quality.q: A team measures completed components against their tolerances and rejects those that fail to conform. Which quality activity is this?
o: Quality planning
Quality control
Quality assurance
Configuration control
Quality.w: Measuring completed outputs against tolerances and rejecting non-conforming items is quality control.

Planning.q: Stakeholder analysis shows a group of community residents to have low influence but high interest. What is the recommended approach?
o: Avoid all engagement until after delivery
Monitor them only if they raise a concern
Manage them closely and involve them in every decision
Keep them informed through regular updates and consultation
Planning.w: Low-influence, high-interest stakeholders should be kept informed to maintain support and prevent misinformation.

Planning.q: Early in the design phase a team produces an estimate with a tolerance of around plus or minus 40%. What does this represent in the estimating funnel?
o: A confirmed contingency figure
A final, validated estimate
A preliminary, high-level estimate
A detailed bottom-up estimate
Planning.w: Wide tolerances such as plus or minus 40% are typical of the preliminary, high-level estimates near the top of the funnel.

Planning.q: At handover, the sponsor asks for evidence that the project met its objectives. Which element should the project manager refer to?
o: The communication plan produced during delivery
The success criteria agreed at project initiation
The work breakdown structure for the project
The procurement strategy used for the project
Planning.w: The success criteria agreed at initiation provide the benchmark against which achievement of the objectives is judged at closure.

Planning.q: Which estimating technique is best suited when detailed information is unavailable and a quick estimate is needed?
o: Analytical estimating
Analogous estimating
Three-point estimating
Parametric estimating
Planning.w: Analogous estimating provides a quick, high-level estimate based on past projects when detailed data is not yet available.

Planning.q: What is the main benefit of using traffic light (RAG) status in project progress reports?
o: It conceals emerging issues from the stakeholders
It communicates status simply using clear visual cues
It replaces the project's earned value calculations
It removes the need for any narrative reporting
Planning.w: RAG status gives a quick, visual indication of performance, making status easy to grasp and supporting rapid decision-making.

Planning.q: Which two dimensions are typically used in an influence/interest matrix for stakeholder analysis?
o: Influence and interest
Support and opposition
Cost and time
Risk and reward
Planning.w: The matrix maps stakeholders by their power to affect the project (influence) and their level of concern (interest).

Planning.q: What is a primary benefit of producing regular project progress reports for the sponsor?
o: They replace the project's risk register entirely
They remove the need to engage with project stakeholders
They finalise the agreed scope of the project
They inform sponsor decisions and enable timely intervention
Planning.w: Regular reports give the sponsor visibility of status, risks and deviations, supporting informed decisions and proactive corrective action.

Planning.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between benefits and outputs?
o: Benefits are the measurable value achieved through using the outputs
Benefits are the deliverables that the project creates
Outputs always exceed the benefits they produce
Outputs are the future outcomes that are derived from benefits
Planning.w: Outputs are what the project delivers; benefits are the measurable value that arises from using those outputs.

Planning.q: What does a flexible deployment baseline allow a team to do in an iterative project?
o: Avoid the need for governance reviews
Work without any documentation or tracking
Respond to evolving user needs as they emerge
Make changes without any impact on the project
Planning.w: A flexible baseline lets an iterative team remain responsive to changing requirements while still planning and tracking work.

Planning.q: Throughout the life of a project, who holds overall ownership of the business case and its continued validity?
o: The project sponsor
The project manager
The project team
The end users
Planning.w: The sponsor owns the business case and is accountable for ensuring the investment remains justified throughout the project.

Planning.q: As sponsor, what should you do if the business case is found to be no longer valid during delivery?
o: Pause the project and update the business case for governance review
Instruct the team to continue with the work regardless
Increase the project's scope to add further value
Remove the project's risk management procedures
Planning.w: The sponsor must keep the business case valid; if it is not, work should be paused and approval sought for any change.

Planning.q: Analysis places a senior regulator as high influence but low interest in day-to-day detail. How should they be engaged?
o: Kept satisfied with concise, high-level updates rather than routine detail
Sent every operational report so nothing is ever withheld from them
Left entirely uninformed until the project has been formally closed
Given full control over prioritising the project team's daily tasks
Planning.w: High-influence, low-interest stakeholders should be kept satisfied with proportionate, high-level information rather than routine detail.

Planning.q: Why are estimates at the top of the estimating funnel less accurate than those produced later?
o: Because the risk register has not yet been created
Because detailed scope and task data are not yet available
Because all projects rely on top-down budgeting at that point
Because agile approaches avoid planning at that stage
Planning.w: Early estimates rest on assumptions and high-level inputs because the detailed scope and work breakdown structure do not yet exist.

Planning.q: At which points in the life cycle do the sponsor and project manager jointly review the business case?
o: Only once the project has been formally closed
Solely at the point a change request is raised
At project initiation and at key decision gates
Only after the benefits have been fully realised
Planning.w: They review the case together at initiation and at decision gates to confirm the justification remains valid.

Planning.q: A product meets every technical specification, yet customer feedback is negative. What most likely went wrong?
o: The deployment baseline was disregarded
The success criteria did not include user satisfaction
Too much emphasis was placed on iterative delivery
Stakeholders were engaged too frequently
Planning.w: Success criteria focused only on technical outputs can omit qualitative measures such as user satisfaction.

Planning.q: At a project board meeting, stakeholders are found to disagree on what constitutes project success. What is the most likely cause?
o: Lessons learned were not reviewed
Too much time was spent on procurement
The project budget was exceeded
Success criteria were not clearly defined and agreed at the start
Planning.w: When success criteria are not defined and agreed early, stakeholders interpret success differently, causing misalignment.

Planning.q: Which of the following is least likely to be a genuine stakeholder in a project management plan?
o: A supplier with no involvement in the project
The project sponsor authorising the plan
The end users who will operate the output
The team members delivering the work packages
Planning.w: A stakeholder has an interest in or is affected by the project; a supplier with no involvement has no such stake in the plan.

Planning.q: Which estimating method is most suitable for a project with high uncertainty in its early planning stage?
o: Analytical estimating
Parametric estimating
Analogous estimating
Three-point estimating
Planning.w: Analogous estimating gives rough early estimates based on prior projects when detail is minimal and uncertainty is high.

Planning.q: Stakeholder analysis identifies a group as both highly influential and highly resistant. What should the engagement strategy prioritise?
o: Reassigning them to a different project
Proactively engaging them to understand concerns and seek alignment
Sending them brief updates by email only
Ignoring them unless they choose to escalate
Planning.w: Highly influential yet resistant stakeholders must be actively engaged to reduce opposition and secure buy-in.

Planning.q: A project manager compares actual cost and progress against the plan approved before delivery to identify variances. What are they comparing against?
o: The risk register
The deployment baseline
The stakeholder analysis
The quality plan
Planning.w: Variances are measured against the deployment baseline, the approved plan for scope, cost and schedule.

Planning.q: Having developed a targeted engagement plan from stakeholder analysis, what is the next logical step?
o: Cancel all project communications until delivery begins
Implement the engagement activities aligned to each stakeholder profile
Replace the risk assessments with stakeholder assessments
Assign the delivery tasks to the project sponsor
Planning.w: The analysis and plan lead into delivering the engagement activities so communication stays relevant and timely for each group.

Planning.q: Beyond control, what wider benefit does transparent progress reporting bring to a project's stakeholders?
o: It builds stakeholder confidence and trust
It ensures no changes are ever requested
It removes the sponsor from the governance chain
It abolishes the need for a communication plan
Planning.w: Open, accurate reporting builds stakeholder confidence and trust in the project's management and direction.

Planning.q: During a gate review of the business case, what is the project manager's main role?
o: To determine the project's strategic alignment
To provide updates on justification and delivery feasibility
To chair the project governance board
To formally approve continued investment in the project
Planning.w: The project manager supplies delivery information that helps the sponsor present the case for continuation; approval rests with governance.

Planning.q: Midway through delivery a previously minor stakeholder gains significant influence. What does this imply for stakeholder analysis?
o: It should be ignored because the original analysis is now fixed
It should be revisited so engagement reflects their changed position
It shows analysis is only ever useful before the project starts
It means engagement should stop until the project is closed
Planning.w: Stakeholder analysis is iterative; as positions change it is revisited so engagement remains effective.

Planning.q: Why is it important to consider success criteria during the handover phase of a project?
o: To benchmark actual outcomes against the planned objectives
To allow the project budget to be closed early
To reassign the project team more quickly
To ensure the client signs off regardless of delivery quality
Planning.w: At handover, success criteria are used to confirm that deliverables and outcomes meet the agreed objectives.

Planning.q: A project manager explains why a linear deployment baseline feels more rigid than an iterative one. Which explanation is correct?
o: Linear fixes it early, while iterative refines it each iteration
Both fix the baseline rigidly before any delivery starts
Both leave the baseline entirely open until closure
Iterative fixes it early, while linear evolves over time
Planning.w: A linear life cycle establishes a firm baseline early, whereas an iterative life cycle refines the baseline across successive iterations.

Planning.q: The project management plan is agreed between the project manager and which party who approves it on behalf of the organisation?
o: The project team members
The external suppliers
The end users
The project sponsor
Planning.w: The PMP is owned by the project manager but approved by the sponsor, who represents the organisation's interests.

Planning.q: Within a project, who is normally responsible for developing and maintaining the project management plan?
o: The end users, who receive and operate the project’s final outputs
The project team members, who deliver the work packages defined within it
The project sponsor, who owns the business case on behalf of the organisation
The project manager, who develops and maintains it throughout delivery
Planning.w: The project manager owns and maintains the project management plan, which sets out how the project will be delivered on behalf of the sponsor.

Planning.q: Which estimating tolerance would you most expect to find towards the bottom of the estimating funnel?
o: Around plus or minus 40%
Around plus or minus 50%
Around plus or minus 25%
Around plus or minus 10% or less
Planning.w: The bottom of the funnel reflects higher confidence and more detailed information, so tolerances narrow to around plus or minus 10% or less.

Planning.q: Why does stakeholder analysis help a project manager use limited engagement time efficiently?
o: It highlights where to focus effort by ranking influence and interest
It confirms that all stakeholders require identical levels of contact
It replaces the need for a communication plan later in delivery
It transfers responsibility for engagement to the project sponsor
Planning.w: By ranking influence and interest, analysis shows where engagement effort will have most value, allowing resources to be focused.

Planning.q: Which of the following best describes a benefit of conducting stakeholder analysis?
o: It improves communication planning by aligning strategy to stakeholder needs
It guarantees that every stakeholder will support the project
It removes the need for a separate risk management plan
It ensures that only internal stakeholders are involved
Planning.w: Understanding influence and interest allows communication and engagement to be aligned to each group's needs.

Planning.q: A sponsor asks what benefits management will contribute once the new system is operational. What is the best answer?
o: It will close the project's contracts with its suppliers
It will track and confirm that the expected improvements are actually achieved
It will approve any further changes to the system's scope
It will build and test the remaining system components
Planning.w: Benefits management tracks and confirms that the expected improvements are actually realised once the output is in use.

Planning.q: A sponsor wants one document setting out why the project is worth doing and what it will cost. Which document meets this need?
o: The business case
The quality plan
The risk register
The communication plan
Planning.w: The business case explains why the project is worthwhile, presenting its justification, costs, benefits and risks in a single document.

Planning.q: While revising the project management plan, a project manager notices there has been no input from the senior supplier. What risk does this pose?
o: Delivery capability and logistics could be misaligned
The project may receive excessive funding
Stakeholder interest will rise unexpectedly
The benefits are likely to be over-delivered
Planning.w: Without supplier input the plan's delivery logistics may be unrealistic or misaligned with the supplier's capacity.

Planning.q: An office build is estimated by applying a known cost per square metre to the floor area. Which estimating method is being used?
o: Expert judgement
Analytical estimating
Analogous estimating
Parametric estimating
Planning.w: Parametric estimating applies a known cost per unit to a measured quantity to derive the total estimate.

Planning.q: Why is it important to establish project success criteria during the initiation phase?
o: To remove the need to prepare a business case
To allow the project to be closed sooner
To allocate individual tasks to team members
To define clear performance expectations that guide later decisions
Planning.w: Defining success criteria early gives a basis for measuring progress, guiding decisions and managing stakeholder expectations.

Planning.q: A delivery partner disputes the agreed timeline partway through the project. Which document validates the originally agreed plan?
o: The stakeholder matrix
The change control log
The deployment baseline
The communication strategy
Planning.w: The deployment baseline holds the agreed timeline and is the authoritative reference for resolving such disputes.

Planning.q: What is the purpose of the estimating funnel in project planning?
o: To identify the benefits associated with each deliverable
To select the most competitive supplier for the work
To measure the performance of the project team
To progressively narrow cost and time estimates as more information becomes available
Planning.w: The estimating funnel refines estimates and reduces tolerance over time as project knowledge increases.

Planning.q: What is the main purpose of a deployment baseline once a project moves into delivery?
o: To provide a fixed reference against which progress and variance are measured
To record the names and contact details of all project stakeholders
To list the recognised standards that the deliverables must comply with
To capture the lessons learned for use on future similar projects
Planning.w: The deployment baseline serves as the benchmark for monitoring performance and identifying variances during delivery.

Planning.q: Why is it important to establish a deployment baseline before project execution begins?
o: It enables scope, cost and time to be measured and controlled
It removes the need to produce a business case
It provides the content for marketing the project
It satisfies post-project reporting obligations only
Planning.w: The deployment baseline provides the reference against which performance is measured and change is controlled during delivery.

Planning.q: Within a business case, the expected benefits are weighed against which two factors to justify proceeding with the investment?
o: The costs and the risks of the investment
The schedule bar chart and the communication plan
The team structure and the individual reporting lines
The test scripts and the recorded defect logs
Planning.w: A business case justifies the investment by weighing the expected benefits against its costs and risks; schedules, team structures and test records are not what the benefits are balanced against.

Planning.q: Within the discipline of benefits management, a 'benefit' is most accurately defined as what?
o: A risk that has occurred and now requires resolution
A tangible product created by the project's delivery work
A task that must be completed before another can begin
A measurable improvement resulting from an outcome, seen as advantageous
Planning.w: A benefit is a measurable improvement, arising from an outcome, that is perceived as advantageous by stakeholders.

Planning.q: Which of the following is the strongest success criterion for a new healthcare IT system?
o: Users agree the system improves the patient experience
Every stakeholder is invited to the project meetings
No existing member of staff changes their role
All project invoices are settled within thirty days
Planning.w: An outcome-focused, user-centred measure such as improved patient experience reflects the benefits the project is intended to deliver.

Planning.q: Why is it inappropriate for a project sponsor to delegate ownership of the business case entirely to the project manager?
o: Delegating it would automatically cancel the project's approved funding
The project manager is not permitted to view the business case at any stage
The project manager already owns the project's risk and quality registers
Ownership must remain with the sponsor, who is accountable for the investment's benefits
Planning.w: The sponsor owns the business case because they are accountable for realising the investment's benefits; that ownership cannot be handed to the project manager.

Planning.q: During development of the project management plan, which stakeholder is most involved in defining scope and quality requirements?
o: The project sponsor
The team leader
The project governance board
The product owner
Planning.w: The product owner articulates what needs to be delivered and sets the associated quality expectations.

Planning.q: During delivery, a team finds that the original success criteria are no longer relevant. What is the best course of action?
o: Abandon the criteria and rely on team discretion
Continue using the original criteria regardless
Replace the criteria without consulting stakeholders
Revise and formally agree the updated criteria with key stakeholders
Planning.w: Success criteria must stay relevant and should be updated through agreed change control involving key stakeholders.

Planning.q: A target of a 30% reduction in complaint-handling time is set for your project. How does this relate to benefits management?
o: It is a deliverable produced during the project
It is a risk mitigation measure
It is a benefit that must be tracked and realised after delivery
It is a constraint placed on the project
Planning.w: The reduction is a measurable benefit that must be tracked and realised to demonstrate the project's value.

Planning.q: An estimate for a new school is based on a similar previous school build, adjusted slightly for inflation. Which estimating method is this?
o: Analytical estimating
Analogous estimating
Three-point estimating
Parametric estimating
Planning.w: Using a comparable completed project as the basis for an estimate, with minor adjustment, is analogous estimating.

Planning.q: At what point in the estimating funnel is a detailed bottom-up estimate typically produced?
o: Immediately after the contract is signed
When the full scope and work breakdown structure are available
After the post-project review is complete
At the initial project concept stage
Planning.w: Bottom-up estimating requires a detailed scope and work breakdown structure, which are available mid-to-late in the funnel.

Planning.q: What is the key difference between parametric estimating and analogous estimating when producing a project estimate?
o: Parametric relies on expert opinion, while analogous applies statistical formulae
Parametric is used only at handover, while analogous is used only at initiation
Parametric suits iterative projects only, while analogous suits linear projects only
Parametric uses historical per-unit data, while analogous compares whole completed projects
Planning.w: Parametric estimating scales historical cost or duration per unit, whereas analogous estimating draws on the overall data from a similar completed project.

Planning.q: How does benefits management differ from simply producing and delivering a project's outputs?
o: It focuses on realising the value the outputs are meant to create
It concentrates only on producing the outputs to specification
It ends the moment the outputs are handed over to users
It ignores the outcomes and measures only delivery on time
Planning.w: Outputs enable outcomes and benefits; benefits management focuses on realising the value rather than merely producing outputs.

Planning.q: A project was delivered on time and within budget, yet a stakeholder claims it was not successful. What most likely caused this disagreement?
o: The risk register was not kept up to date
The project board was disbanded too early
Lessons learned were not formally recorded
Success criteria were not clearly defined and agreed at the start
Planning.w: Without clear, agreed success criteria at the outset, stakeholders can hold conflicting views of what constitutes success.

Planning.q: At handover, the operations team asks how it will be judged whether the project met its goals. What should they be shown?
o: The agreed project success criteria
The project communication plan
The project risk register
The project stakeholder map
Planning.w: The agreed success criteria are the standard against which the project's achievement of its goals is judged at handover.

Planning.q: Which statement best describes the purpose of the estimating funnel within a project?
o: It maps the costs of each resource against the responsible stakeholders
It limits the number of estimates that may be produced to three
It illustrates how the accuracy of estimates improves as the project matures
It applies only within iterative project environments that use sprints
Planning.w: The estimating funnel shows that estimates become more accurate and their range narrows as more information becomes known through the life cycle.

Planning.q: Which statement best describes analytical, or bottom-up, estimating as used to produce a project estimate?
o: Producing a top-down figure based on the overall size of the project
Building a total estimate by summing the estimated costs of individual tasks
Comparing the project with a previous initiative of broadly similar scope
Reaching a figure through repeated rounds of anonymous expert consensus
Planning.w: Analytical, or bottom-up, estimating totals the estimates for individual tasks or work packages to produce an overall project estimate.

Planning.q: Before a project is authorised, what is the main reason an organisation requires a business case to be produced?
o: To justify the investment by setting out its costs, benefits and risks
To list every task and dependency needed to build the product
To assign the day-to-day responsibilities across the whole project team
To record the detailed technical design of the final project deliverable
Planning.w: The business case justifies the investment by presenting the costs, benefits, risks and options, providing the basis for the decision to proceed.

Planning.q: Which of the following statements best defines the term 'benefits management' in a project context?
o: The production and testing of the project's outputs before handover
The identification, planning, tracking and realisation of a project's benefits
The scheduling of tasks so the project finishes by its agreed deadline
The control of changes to the project's approved scope baseline
Planning.w: Benefits management is the identification, definition, planning, tracking and realisation of the benefits a project is intended to deliver.

Planning.q: A business case presents only one delivery option. What weakness does this introduce?
o: It demonstrates that the approach is more agile
It removes the need for any stakeholder input
It automatically makes the project easier to fund
It limits consideration of alternatives and weakens the justification
Planning.w: Without alternatives to compare against, the case cannot demonstrate that the chosen option delivers the best value.

Planning.q: An estimate based on an industry-average unit cost is challenged as insufficiently accurate. How could its accuracy best be improved?
o: By breaking the work down and applying analytical estimating
By relying on expert guesswork instead
By substituting an analogous estimate
By adding a fixed contingency percentage
Planning.w: Analytical, bottom-up estimating improves accuracy by evaluating each component individually rather than applying a single average rate.

Planning.q: A sponsor complains they only hear about problems once they are severe. Which reporting improvement would most directly address this?
o: Reporting exclusively on completed deliverables
Reporting only when the sponsor formally requests it
Reporting only at the project's closure stage
Reporting progress regularly with early variance alerts
Planning.w: Regular reporting with timely variance information gives early warning, preventing problems from being discovered only when severe.

Planning.q: An agile team forecasts remaining effort by extrapolating from its established average sprint velocity. Which estimating method does this represent?
o: Parametric estimating
Three-point estimating
Analytical estimating
Analogous estimating
Planning.w: Applying a known unit rate, such as story points per sprint, to extrapolate a total is a form of parametric estimating.

Planning.q: During initiation the project manager drafts cost and risk information while the sponsor decides on strategic justification. What does this show?
o: The two roles collaborate, with the manager informing and the sponsor owning the case
The two roles entirely duplicate each other's responsibilities and effort
The project manager holds ultimate accountability for the whole investment
The sponsor is responsible only for producing the detailed cost estimates
Planning.w: Developing the business case is collaborative: the project manager provides delivery information while the sponsor owns and justifies the investment.

Planning.q: What is one benefit of defining clear success criteria at the beginning of a project?
o: They remove the need to produce a stakeholder map
They guarantee that the schedule cannot slip
They avoid the need for a post-project review
They provide a clear benchmark for evaluating performance
Planning.w: Clear success criteria give a measurable benchmark for judging whether objectives were achieved and for justifying decisions.

Planning.q: Which statement best characterises how estimate tolerance behaves as a project moves through the estimating funnel?
o: Tolerance stays constant from concept through to delivery
Tolerance widens steadily as the project progresses
Tolerance is only ever expressed as a single fixed value
Tolerance narrows progressively as knowledge and detail increase
Planning.w: Estimate tolerance narrows progressively through the funnel as increasing knowledge and detail reduce uncertainty.

Planning.q: A team switching from a linear to an iterative approach asks how their deployment baseline will now behave. What is the best answer?
o: It will be locked for the entire project duration
It will be updated as requirements emerge each iteration
It will be removed because iterative work has no plan
It will be signed off only at the concept stage
Planning.w: Iterative delivery updates the deployment baseline as requirements emerge and are prioritised in each iteration, rather than locking it once.

Planning.q: How does the estimating funnel help justify revisiting cost estimates at each stage of a project?
o: It demonstrates that later estimates are inherently less trustworthy
It confirms estimates should only ever be produced at project closure
It proves that the first estimate given should be treated as final
It shows that increasing knowledge legitimately allows estimates to be refined over time
Planning.w: The funnel shows that greater knowledge at each stage legitimately allows estimates to be refined, justifying revisiting them.

Planning.q: A project manager analyses delivery options and their associated risks for the business case. How does this help the sponsor?
o: It improves the credibility and delivery accuracy of the business case
It guarantees the sponsor's independence from delivery
It allows the project manager to approve the project budget
It removes the need for any governance review of the case
Planning.w: By supplying delivery detail, the project manager helps the sponsor produce a credible, evidence-based justification.

Planning.q: Which statement best describes the shared responsibility of the sponsor and project manager in developing the business case?
o: The project manager owns it and the sponsor merely signs it off
The sponsor owns it and the project manager contributes delivery detail
The finance team writes it without involving either role
The PMO is solely responsible for writing and approving it
Planning.w: The sponsor owns the business case while the project manager supports its development with delivery-focused content.

Planning.q: Which of the following would you typically expect to find within a well-structured business case?
o: The project closure checklist and lessons learned
Options analysis, investment appraisal and success criteria
A record of every risk the project has identified
A detailed daily stand-up schedule for the team
Planning.w: A business case typically sets out the options considered, the investment appraisal and the success criteria that justify proceeding.

Planning.q: Which of the following is least likely to form part of a business case?
o: The investment appraisal
The project rationale
The options analysis
A detailed stakeholder engagement matrix
Planning.w: Detailed stakeholder engagement planning sits within the project management plan rather than the business case.

Planning.q: Why does benefits management typically continue after a project has been formally closed?
o: Because outstanding project risks can only be reviewed after closure
Because many benefits are realised during operational use rather than during delivery
Because the project baseline must be recalculated once delivery ends
Because the next phase of delivery must be planned after handover
Planning.w: Benefits such as cost savings or improved service are usually realised once outputs are in operational use, so benefits management extends beyond project closure.

Planning.q: Why should the project sponsor be actively involved as a stakeholder in agreeing the project management plan?
o: Because the sponsor owns the business case and provides direction
Because the sponsor writes each work package personally
Because the sponsor tests each deliverable for quality
Because the sponsor performs the day-to-day delivery tasks
Planning.w: The sponsor owns the business case and provides strategic direction, so their agreement ensures the plan aligns with the organisation's aims.

Planning.q: Why is the sponsor, rather than the project manager, held accountable for the business case throughout the project?
o: Because the sponsor produces the detailed cost estimates used in delivery
Because the sponsor manages the project's day-to-day activities and tasks
Because the sponsor writes the technical specification of the product
Because the sponsor owns the investment and is answerable for its benefits
Planning.w: The sponsor owns the investment and is accountable for realising its benefits, which is why the business case sits with them, not the project manager.

Planning.q: When reviewing a colleague's draft business case, which of the following would you expect to be a core component?
o: The finalised test scripts to be used in verifying each deliverable
The individual holiday schedules of every member of the project team
The minutes of every project progress meeting held to date
The expected benefits, costs, timescales and risks of the proposed investment
Planning.w: A business case sets out the anticipated benefits, costs, timescales and risks of the investment; test scripts, holiday schedules and meeting minutes are not core content.

Planning.q: Which statement best describes the way in which regular progress reporting supports effective control of a project?
o: It transfers accountability from the sponsor to users
It fixes the deployment baseline permanently in place
It measures progress so deviations can be corrected
It records lessons only after the project has closed
Planning.w: By measuring progress against plan, reporting exposes deviations so the project manager can take corrective action, supporting control.

Planning.q: When developing the communication content of a project management plan, which group most needs clearly defined roles and timely updates in order to deliver the work?
o: The project team members
The regulatory authorities
The general public
The external suppliers
Planning.w: Project team members carry out the work, so they require clear responsibilities and regular, relevant updates to perform effectively.

Planning.q: A sponsor asks for a summary of how the project is performing against its key milestones. Which document best provides this?
o: The work breakdown structure
The project progress report
The lessons learned log
The project risk register
Planning.w: The progress report summarises current status against milestones, budget and performance indicators for decision-makers.

Planning.q: What is the primary purpose of a business case in the context of project management?
o: To define the engagement approach for each stakeholder
To justify the investment by weighing benefits, costs and risks
To schedule the daily activities of the delivery team
To assign roles and responsibilities across the project team
Planning.w: The business case provides the justification for investment, setting out expected benefits against the associated costs and risks.

Planning.q: During delivery, a scope change is identified that will affect cost and schedule. What is the first step the project manager should take?
o: Continue as planned and ignore the change
Reassign the work without recording it
Compare the proposed change against the deployment baseline
Notify stakeholders that the project will close
Planning.w: Proposed changes are first assessed against the deployment baseline to determine their impact and whether approval is required.

Planning.q: At which point in a project is analogous estimating typically most useful?
o: Late in delivery when every work package is fully specified
Early on, when little detail exists but similar past projects do
Only after the critical path has been finalised
Only once the product has been handed over to operations
Planning.w: Analogous estimating draws on similar completed projects, making it valuable early when detailed information is scarce.

Planning.q: When identifying the stakeholders of a project management plan, which of the following would not normally be included?
o: An external auditor
The product owner
A project team member
The project sponsor
Planning.w: The project management plan focuses on delivery stakeholders; an external auditor is not typically among them.

Planning.q: A project manager is planning a new construction project. Who should be consulted to ensure operational handover requirements are captured in the plan?
o: The wider project team
The programme director
The end users
The project management office
Planning.w: End users define the operational needs that must be met for a successful handover into use.

Planning.q: During the early planning of a project with little detailed information, which estimating method is most appropriate?
o: Parametric estimating
Three-point estimating
Analytical estimating
Analogous estimating
Planning.w: Analogous estimating suits early planning, using high-level comparison with previous projects when detail is scarce.

Planning.q: Why is stakeholder analysis important during the planning phase of a project?
o: It removes all project risks before delivery begins
It ensures all project tasks are assigned to the project manager
It identifies stakeholder interests so engagement can be tailored accordingly
It completes the procurement documentation ahead of time
Planning.w: Stakeholder analysis reveals interest and influence, enabling engagement to be targeted for smoother delivery.

Planning.q: Why should an early-stage estimate be presented as a range rather than a single figure, according to the estimating funnel?
o: Because the range will always prove more accurate than the final cost
Because presenting a range removes the need for any later estimates
Because limited information at that stage means the estimate carries wide uncertainty
Because single-figure estimates are never permitted under APM guidance
Planning.w: At an early stage limited information means the estimate carries wide uncertainty, so the funnel shows it is best expressed as a broad range.

Planning.q: A total cost is built up from detailed specifications and individual work package estimates. Which estimating method does this describe?
o: Analytical (bottom-up) estimating
Analogous estimating
Three-point estimating
Parametric estimating
