Planning.w: Analytical, or bottom-up, estimating aggregates detailed estimates from individual work packages to produce the overall figure.

Planning.q: What information is typically contained within a formal project progress report?
o: A complete list of the project's suppliers
Progress against plan, key risks, issues and forecast to complete
A post-project analysis of the benefits realised
The scope baseline and a full stakeholder map
Planning.w: A progress report typically sets out current status against the plan, key risks and issues, and a forecast of the outcome.

Planning.q: An app is being built in agile using short sprints, with priorities changing after each review. What does this mean for the deployment baseline?
o: It is defined fully at the start and never altered
It does not exist on agile projects
It is flexible and reviewed frequently
It contains only the cost baseline
Planning.w: In iterative and agile approaches the baseline is flexible and reviewed regularly as the project progresses.

Planning.q: In a project to digitise patient records, which activity best demonstrates benefits management?
o: Tracking supplier invoices during the system rollout
Identifying, measuring and realising improvements in access to patient data
Ensuring clinical staff are trained before the system goes live
Producing the project's quality register
Planning.w: Benefits management focuses on identifying, measuring and realising value, such as improved access to patient data.

Planning.q: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of establishing success criteria at the start of a project?
o: It aligns the expectations of the project stakeholders
It removes the need for formal project governance
It guides decisions about scope and quality
It provides clear measures for evaluating performance
Planning.w: Success criteria support evaluation, alignment and decision-making, but they do not replace the need for governance structures.

Planning.q: A trade union group with a history of resisting change is assessed as high influence and high interest. What is the most suitable engagement strategy?
o: Delay engagement until executive approval is granted
Withhold project documents from them
Assign a junior team member to manage the relationship
Engage them early and involve them in planning to address concerns
Planning.w: High-influence, high-interest stakeholders should be engaged closely and early to reduce resistance and gain their input.

Planning.q: How does understanding stakeholders' interests through analysis improve project communication?
o: It removes the need to consider how messages are received
It allows the same generic message to be issued to everyone
It enables messages to be shaped to each group's needs and concerns
It ensures only good news is ever shared with stakeholders
Planning.w: Knowing each group's interests allows communications to be shaped to their needs, supporting more effective engagement.

Planning.q: A team agrees its delivery scope, timeline and budget, and this is recorded and approved before work begins. What has been established?
o: A procurement strategy
A risk threshold
A communication plan
A deployment baseline
Planning.w: An agreed and approved reference for scope, time and cost before execution describes the deployment baseline.

Planning.q: A sponsor asks the project manager to refresh the cost and benefit figures within the business case. Why is this appropriate?
o: The manager is taking over ownership of the case from the sponsor
The manager alone now decides whether the project should continue
The manager supplies delivery information so the sponsor can keep it current
The manager becomes accountable for the realisation of the benefits
Planning.w: The project manager provides updated delivery information to help the sponsor keep the business case current; ownership and accountability remain with the sponsor.

Planning.q: A deliverable is completed on time and within budget, yet the customer is dissatisfied. Which success criteria were most likely overlooked?
o: Measures reflecting the schedule's baseline dates
Measures reflecting the supplier payment terms
Measures reflecting the project's risk tolerance
Measures reflecting user acceptance and satisfaction
Planning.w: Success criteria should capture user acceptance and satisfaction, not only time and cost, so that the outcome genuinely meets the customer's needs.

Planning.q: A sponsor of a linear construction project asks how often the deployment baseline will change during delivery. What is the most accurate reply?
o: Rarely, and only through formal change control
Weekly, as part of routine iteration planning
Never, even where formal changes are approved
Constantly, after every single working day
Planning.w: In a linear life cycle the baseline is fixed early and only altered through formal change control, so changes are infrequent.

Planning.q: Which of the following would be the weakest choice of project success criterion?
o: Delivery within the approved budget tolerance
Achievement of the required technical specification
Stakeholder satisfaction above an agreed threshold
An improvement in team morale during the project
Planning.w: Team morale is subjective and not directly tied to the project's deliverables, making it a poor, hard-to-measure success criterion.

Planning.q: Which of the following activities best reflects the sponsor's particular role in relation to the project's business case?
o: Testing the completed deliverables against their acceptance criteria
Championing and defending the investment at senior decision-making levels
Maintaining the project's day-to-day risk and issue registers
Producing the detailed schedule and resource plan for the delivery work
Planning.w: The sponsor champions and defends the business case at senior level; scheduling, testing and register maintenance are project manager or team responsibilities.

Planning.q: At handover a customer claims the product is unacceptable while the team believes it is complete. Which reference best resolves this dispute?
o: The agreed success criteria
The procurement strategy
The communication plan
The risk register
Planning.w: Pre-agreed success criteria give an objective standard against which acceptance at handover can be judged, resolving such disputes.

Planning.q: A project manager combines a per-square-metre rate with a similar building's actual cost to sense-check figures. Which two methods are being used?
o: Bottom-up and comparative estimating
Qualitative and residual estimating
Parametric and analogous estimating
Analytical and Delphi estimating
Planning.w: Applying a unit rate is parametric, while comparing against a similar building's actuals is analogous estimating.

Planning.q: Midway through an iterative project, stakeholders reprioritise features. What effect does this typically have on the deployment baseline?
o: It invalidates the baseline, so it must be deleted
It freezes the baseline until the project closes
It has no effect, as the baseline is permanently fixed
It updates the baseline to reflect the revised priorities
Planning.w: An iterative deployment baseline is expected to evolve, so reprioritised features are absorbed by updating the baseline for the next iterations.

Planning.q: A sponsor insists that stakeholder feedback be included as a success measure. What does this illustrate about effective success criteria?
o: They must always be expressed in financial terms
They should include both objective and subjective elements
They should exclude any measure of user experience
They are best defined at project closure
Planning.w: Good success criteria combine measurable, objective outcomes with subjective elements such as stakeholder satisfaction.

Planning.q: At closure, a team wants to confirm whether the expected objectives and benefits have been achieved. Which element should they refer to?
o: The stakeholder matrix
The work breakdown structure
The success criteria agreed during initiation
The change control log
Planning.w: The success criteria agreed at initiation provide the benchmark for evaluating whether outcomes and benefits have been delivered.

Planning.q: In a linear project the baseline for time, cost and scope is set at the start. What is the key challenge if significant changes are later needed?
o: There is no means of tracking the change
The whole project has to be restarted
Baselines cannot be documented at all
Any change must pass through formal change control
Planning.w: In a linear life cycle changes to the fixed baseline must be formally assessed and approved through change control.

Planning.q: A sponsor requests a rough cost estimate while the project is still at the concept stage. Where in the estimating funnel does this sit?
o: A narrow-tolerance estimate at the bottom of the funnel
A detailed bottom-up estimate stage
A final validated estimate stage
A wide-tolerance estimate near the top of the funnel
Planning.w: The top of the estimating funnel produces high-level, wide-tolerance estimates because little detail is yet available.

Planning.q: In what way can parametric estimating help to improve the accuracy of a project estimate?
o: By applying historical cost-per-unit data and scaling it to the work required
By relying on group brainstorming sessions to reach an agreed figure
By assigning a single fixed cost to every stage of the project
By comparing the whole project against one broadly similar completed project
Planning.w: Parametric estimating applies measured historical rates per unit of work, which can be scaled to give a more accurate and defensible estimate.

Planning.q: Midway through delivery, a steering group relies on progress reports to make decisions. Which benefit of reporting does this best illustrate?
o: It removes all risk from the project entirely
It enables informed, timely decision-making
It guarantees the project finishes ahead of time
It replaces the project's governance arrangements
Planning.w: Progress reporting gives stakeholders timely, accurate information, enabling informed decisions and effective control.

Planning.q: A project manager omits the senior user when producing the project management plan. What is the most likely consequence?
o: Delivery costs will automatically increase tenfold
The plan may not reflect genuine user requirements
The sponsor loses all accountability for benefits
The schedule will no longer require any milestones
Planning.w: The senior user represents those who will use the output; omitting them risks a plan that does not reflect real user needs.

Planning.q: In a linear life cycle the scope, timeline and budget are fixed at the start and rarely change. What does this indicate about the deployment baseline?
o: It changes on a daily basis
It is used only after the project closes
It is set early and used to manage performance
It is created during the benefits review
Planning.w: In a linear life cycle the deployment baseline is fixed early and used as a stable reference for controlling delivery.

Planning.q: A business case compares 'do nothing', 'do the minimum' and 'do something' approaches. Why is this comparison valuable?
o: It defines the criteria for project handover
It reduces the overall scope of the project
It demonstrates value for money and the case for change
It accelerates the procurement of suppliers
Planning.w: Comparing these options shows the value of proceeding and supports the strategic case for change.

Planning.q: Which scenario best illustrates poor stakeholder engagement caused by inadequate analysis?
o: A key regulator halted work because it was not consulted during planning
A quality report was produced in the wrong format
A supplier failed to deliver a component on time
The team did not complete the project risk register
Planning.w: Overlooking a key regulator during analysis and engagement planning can lead to serious blocks on delivery.

Planning.q: After stakeholder analysis, the project manager groups stakeholders for communication purposes. Why is this important?
o: It removes low-priority stakeholders from the project records
It establishes distinct categories of project risk
It creates a new reporting hierarchy within the project team
It tailors communication and engagement methods to each stakeholder type
Planning.w: Grouping stakeholders lets communication be made relevant, timely and appropriate to each group's level of involvement.

Planning.q: Which group of stakeholders should contribute to a project management plan to ensure the delivered output can be operated after handover?
o: Regulatory auditors external to the organisation
Competitors within the same market sector
End users and operational staff
Members of an unrelated project's team
Planning.w: End users and operational staff must contribute so the plan reflects requirements needed for successful operation and handover.

Planning.q: What is the role of success criteria when they are set out within a business case?
o: To set performance targets for individual team members
To clarify the benefits the project must deliver to be considered worthwhile
To record the communication preferences of the team
To track the duration of each scheduled task
Planning.w: Success criteria define what the project must achieve to justify the investment and deliver worthwhile value.

Planning.q: How does the deployment baseline relate to the project management plan?
o: It replaces the plan once the project enters the delivery phase
It is the approved reference set for scope, time and cost drawn from the plan
It is produced by operations after the outputs are handed over
It records only the risks and issues identified during planning
Planning.w: The deployment baseline is the fixed, approved set of scope, time and cost derived from the project management plan and used to control delivery.

Planning.q: A customer is uncertain whether the final deliverable meets their original needs. Which early activity would most likely have prevented this?
o: Holding more frequent team retrospective meetings
Assigning additional members to the project team
Producing a more detailed schedule as a Gantt chart
Defining the success criteria collaboratively with the customer
Planning.w: Agreeing success criteria with the customer early ensures a shared, documented understanding of the intended outcome.

Planning.q: Why is it important to tailor progress reports to different stakeholder groups?
o: To provide information relevant to each group's interest and influence
To remove the need for formal governance meetings
To avoid carrying out any project audits
To reduce the amount of communication within the team
Planning.w: Stakeholders have differing interests and influence, so tailoring reports ensures each group receives meaningful and relevant information.

Planning.q: As your project's outputs are handed over to the operational team, what role does benefits management play?
o: It becomes irrelevant once the project has closed
It ensures the expected value outcomes continue to be tracked in operations
It finalises the outstanding contract negotiations
It replaces the project's risk register
Planning.w: Benefits are often realised after handover, so benefits management ensures value continues to be tracked in operation.

Planning.q: Which combination of elements is typically fixed within a project's deployment baseline?
o: Quality standards, audits and benefit reviews
Scope, schedule and cost agreed for delivery
Team roles, supplier contracts and lessons learned
Stakeholder interests, risks and communication channels
Planning.w: The deployment baseline captures the approved scope, schedule and cost that define what will be delivered.

Planning.q: Why might a deployment baseline change more frequently in an iterative life cycle than in a linear one?
o: Change control is not used on iterative projects
Requirements evolve throughout the development
Schedules are disregarded in iterative delivery
Project governance is not required at all
Planning.w: Iterative life cycles use feedback and evolving requirements, so the baseline is regularly updated.

Planning.q: Which stakeholder is primarily responsible for ensuring that the project management plan aligns with the organisation's strategic objectives?
o: A project team member
A supplier
The project sponsor
The product owner
Planning.w: The sponsor owns the business case and ensures the project remains aligned with the organisation's strategic goals.

Planning.q: The sponsor is concerned that delivery risks are under-represented in the business case. What should the project manager do?
o: Remove the risk section and emphasise the benefits
Work with the team to supply accurate risk data and mitigation plans
Transfer ownership of the business case to governance
Wait until the next stage gate before raising it
Planning.w: The project manager supports the sponsor by providing accurate delivery risk information to inform the case.

Planning.q: In which type of life cycle is the deployment baseline expected to evolve frequently as the solution develops?
o: Linear
Iterative
Waterfall
Extended
Planning.w: In iterative life cycles the baseline evolves as understanding grows and the solution is progressively refined.

Planning.q: At what point should a project's deployment baseline normally be agreed and approved?
o: During the concept phase, before any planning is done
After the project has been formally closed
Before delivery begins, at the end of planning
Only when a change request is first raised
Planning.w: The baseline is set and approved once planning is complete and before delivery begins, so performance can be measured from that point.

Planning.q: Two projects run side by side: one linear, one iterative. Which difference in their deployment baselines should the project manager expect?
o: The linear baseline flexes weekly; the iterative stays fixed
Both baselines remain completely unchanged throughout
The iterative baseline flexes; the linear stays largely fixed
Neither project establishes a baseline at any point
Planning.w: The iterative project's baseline evolves with each iteration, while the linear project's baseline is largely fixed after early approval.

Planning.q: A team defines the improvements expected, then tracks whether they materialise after go-live. Which discipline are they applying?
o: Quality control
Configuration management
Critical path analysis
Benefits management
Planning.w: Defining expected improvements and tracking their realisation is the essence of benefits management.

Planning.q: What key function does the deployment baseline serve in relation to change control?
o: It sets the duration of the supplier contract
It provides a reference point for evaluating proposed changes
It guarantees that no changes will ever be permitted
It allows stakeholders to be removed without approval
Planning.w: All proposed changes are compared against the baseline so their impact can be assessed and approval sought.

Planning.q: Why is it important that a business case documents its key assumptions and constraints?
o: They define the decision-making authority of governance
They remove the need for ongoing performance tracking
They are legally binding on all parties to the project
They help stakeholders judge feasibility and where risk may lie
Planning.w: Stated assumptions and constraints let stakeholders assess how realistic the proposal is and where key risks are concentrated.

Planning.q: Stakeholders disagree over the project's success criteria partway through delivery. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Proceed with the original criteria and ignore the concerns
Revise and agree updated criteria through change control
Suspend all activity until full consensus is achieved
Replace the success criteria with the business case
Planning.w: Success criteria may need revising as expectations evolve, and any change should be agreed through the formal change control process.

Planning.q: The project manager has supplied updated risk analysis for the business case. Who decides whether the case is formally revised?
o: The project sponsor, as owner of the business case
The project manager, as author of the analysis
The project team, as producers of the work
The end users, as recipients of the benefits
Planning.w: The project manager provides the analysis, but the sponsor owns the business case and decides whether it is formally revised.

Planning.q: In an agile project, which stakeholder clarifies the acceptance criteria and ensures user needs are reflected in the plan?
o: The PMO analyst
The product owner
The scrum master
The project sponsor
Planning.w: The product owner represents the customer and defines the requirements, including what acceptable delivery looks like.

Planning.q: When developing a business case, which pairing of responsibilities to roles is correct?
o: Owning and championing it — the sponsor; providing information to develop it — the manager
Owning it — the manager; approving the funding — the sponsor
Producing the estimates — the sponsor; deciding strategic fit — the manager
Approving it — the end users; writing it — the project team
Planning.w: The sponsor owns and champions the business case, while the project manager provides the information needed to develop it.

Planning.q: What is one benefit of applying a standard estimating funnel across an organisation's projects?
o: It replaces the need for bottom-up estimating
It fixes all estimates at the start of each project
It promotes consistent refinement of estimates across project phases
It removes the need for any contingency planning
Planning.w: A standard funnel provides a consistent approach to refining estimates as knowledge grows, aiding comparison across projects.

Planning.q: Which estimating method would give the most accurate figure once detailed design information is available?
o: A high-level judgement made at the concept gate
Analytical (bottom-up) estimating of each work package
Analogous estimating based on a past project
A rough order-of-magnitude estimate
Planning.w: Bottom-up estimating uses detailed component information, so it is most accurate once that detail exists.

Planning.q: Which of the following is typically included in a benefits management plan?
o: The ownership, timing and measurement of each benefit
The baseline schedule data for the project
The list of items excluded from scope
The communication escalation procedures
Planning.w: A benefits management plan sets out who owns each benefit, when it is expected and how it will be measured.

Planning.q: A sponsor is frustrated that the concept-stage estimate later changed. How does the estimating funnel explain this?
o: The original estimate should never have been shared with the sponsor
Estimates are fixed once given and any change indicates poor planning
Early estimates are broad and refine as project detail increases
Later estimates are always less reliable than earlier ones
Planning.w: The funnel shows that early estimates are indicative and legitimately refine as more detail emerges through the life cycle.

Planning.q: Why is a single, tightly controlled deployment baseline more workable in a linear life cycle than in an iterative one?
o: Linear projects have no stakeholders to satisfy
Linear projects deliver nothing until the very end
Linear requirements are defined and stable up front
Linear projects never encounter any change requests
Planning.w: Linear life cycles define requirements up front and expect them to remain stable, so a single controlled baseline is appropriate; iterative requirements evolve.

Planning.q: What is a recognised disadvantage of using analogous estimating during a project?
o: It can only be applied once the project is nearing completion
It is based on judgement and can therefore be subjective and less accurate
It demands fully detailed specifications before any estimate is produced
It requires extensive historical unit-rate data to be collected first
Planning.w: Analogous estimating relies on comparison and expert judgement, so it is quick but tends to be subjective and less accurate than data-driven methods.

Planning.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between progress reporting and stakeholder confidence?
o: Frequent reports remove the need for stakeholder input
Clear, honest reports build trust and transparency
Reports should be withheld to avoid raising concerns
Reporting is the main cause of project scope creep
Planning.w: Transparent and honest reporting keeps stakeholders informed and engaged, which builds trust and confidence in the project.

Planning.q: In which situation should analytical (bottom-up) estimating be preferred over analogous or parametric methods?
o: When only high-level assumptions are available
When detailed work package data is available
When an estimate is needed very quickly
When no historical data exists
Planning.w: Analytical estimating gives the most accurate result when detailed task and resource data at work package level is available.

Planning.q: A plan setting out the agreed scope, cost, schedule and resources for delivery, signed off by the stakeholders, is known as what?
o: The benefit profile
The change request log
The work breakdown structure
The deployment baseline
Planning.w: The deployment baseline records the agreed parameters for delivery, including scope, cost and schedule.

Planning.q: How does an early stakeholder analysis help a project manager anticipate potential opposition to a project?
o: By guaranteeing that no stakeholder will ever oppose the project's aims
By transferring responsibility for opposition to the project sponsor
By removing any need to communicate with opposing stakeholders
By revealing which stakeholders may resist, so their concerns can be addressed early
Planning.w: Analysis reveals which stakeholders may resist, allowing their concerns to be understood and addressed early in engagement.

Planning.q: Which statement best describes the way parametric estimating is used to produce a project estimate?
o: Reaching an estimate through the anonymous consensus of experts
Adding up separate estimates for every individual work package
Applying a measured rate to the number of units of work required
Basing the whole estimate on one similar completed project
Planning.w: Parametric estimating multiplies a known rate per unit by the quantity of units required.

Planning.q: Which of the following best describes how the deployment baseline behaves within an iterative project life cycle?
o: An evolving reference updated as the solution develops
A document produced only at project handover
A fixed reference set once and never changed
A record that applies solely to linear projects
Planning.w: In iterative delivery the deployment baseline evolves, being revised as each increment develops the solution.

Planning.q: A sponsor asks why an estimate's tolerance has narrowed from around plus or minus 40% to plus or minus 10%. What best explains this?
o: More project detail became available, moving the estimate down the funnel
An error in the original estimate was corrected
A different comparison project was selected
A change request reduced the overall project cost
Planning.w: As a project progresses and more detail emerges, estimates become more accurate and their tolerances narrow down the estimating funnel.

Planning.q: The sponsor asks the project manager to update the delivery milestones in the business case. What does this indicate about their relationship?
o: The sponsor leads strategy while the project manager supplies delivery detail
Project governance is being deliberately bypassed
The project manager holds ownership of the strategic goals
The sponsor is performing the project manager's role
Planning.w: This reflects appropriate collaboration: the sponsor leads on strategy and the project manager provides delivery information.

Planning.q: An iterative project has a loosely defined baseline at the outset. How is performance typically monitored?
o: By means of a post-project audit only
Through frequent comparison against the evolving baseline
Against a fixed plan set at project initiation
Against the supplier contract terms only
Planning.w: In iterative life cycles performance is monitored against a baseline that is reviewed and updated regularly.

Planning.q: A sponsor asks how delivery progress will be monitored. Which document should the project manager refer to as the key benchmark?
o: The organisational chart
The procurement policy
The deployment baseline
The risk log
Planning.w: The deployment baseline holds the agreed scope, time, cost and resources against which progress is compared.

Planning.q: A stakeholder group is assessed as low influence and low interest. What engagement approach does the analysis suggest?
o: Monitor them with minimal effort, informing them only if needed
Treat them as the primary audience for detailed reporting
Escalate all issues to them before any action is taken
Involve them in every decision to secure their formal approval
Planning.w: Low-influence, low-interest stakeholders are monitored with minimal effort, receiving information only when necessary.

Planning.q: In which life cycle is the deployment baseline most likely to be established firmly at a single point early in delivery?
o: A linear life cycle with defined, stable requirements
Any life cycle where requirements keep changing
An iterative life cycle using repeated increments
A life cycle that omits planning altogether
Planning.w: A linear life cycle sets a firm baseline early because requirements are defined and stable, unlike the evolving baseline of iterative delivery.

Planning.q: What does the estimating funnel primarily illustrate about project estimates over time?
o: Estimates become less reliable as the project progresses
Accuracy improves and tolerance ranges narrow as more becomes known
Costs always fall steadily throughout the life cycle
The number of estimates required reduces to a single figure at the start
Planning.w: The estimating funnel shows that estimate accuracy improves and tolerance ranges narrow as more detailed information becomes available.

Planning.q: Stakeholder analysis identifies a sponsor as high influence and high interest. What engagement does this indicate?
o: Contact limited strictly to the closure phase of the project
Occasional, low-detail updates issued only at major milestones
No direct contact, relying on others to relay information to them
Close, active engagement and full involvement throughout delivery
Planning.w: High-influence, high-interest stakeholders should be actively engaged and closely managed throughout the project.

Planning.q: Which of the following would not normally form part of a deployment baseline?
o: The planned resource requirements
The agreed delivery schedule
The defined scope of work
Benefits realisation tracking
Planning.w: Benefits realisation occurs after delivery within the extended life cycle and is not part of the deployment baseline.

Planning.q: Which statement best describes what is meant by a deployment baseline in project management planning?
o: The initial draft of the business case prepared before the project is approved
The register of risks and issues maintained throughout the delivery phase
The formally agreed scope, cost, schedule and resources against which delivery is managed
The record of lessons learned captured once the project has been handed over
Planning.w: A deployment baseline is the agreed reference for scope, time, cost and resources against which delivery is measured and controlled.

Planning.q: Which of the following best describes the role of success criteria at project handover?
o: They determine which team members remain on the project
They confirm that the business case is now obsolete
They serve as a benchmark for confirming that objectives have been met
They replace the need for a final project report
Planning.w: At handover, success criteria provide the measurable benchmark against which project outcomes are evaluated.

Planning.q: Which estimating method relies on decomposing the work and estimating each component before summing the totals?
o: Analogous estimating
Parametric estimating
Analytical (bottom-up) estimating
Delphi estimating
Planning.w: Analytical, or bottom-up, estimating breaks work into components, estimates each and aggregates the totals.

Planning.q: In the early stages of a project, who is primarily responsible for justifying the investment and championing the business case?
o: The PMO analyst
The delivery team member
The project sponsor
The project manager
Planning.w: The sponsor owns the business case, ensures alignment with strategic objectives and secures the funding.

Planning.q: A progress report shows costs are running fifteen per cent above baseline. What should the project manager do next?
o: Escalate the variance through the appropriate governance route
Disregard the variance because quality remains high
Halt the project immediately without further review
Amend the budget quietly to hide the overspend
Planning.w: A significant variance should be escalated through the agreed governance route so that it can be reviewed and a decision taken.

Planning.q: When a business case is being developed, what is the project manager's typical contribution to that process?
o: Deciding whether the project aligns with the corporate strategy
Approving the funding and committing the organisation's resources
Accepting personal accountability for the realisation of the benefits
Providing analysis such as options, costs and risks to inform the case
Planning.w: The project manager supplies delivery analysis, such as options, costs and risks, to help the sponsor develop and maintain the business case.

Planning.q: Why are success criteria considered at the start, during and at the handover of a project rather than only once?
o: To ensure they remain relevant and are used to steer and finally judge the project
To increase the number of governance gates the project must pass through
To allow the project budget to be revised at each of the three points
To transfer ownership of the criteria to a different stakeholder each time
Planning.w: Revisiting success criteria across the life cycle keeps them relevant and ensures they both guide delivery and provide the final measure of success.

Planning.q: In a project management plan, which role is chiefly concerned with confirming that the delivered outputs are usable and meet the needs of the business?
o: The project governance board
The product owner
The delivery team members
The end users
Planning.w: End users use the outputs in operation, so they are best placed to confirm the deliverables are fit for purpose and meet business needs.

Planning.q: How does agreeing the success criteria at the outset help to secure early stakeholder buy-in to a project?
o: It lets each stakeholder pursue their own personal project goals
It removes the need to prepare a formal business case
It secures procurement discounts from the preferred suppliers
It aligns stakeholder expectations with the agreed project objectives
Planning.w: Involving stakeholders in setting success criteria aligns their expectations with the project's objectives from the start, encouraging commitment.

Planning.q: An estimate is produced by applying a known average cost per feature module across the number of modules required. Which method is being used?
o: Parametric estimating
Three-point estimating
Analytical estimating
Analogous estimating
Planning.w: Parametric estimating scales a known cost-per-unit value by the quantity of units to reach a total estimate.

Planning.q: A team lists its stakeholders then rates each on power and interest. What does this rating enable them to do?
o: Remove any stakeholder who might disagree with the project
Record only the contact details needed to send invitations
Plan an engagement approach proportionate to each stakeholder's position
Confirm the exact final cost of the project to the last item
Planning.w: Rating power and interest lets the team plan engagement that is proportionate to each stakeholder's position.

Planning.q: Your sponsor asks for the business case to be updated to reflect recent inflation. Which section should you review first?
o: The investment appraisal
The record of team roles
The success criteria
The scope statement
Planning.w: Inflation affects forecast costs, so the investment appraisal is the section that must be revisited.

Planning.q: In which section of a business case would you expect to find the project's forecast financial return?
o: The quality plan
The executive summary
The investment appraisal
The communication plan
Planning.w: The investment appraisal presents the financial justification, such as cost–benefit analysis or return on investment.

Planning.q: Which estimating method is most appropriate when reliable data from a similar completed project is available?
o: Parametric estimating
Analogous estimating
Three-point estimating
Analytical estimating
Planning.w: Analogous estimating draws on data from a similar previous project to produce an estimate for the current one.

Planning.q: What is the key purpose of success criteria during the delivery phase of a project?
o: To measure project performance against its objectives
To develop contracts with external suppliers
To validate the entries in the risk register
To justify increasing the contingency budget
Planning.w: During delivery, success criteria act as a benchmark for assessing performance and keeping the project on track.

Planning.q: When agreeing a project management plan, why is it important to involve the stakeholders who will provide the project's resources?
o: So they can approve the sponsor's business case
So the plan's resource assumptions are realistic and committed
So they take over the project manager's daily duties
So they can remove the need for a schedule
Planning.w: Resource providers must be engaged so the plan's assumptions on availability and commitment are realistic and agreed.

Planning.q: What is a key difference in how deployment baselines are managed in linear versus iterative life cycles?
o: Linear projects avoid the use of baselines completely
Linear projects rely on a fixed baseline, while iterative projects expect it to evolve
Iterative life cycles set one baseline and never change it
Both approaches exclude stakeholders from creating the baseline
Planning.w: Linear life cycles seek stability through a fixed baseline, whereas iterative life cycles embrace an evolving one.

Planning.q: Which estimating method is least effective when no historical data is available?
o: Analytical (bottom-up) estimating
Delphi (expert) technique
Three-point estimating
Parametric estimating
Planning.w: Parametric estimating requires reliable historical unit data to function, so it is least effective when no such data exists.

Planning.q: Which three methods are recognised as typical estimating approaches within project planning?
o: Predictive, iterative and hybrid estimating
Analytical, analogous and parametric estimating
Levelling, smoothing and crashing estimating
Qualitative, quantitative and residual estimating
Planning.w: Analytical, analogous and parametric are the standard estimating methods identified in the APM Body of Knowledge.

Planning.q: A benefit register entry reads 'annual IT maintenance savings of £50,000 by Year 2'. What does this represent?
o: A project deliverable
A change request
A project risk
A quantifiable benefit
Planning.w: This is a measurable, time-bound financial benefit that should be tracked to assess the project's value.

Planning.q: One project is linear with a fixed baseline and another is iterative with rolling planning. What difference should you expect in how change is handled?
o: The iterative project avoids making any changes
Neither project requires change control at all
Only the linear project makes use of baselines
The linear project resists change, while the iterative one embraces it
Planning.w: Linear life cycles rely on stability, whereas iterative life cycles accommodate change more readily through adaptive planning.

Planning.q: Which of the following is a genuine benefit of regular progress reporting to the project manager?
o: It removes the requirement to hold a baseline
It eliminates the need to manage project risks
It guarantees stakeholders will never raise issues
It provides early warning of emerging variances
Planning.w: Regular reporting highlights variances early, allowing corrective action before problems escalate.

Planning.q: A senior user reviews the project management plan and questions the schedule. Why is their involvement important?
o: They represent end-user needs and shape quality expectations
They manage all of the third-party procurement
They are accountable for allocating project risk
They take over the project manager's role if delays occur
Planning.w: Senior users ensure the plan reflects business needs and the quality expectations of those who will use the deliverables.

Planning.q: During delivery, how can regularly checking work against the success criteria benefit the project manager?
o: It fixes the deployment baseline so that no change can occur
It confirms that delivery is still heading towards the agreed definition of success
It removes the requirement to report progress to the sponsor
It guarantees that all of the identified risks will not materialise
Planning.w: Comparing progress with the success criteria during delivery confirms the project remains on course to meet its agreed objectives.

Planning.q: Why do estimates near the bottom of the estimating funnel carry tighter tolerances than earlier ones?
o: Contingency has been deliberately stripped out of them
More detailed scope and information are available by that stage
Fewer stakeholders remain involved to challenge them
The sponsor insists later estimates match the first figure given
Planning.w: As the project progresses, greater scope definition and information reduce uncertainty, allowing tighter estimate tolerances.

Planning.q: Who is typically responsible for ensuring that a project's benefits are realised after its outputs have been delivered?
o: The project quality manager
An individual project team member
The project sponsor or business owner
The project manager
Planning.w: The project manager delivers the outputs, but the sponsor or business owner owns the realisation of benefits once the project is complete.

Planning.q: What is the primary purpose of benefits management within the delivery of a project?
o: To reduce the project's overhead costs
To ensure that suppliers are paid on time
To keep the project delivery on schedule
To define, track and realise the intended value of the project
Planning.w: Benefits management ensures the project delivers measurable value that supports the organisation's business objectives.

Planning.q: In a project using iterative delivery, which aspect of the deployment baseline is most likely to change frequently?
o: The governance structure
The procurement method
The sponsor's role
The scope definition and priorities
Planning.w: Scope and priorities evolve throughout an iterative project, so the baseline adjusts to reflect them.

Planning.q: Before work begins, a project manager agrees measurable success criteria with all parties. What does this primarily achieve?
o: It transfers accountability for the benefits to the operational teams
It guarantees that the project will be delivered within its budget
It removes the need to produce a business case for the investment
A shared, agreed definition of what success will look like for the project
Planning.w: Agreeing success criteria at the outset gives every party a common, agreed understanding of what the project must achieve.

Planning.q: If the sponsor fails to check that the business case remains valid, what is the most likely consequence?
o: Stakeholder support for the project will automatically increase
The project schedule will adjust itself to stay on track
The delivery team is likely to over-deliver on scope
The project may continue without justification, wasting resources
Planning.w: Continued validation keeps the project aligned to its objectives; without it the project may run on without justification and waste resources.

Planning.q: A business case usually evaluates alternative ways of meeting the identified need. What is this particular section commonly called?
o: The risk register
The options appraisal
The responsibility matrix
The configuration log
Planning.w: Comparing alternative approaches, such as 'do nothing', 'do minimum' and 'do something', forms the options appraisal within the business case.

Planning.q: Beyond gaining initial approval, what continuing purpose does the business case serve as the project progresses through delivery?
o: It replaces the need to maintain a project schedule during delivery
It records the version history of each of the configuration items
It provides the reference for checking that the investment remains justified
It sets out the acceptance tests to be run on the final product
Planning.w: The business case is reviewed throughout delivery to confirm the investment remains viable and continues to justify the project's continuation.

Planning.q: Which document does the sponsor use to demonstrate the strategic value of a proposed project to the organisation?
o: The quality register
The risk register
The business case
The work breakdown structure
Planning.w: The business case sets out the value proposition and links the project to the organisation's strategic goals.

Planning.q: Which tool is most commonly used to support stakeholder analysis during project planning?
o: The risk register
The influence/interest matrix
The deployment baseline
The work breakdown structure
Planning.w: The influence/interest matrix categorises stakeholders so the project manager can plan how best to engage each one.

Planning.q: Beyond identifying who the stakeholders are, what further insight does a stakeholder analysis provide to guide engagement?
o: The final acceptance date agreed for every project deliverable
The exact budget each stakeholder is willing to contribute
Each stakeholder's likely attitude, expectations and level of support
The precise technical solution each stakeholder must build
Planning.w: Analysis assesses stakeholders' attitudes, expectations and support, informing how each should be engaged.

Planning.q: How does regular progress reporting support accurate forecasting of likely outcomes on a project?
o: By removing closed risks from the project’s risk register automatically
By increasing the volume of procurement activity across the project
By extending the planning phase until all uncertainty is removed
By highlighting performance trends that help predict likely future outcomes
Planning.w: Progress reporting captures trend data that allows the project manager to forecast likely outcomes and take timely corrective action.

Planning.q: A key stakeholder is unaware of a recent schedule delay. What has most likely been lacking on the project?
o: Effective project progress reporting
A change to the project's resource allocation
Completion of all the project deliverables
A fully updated project business case
Planning.w: Regular, clear progress reporting keeps stakeholders informed of the current status, including any delays.

Planning.q: A sponsor wants a quick, high-level estimate based on a similar project completed last year. Which method should be used?
o: Analytical estimating
Parametric estimating
Analogous estimating
Three-point estimating
Planning.w: Analogous estimating uses data from a comparable past project to give a fast, high-level estimate.

Planning.q: Which of the following is essential for parametric estimating to produce reliable results?
o: A fully completed work breakdown structure
Accurate historical data for unit costs or durations
Consensus reached through expert judgement
An approved stakeholder engagement plan
Planning.w: Parametric estimating depends on accurate historical cost or duration data per unit in order to scale estimates reliably.

Planning.q: During delivery, what does regular progress reporting mainly allow a project manager to compare?
o: Actual performance against the agreed baseline
The business case against the risk register
Team roles against Belbin behavioural profiles
Supplier prices against the wider market
Planning.w: Progress reporting chiefly compares actual performance against the agreed baseline so variances can be identified and managed.

Planning.q: A project manager issues weekly reports on progress against cost and schedule. What key purpose does this serve?
o: It tracks variance against the agreed project plan
It replaces the need for the project brief
It allocates performance bonuses to the team
It approves the project's procurement contracts
Planning.w: Reporting against the plan identifies variances early, allowing the project manager to take timely corrective action.

Planning.q: A cost estimate is produced by applying a standard cost per metre of road drawn from industry data. Which estimating method is this?
o: Parametric estimating
Expert judgement
Analogous estimating
Analytical estimating
Planning.w: Parametric estimating applies a known unit rate to a measured quantity, using historical or industry data.

Planning.q: Which of the following statements about the deployment baseline is correct?
o: It is only ever used on agile projects
It supports the tracking of project performance during execution
It is identical in content to the business case
It becomes irrelevant once the concept phase ends
Planning.w: The deployment baseline is a live reference used to track and control delivery performance throughout execution.

Planning.q: What most clearly distinguishes a deployment baseline from an ordinary version of the project plan?
o: It lists the personal contact details of every project stakeholder
It records only the risks identified before delivery began
It is an informal draft that the team may amend at any time
It has been formally approved and fixed as the reference for measuring delivery
Planning.w: The deployment baseline is the approved, fixed version of scope, time and cost used as the reference against which delivery is measured.

Planning.q: Benefits management covers a benefit from its first identification through to which final point?
o: Its realisation and review once the outputs are in use
The completion of the project's detailed schedule
The approval of the project's initial business case
The moment the project's outputs are handed over
Planning.w: Benefits management spans from identification through to the realisation and review of benefits once outputs are in use.

Planning.q: When should a project's success criteria be reviewed during the life cycle?
o: At initiation, regularly during delivery, and again at handover
Only once the benefits have been realised
Only at project closure
Only at the start of the project
Planning.w: Success criteria should be defined early, monitored during delivery to maintain alignment, and evaluated at handover.

Planning.q: Midway through delivery a project manager faces a trade-off between two options. How can the agreed success criteria help?
o: They remove the need to consult the project sponsor about the choice
They provide a reference to guide the decision towards the intended outcome
They automatically approve whichever option costs the least money
They replace the change control process for that particular decision
Planning.w: During delivery, success criteria act as a reference point that keeps decisions aligned with the project's intended outcomes.

Planning.q: A linear project fixes its deployment baseline once at the outset. How is the iterative equivalent best described by comparison?
o: Fixed once and never revisited after approval
Re-baselined progressively as each iteration completes
Abandoned entirely because iterative work needs no baseline
Set only after the final product has been delivered
Planning.w: In an iterative life cycle the deployment baseline evolves and is re-established as successive iterations refine the solution, unlike the single fixed baseline of a linear project.

Planning.q: A senior executive asks why several delivery options are presented in the business case. What is the best explanation?
o: To provide the delivery team with additional tasks to complete
To satisfy a mandatory legal audit of the procurement route
To evaluate and justify the recommended approach against value and risk
To demonstrate that the cheapest option was selected
Planning.w: Options analysis allows the recommended approach to be justified on the basis of value, cost and feasibility rather than cost alone.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following is a common responsibility of a project management office (PMO)?
o: Providing assurance and support across multiple projects
Owning and controlling the project budget
Managing the scope and deliverables of each project
Acting as the primary user of the deliverables
Roles & Responsibilities.w: A PMO offers governance, assurance, reporting and consistent support across projects or programmes.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between the project sponsor and the project manager?
o: The sponsor sets direction and governance while the manager delivers
The sponsor manages daily delivery while the manager sets strategy
The two roles operate independently with no formal relationship
The sponsor handles finance while the manager makes technical choices
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The sponsor provides strategic direction and governance, while the project manager delivers the project within those boundaries.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Within a project, what is the primary responsibility of the project governance arrangements?
o: To carry out the day-to-day technical tasks defined in the work packages
To provide the framework of oversight, authority and accountability for the project
To gather user feedback after each iteration is completed
To produce the deliverables that make up the final product
Roles & Responsibilities.w: Project governance provides the structure of oversight, decision-making authority and accountability within which the project is directed and controlled.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: A developer finds that a technical constraint will prevent on-time delivery of a feature. What should they do next?
o: Raise the issue with the project manager and suggest options
Withdraw from the task and await reassignment
Notify the project sponsor of the problem directly
Escalate to the governance board for a decision
Roles & Responsibilities.w: Team members are expected to raise emerging issues with the project manager and collaborate on possible solutions.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following best describes the responsibility of a project team member?
o: Providing specialist skills and completing assigned tasks
Defining and owning the project business case
Approving transitions between project phases
Authorising procurement contracts with suppliers
Roles & Responsibilities.w: Team members apply their specialist skills to complete assigned work packages and report progress to the project manager.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: During delivery, who is best placed to confirm whether a new process will actually be workable in daily operation?
o: The project sponsor
The end users
The project governance board
The finance department
Roles & Responsibilities.w: End users operate the outputs day to day, so they are best placed to confirm the solution is usable and fit for purpose.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: During delivery, which task most directly reflects what a project team member is responsible for?
o: Deciding whether the project should proceed past each gate
Championing the project at senior board level
Completing assigned work packages to the required standard
Approving the project's business case before work starts
Roles & Responsibilities.w: Project team members are responsible for carrying out the assigned work packages and producing outputs to the required standard.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Which statement best describes the difference between a product owner and a project sponsor?
o: The sponsor provides strategic oversight, while the product owner manages feature value
The product owner approves gateway reviews, while the sponsor delivers the outputs
The sponsor manages the backlog, while the product owner controls the funding
The product owner owns the business case, while the sponsor manages delivery tasks
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The sponsor secures funding and strategic alignment, whereas the product owner focuses on feature value and customer priorities.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following is a core responsibility of the project manager?
o: Chairing the project steering group
Owning the business case and justifying the benefits
Authorising the release of project funding
Managing delivery against time, cost and quality
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The project manager is responsible for delivering the project within the agreed constraints of time, cost and quality.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: A PMO analyst finds that three portfolio projects are reporting schedule delays and inconsistent risk data. What is the most appropriate PMO action?
o: Replace the affected project managers without delay
Compile the performance data and escalate the trends to governance
Cancel the three projects that are reporting delays
Take over delivery responsibility for the projects
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The PMO monitors and reports performance trends so that governance bodies can make informed decisions.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following is a key responsibility of the project sponsor?
o: Writing the detailed work breakdown structure
Maintaining the day-to-day project issue log
Producing the project communication plan
Approving key decisions and owning the business case
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The sponsor provides direction, owns the business case and approves the major decisions and investment for the project.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: On an agile project, which responsibility most clearly belongs to the product owner rather than the project manager?
o: Managing the project's overall budget and schedule
Reporting overall delivery progress to the project board
Prioritising the backlog so it reflects the greatest user value
Securing the resources needed for the delivery team
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The product owner owns and prioritises the backlog to maximise value delivered to users, distinct from the project manager's delivery oversight.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: In an agile project a stakeholder maintains the product backlog and decides which features are developed next. Which role is this person performing?
o: Project sponsor
Scrum master
Product owner
Project manager
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The product owner owns the backlog and maximises value by deciding the order in which features are delivered.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: A change in organisational strategy puts a project at risk of cancellation. Who is responsible for deciding whether it should continue?
o: Project sponsor
Project manager
Product owner
Project planner
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The sponsor assesses continued strategic alignment and has the authority to continue or cancel the project.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Early feedback on a new IT system shows that users are confused by the interface wording. Which action best supports successful adoption?
o: Reassign the technical work to the users themselves
Transfer the concern to the sponsor as a risk
Arrange further end user engagement and training
Update the project governance plan
Roles & Responsibilities.w: Engaging and training end users after handover helps embed the solution and maximise the benefits realised.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following would not typically be the responsibility of a project team member?
o: Providing progress updates to the project manager
Contributing specialist technical expertise
Delivering assigned tasks to the agreed specification
Tracking organisational benefits after handover
Roles & Responsibilities.w: Tracking benefits after handover is a sponsor responsibility, not part of a team member's delivery role.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: A late supplier delivery has caused a critical delay. What is the most appropriate first action for the project manager?
o: Notify procurement that the project will be cancelled
Assess the impact and update the risk register and schedule
Escalate straight to the sponsor without any analysis
Reassign the whole project to the product owner
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The project manager should first assess the impact and update the relevant records before recommending action or escalating.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: A project manager needs a standard risk register template and guidance on preparing for a gateway review. Which role usually provides this support?
o: The scrum master
The project sponsor
The project governance board
The project management office (PMO)
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The PMO provides templates, tools, assurance and support to help projects plan and prepare for reviews.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: What is the primary responsibility of the product owner in an agile environment?
o: Producing the detailed technical documentation
Monitoring the delivery team's performance metrics
Prioritising the product backlog according to business value
Negotiating and managing the supplier contracts
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The product owner ensures the most valuable features are delivered by managing and prioritising the backlog.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: A development team is waiting for its next batch of prioritised work. Who is responsible for keeping the backlog updated and correctly ordered?
o: The project manager
The product owner
The scrum master
The project sponsor
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The product owner maintains the backlog and ensures the most valuable items are ready for the team to develop.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: A PMO introduces a lessons learned process across all completed projects. What is the primary benefit of doing this?
o: It identifies who to blame for previous project failures
It speeds up future procurement decisions
It supports continuous improvement across the project portfolio
It justifies staff changes within the delivery teams
Roles & Responsibilities.w: Capturing lessons learned helps future projects avoid repeat mistakes and adopt proven good practice.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: On a new IT project you gather requirements, attend progress meetings and support testing. Which role are you performing?
o: Project sponsor
Product owner
End user
Project team member
Roles & Responsibilities.w: A project team member completes assigned tasks and contributes specialist or technical input to the delivery of the project.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Before handover is approved, the board requires confirmation that all deliverables meet the agreed scope and quality standards. What mechanism is this?
o: A risk escalation process
A work package authorisation
An issue log update
A decision gate review
Roles & Responsibilities.w: A decision gate lets governance confirm that agreed criteria are met before the project is authorised to proceed.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Which statement correctly separates the responsibilities of the project sponsor from those of the project manager?
o: The sponsor delivers the work packages while the manager owns the business case
Both roles share identical accountability for producing the deliverables
The sponsor owns the business case and benefits; the manager delivers the outputs
The manager secures funding while the sponsor schedules daily tasks
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The sponsor is accountable for the business case and benefits realisation, while the project manager is responsible for day-to-day delivery of the outputs.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following is not normally a responsibility of an end user during a project?
o: Controlling the project budget and schedule
Taking part in user acceptance testing
Providing feedback on usability and functionality
Adopting the new system or process after handover
Roles & Responsibilities.w: Controlling budget and schedule is a project management responsibility and falls outside the end user's role.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Staff using a newly delivered finance system report confusion over some features and ask for more training. What is the most appropriate project response?
o: Log the feedback and assess the options for supporting the users
Disregard the request because the project has already closed
Escalate the concern straight to the governance board
Amend the business case to add the requested features
Roles & Responsibilities.w: End user feedback should be acknowledged and addressed through support, training or further improvement to aid successful adoption.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: A team member misses a critical deadline, affecting the schedule. What is the most appropriate response from the project manager?
o: Discuss the issue, find root causes and support recovery
Ignore it and quietly extend the project deadline
Assign the overdue task to the governance board
Escalate immediately to the sponsor for dismissal
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The project manager should address the shortfall constructively, understanding the causes and working to recover the schedule.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Having approved the business case and committed funding, what should be a project sponsor's next priority?
o: Monitoring task-level performance of the team
Issuing procurement requests to suppliers
Developing the detailed project schedule
Ensuring strategic alignment and effective governance
Roles & Responsibilities.w: A key sponsor responsibility is keeping the project aligned to strategic objectives and supporting sound governance.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Which decision would most appropriately sit with the project's governance arrangements rather than the project manager?
o: How a specific technical task should be carried out
Which team member is assigned to a particular work package
The wording of a routine weekly status update
Whether the project should continue past a decision gate
Roles & Responsibilities.w: Decisions about whether the project proceeds at a gate rest with governance, keeping strategic authority separate from day-to-day delivery.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following would typically fall outside the responsibilities of the project manager?
o: Tracking and reporting project progress
Managing the day-to-day project risks
Approving strategic funding and benefits realisation
Leading the creation of the project schedule
Roles & Responsibilities.w: Approving funding and owning benefits realisation are sponsor responsibilities, not those of the project manager.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: An executive secured the funding and holds overall accountability for delivering the project's benefits. Which role is being described?
o: End user
Project manager
Project sponsor
Product owner
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The project sponsor owns the business case, secures funding and is accountable for the realisation of the benefits.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: A gateway review finds the deliverables no longer align with business strategy. Who is responsible for recommending that the project stops or is redirected?
o: Project governance board
Project team
Project manager
PMO administrator
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The governance board has the authority to intervene when a project no longer aligns to strategy or exceeds risk thresholds.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: A board has been assembled to oversee compliance, strategic fit and risk exposure ahead of a major investment decision. What role is it fulfilling?
o: Project management office
Product ownership
Project governance
Project team
Roles & Responsibilities.w: Project governance provides oversight, authorises decisions and ensures the project complies with agreed standards.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: A product owner postpones a planned feature so that a newly requested customer feature can be developed first. What does this decision demonstrate?
o: Formal change control escalation
Project risk avoidance
Backlog prioritisation and refinement
Project closure planning
Roles & Responsibilities.w: Reordering the backlog in response to customer value is a core product owner responsibility.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: You manage the day-to-day activities of a project, control its risks and ensure deliverables are completed on time. Which role are you performing?
o: Project team member
Project manager
Product owner
Project sponsor
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The project manager runs the project day to day, managing time, cost, quality and coordination of the work.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: What distinguishes a project management office from a project manager?
o: The PMO provides oversight and tools across projects, while the manager delivers one project
The PMO reports to the project manager on each project by default
The PMO owns every work package, while the manager owns the schedule
The PMO leads stakeholder engagement, while the manager owns governance
Roles & Responsibilities.w: The PMO supports governance and consistency across projects, while the project manager is accountable for delivering a specific project.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: The sponsor has requested a progress report on the project. What should the project manager most appropriately include?
o: Updates on schedule, budget, risks and key deliverables
Strategic alignment assessments and funding approvals
Benefit realisation figures and post-project audit results
Detailed staffing contracts and future hiring plans
Roles & Responsibilities.w: Progress reporting communicates performance against schedule, budget, risks and deliverables so decisions can be made.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following would not typically be a project governance responsibility?
o: Scheduling the team's day-to-day working meetings
Reviewing performance against project objectives
Providing strategic oversight of the project
Approving transitions between project phases
Roles & Responsibilities.w: Arranging routine team meetings is an operational matter for the project manager, not a governance function.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Which statement best describes the role of end users within a project?
o: They own the business case and ensure the benefits are realised
They define the strategic objectives and agreed scope of the project
They direct governance activities and approve the supplier contracts
They use the final product or service and give feedback during development
Roles & Responsibilities.w: End users interact with the deliverables and provide feedback that helps ensure the product or service is practical, usable and effective.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following statements best describes the overall function of project governance?
o: Creating the detailed work breakdown structure
Running the daily stand-ups and team meetings
Ensuring strategic direction, decision-making and control
Maintaining the project's daily risk log
Roles & Responsibilities.w: Governance ensures the project stays aligned to strategy and follows agreed controls, decision-making and oversight.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Warehouse staff who will operate a new inventory system daily are asked to test a prototype and give feedback. Which role are they performing?
o: Project manager
Project sponsor
Product owner
End users
Roles & Responsibilities.w: End users are the people who will work with the project's deliverables day to day and can give practical feedback.
